HIPAA Security Rule.description: 164.308(a)(3): Workforce security; 164.308(a)(5): Security awareness and training, both requiring documented rules for acceptable use.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.description: CC6.1: The entity implements logical access security measures; CC6.2: The entity restricts access to authorized users, consistent with acceptable use policy requirements.

title: Return of assets
description: Personnel and other interested parties as appropriate shall return all the organization assets in their possession upon change or termination of their employment, contract or agreement.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 Control A.5.11, organizations must establish a structured process that ensures all assets issued to personnel and third parties are returned upon termination or change of employment/contract. Technically, this involves maintaining a centralized and regularly updated asset inventory system that tracks assignment and return of physical (e.g., laptops, access cards) and logical (e.g., software licenses, VPN tokens) assets. The process should be integrated with HR's offboarding workflows, automatically alerting IT and Facilities teams when an exit event is triggered. During offboarding, conduct an in-person or remote asset check, using a standardized checklist, to verify the condition and completeness of returned items. Immediate revocation of system and application access is crucial to prevent unauthorized data exposure. Documentation requirements include signed asset return forms, updated asset inventory records, and logs of access revocation. Common pitfalls include incomplete asset inventories, lack of formal procedures, poor coordination between departments, and failing to document exceptions (e.g., lost or damaged assets). Organizations should regularly audit the asset return process to identify and remediate gaps, ensuring that no assets—especially those that could contain sensitive or proprietary information—remain with former employees or contractors. This approach not only supports compliance but also reduces the risk of data breaches and asset loss.

compliance_steps.step: Create and maintain a comprehensive asset inventory that includes all assets issued to personnel (e.g., laptops, mobile phones, access cards, software licenses).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Up-to-date asset inventory records linked to individual users.

compliance_steps.step: Establish a formal asset return procedure integrated with offboarding, covering both voluntary and involuntary terminations.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Documented asset return procedure; offboarding checklists.

compliance_steps.step: Notify relevant departments of impending employment or contract changes to initiate the asset return process prior to termination.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Notification logs; workflow records showing timely alerts.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct a physical and logical asset return audit during exit interviews or contract close-out, verifying each asset's condition and completeness.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Signed asset return forms; audit checklist completed for each individual.

compliance_steps.step: Revoke access rights to organizational systems, applications, and cloud services immediately after asset return confirmation.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Access revocation logs; updated user access lists.

compliance_steps.step: Update asset inventory to reflect returned, missing, or damaged assets, and initiate follow-up for outstanding items.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Asset inventory update records; issue tracking logs for unreturned assets.

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and test the efficacy of asset return procedures at least annually to ensure compliance and address gaps.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Internal audit reports; records of procedure reviews and improvements.

NIST CSF.Description: Ensures personnel and other parties are removed and assets are returned when employment changes or ends; related to identity management and asset handling.

GDPR Articles.Description: Requires measures to ensure security of personal data, including protection and return of assets that may contain such data upon employment or contract termination.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Termination procedures for workforce members; device and media controls including return and removal of access to PHI.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: Addresses removal of access and return of assets upon termination or changes in employment or contract status.

title: Classification of information
description: Information shall be classified according to the information security needs of the organization based on confidentiality, integrity, availability and relevant interested party requirements.
guidance: Effective implementation of ISO 27001:2022 Control A.5.12 requires organizations to establish a robust information classification system that meets both technical and process requirements. Begin by developing a formal classification policy, clearly defining levels such as Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted, and setting criteria based on confidentiality, integrity, availability, and stakeholder needs. Conduct a comprehensive inventory of all information assets, ensuring each has an identified owner responsible for its classification. Technically, leverage data labeling within systems, configure access controls in line with classification levels, and deploy data loss prevention (DLP) solutions to prevent unauthorized disclosure. Process-wise, ensure that classification is integrated into the asset lifecycle, from creation and storage to transmission and disposal. Continuous training for employees and third parties is essential to prevent accidental mishandling, and regular audits should be scheduled to identify misclassifications or policy deviations. Documentation should capture the policy, inventory, classification decisions, training records, and audit findings. Common pitfalls include overly complex classification schemes, lack of regular reviews, insufficient technical controls, and failing to integrate classification into daily workflows. Avoid these by keeping classification levels manageable, regularly updating policies and inventories, automating technical enforcement where possible, and embedding classification requirements into all relevant processes.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and formally approve an Information Classification Policy that defines classification levels (e.g., Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted) and criteria based on confidentiality, integrity, availability, and interested party requirements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved policy document; meeting minutes of policy approval

compliance_steps.step: Conduct an inventory of all information assets, including documents, databases, emails, and digital files, identifying asset owners for each.
compliance_steps.evidence: Up-to-date asset inventory list with asset owners assigned

compliance_steps.step: Classify all information assets according to the defined policy, documenting the classification for each asset in the inventory.
compliance_steps.evidence: Asset inventory with classification tags; completed classification records

compliance_steps.step: Implement technical controls to enforce classification such as labeling files, configuring access controls, and using data loss prevention (DLP) tools.
compliance_steps.evidence: Screenshots of labels, access control lists, DLP configuration reports

compliance_steps.step: Train all employees and relevant third parties on the information classification policy, procedures, and how to handle each classification type.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training attendance records; training materials; completion certificates

compliance_steps.step: Review and update classifications and the policy at least annually or when significant changes occur, ensuring ongoing relevance and compliance.
compliance_steps.evidence: Review logs; updated policy documents; change records

compliance_steps.step: Monitor and audit the effectiveness of classification implementation, including spot checks and automated scans for misclassified information.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit reports; scan results; remediation action logs

NIST CSF.Description: Data-at-rest is protected; includes data classification as part of data protection

GDPR Articles.Description: Requires data controllers/processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures, including classification, to ensure data security

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Requires identification and classification of ePHI assets to assess risks and safeguards

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: The entity identifies, inventories, and classifies information assets to protect them according to their sensitivity

title: Labelling of information
description: An appropriate set of procedures for information labelling shall be developed and implemented in accordance with the information classification scheme adopted by the organization.
guidance: To effectively implement control A.5.13: Labelling of Information, organizations must first establish a robust information classification scheme that clearly defines what types of information exist, the sensitivity levels, and criteria for classification. Once classifications are established, technical requirements involve configuring systems (such as document management, email platforms, DLP solutions) to support and enforce labelling—ensuring that classification labels are visible, embedded in metadata, and cannot be easily removed or altered without authorization. Process requirements include developing and communicating labelling procedures, distributing labelling templates, and ensuring that all users know how and when to apply, update, or remove labels. Comprehensive documentation is vital: maintain records of the classification scheme, labelling procedures, training materials, audit results, and remediation actions. Common pitfalls to avoid include inconsistent labelling across systems, lack of automation (resulting in human error), failing to train staff adequately, and neglecting periodic reviews that account for changes in data types or systems. Ensure that labelling mechanisms are tested regularly, and integrate labelling compliance checks into routine audits. Finally, establish clear escalation and correction processes for mislabelled or unlabelled information to prevent data leakage or mishandling. This approach ensures information is consistently protected according to its sensitivity and regulatory requirements.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and document an information classification scheme that defines classification levels (e.g., Public, Internal, Confidential, Restricted) and associated labelling requirements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved classification policy and procedure documents

compliance_steps.step: Create standardized labelling templates and guidelines for both physical and electronic information (e.g., document headers, metadata tags, email footers).
compliance_steps.evidence: Labelling templates, published guidelines, sample labelled documents

compliance_steps.step: Configure automated labelling mechanisms in digital systems (e.g., DLP, email systems, document management platforms) to enforce and verify correct labelling based on classification.
compliance_steps.evidence: System configuration documentation, screenshots, audit logs of automated labelling

compliance_steps.step: Train employees and relevant third parties on how to correctly label information according to the classification scheme, including when to apply, remove, or change labels.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training records, attendance sheets, training materials

compliance_steps.step: Conduct periodic audits of labelled information (both physical and electronic) to ensure consistency and compliance with the defined labelling procedures.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit reports, non-compliance findings, remediation plans

compliance_steps.step: Establish a process for reporting and correcting mislabelled or unlabelled information, including escalation procedures for repeated non-compliance.
compliance_steps.evidence: Incident logs, corrective action records, communication to staff

compliance_steps.step: Review and update labelling procedures and technologies annually or when significant changes occur (e.g., new system rollout, classification scheme update).
compliance_steps.evidence: Change management records, updated procedures, review meeting minutes
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Manager / IT Change Manager

GDPR Articles.description: Requires data protection by design and default, including appropriate labelling and handling of personal data according to risk and classification.

HIPAA Security Rule.description: Access control and security management processes require identification, labelling, and appropriate handling of ePHI.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.description: The entity classifies information assets and applies appropriate security measures, including labelling and handling controls.

title: Information transfer
description: Information transfer rules, procedures, or agreements shall be in place for all types of transfer facilities within the organization and between the organization and other parties.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.14 (Information Transfer), organizations must adopt a holistic approach that encompasses technical, procedural, and contractual safeguards. Begin by conducting a thorough mapping of all information transfer channels, including internal communications, external exchanges, APIs, and physical media. Classify data according to sensitivity, as this dictates the level of control required. Technically, ensure all transfers—especially those across untrusted networks—utilize strong encryption protocols (such as TLS 1.2+, SFTP, or VPNs) and deploy data loss prevention (DLP) solutions to monitor and restrict unauthorized transfers. For external parties, incorporate robust data transfer clauses in contracts, addressing not only the security measures but also incident notification and responsibility demarcation. Process-wise, establish clear, documented procedures for initiating, approving, and recording information transfers, and ensure these are communicated to all relevant staff via targeted training. Maintain detailed logs of information transfer activities, and routinely review them for anomalies or breaches, integrating these activities into your broader monitoring and audit regime. Documentation is essential—retain evidence of policies, procedures, agreements, training, and monitoring activities. Common pitfalls to avoid include neglecting informal transfer channels (such as instant messaging or personal email), failing to update agreements when systems change, and overlooking the need for user awareness. Regular reviews and updates, especially in response to business or technology changes, are critical to maintaining compliance and security resilience.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and document an Information Transfer Policy covering all types of internal and external information transfers (e.g., email, file sharing, APIs, portable media).
Identify and classify all information transfer channels and facilities, including third-party integrations, and map them to data sensitivity levels.
Implement technical security controls for transfers (e.g., encryption in transit, secure protocols like SFTP/HTTPS, DLP tools) based on data classification.
Establish formal agreements or data transfer clauses with external parties addressing transfer mechanisms, security requirements, and responsibilities.
Communicate and enforce information transfer procedures through staff training and awareness campaigns.
Monitor and log information transfers, especially those involving sensitive data or external parties, and regularly review audit logs for anomalies.
Review and update information transfer rules and controls annually or upon significant changes to systems or business processes.

GDPR.Art. 32: Security of processing—Requires security measures for data in transit.
GDPR.Art. 44: Transfers of personal data to third countries—Requires safeguards and agreements.

NIST CSF.PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected (Securing transfer channels).

HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D): Information system activity review—Regularly review logs of information transfers.

title: Access control
description: Rules to control physical and logical access to information and other associated assets shall be established and implemented based on business and information security requirements.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.15, organizations must establish robust access control procedures that address both physical and logical access. Technically, this requires configuring systems to support role-based access control (RBAC), strong authentication mechanisms (e.g., unique IDs, passwords, MFA), and ensuring physical barriers (e.g., badge systems, locked server rooms) are in place. Processes should include formalized onboarding and offboarding protocols, periodic access reviews, and clear escalation paths for exceptions. Documentation is critical: maintain up-to-date access control policies, asset inventories, user access lists, approval records, and change logs. Train staff regularly on procedures and monitor access logs for anomalies or unauthorized attempts. Common pitfalls include failure to promptly revoke access for terminated employees, lack of periodic reviews, and undocumented exceptions. Avoid over-privileging users and ensure the principle of least privilege is enforced. Without clear process ownership, access reviews and updates may be neglected, leading to compliance gaps. Automate where possible (e.g., user provisioning/deprovisioning, log monitoring) but ensure manual oversight for sensitive roles and assets. By combining technical controls, documented processes, and continuous monitoring, organizations can demonstrate compliance and reduce risk associated with inappropriate access.

compliance_steps.step: Identify and classify all information assets and associated systems that require access control.
compliance_steps.evidence: Asset inventory documentation, classification records

compliance_steps.step: Define and document access control policies specifying who can access what information, under which conditions, and the approval process.
compliance_steps.evidence: Access control policy document, approval workflows

compliance_steps.step: Implement technical controls such as user authentication, role-based access control (RBAC), and physical controls (badges, locks) aligned with the access control policy.
compliance_steps.evidence: System configuration screenshots, access logs, physical access records

compliance_steps.step: Perform regular user access reviews (at least quarterly) to verify that only authorized individuals maintain access to information and assets.
compliance_steps.evidence: Access review reports, user access change logs

compliance_steps.step: Ensure all access requests, changes, and removals follow a formal documented process with management approval.
compliance_steps.evidence: Access request forms, approval records, termination checklists

compliance_steps.step: Monitor and log access to critical systems and information; review logs for unauthorized access attempts.
compliance_steps.evidence: Access logs, monitoring tool reports, incident records

compliance_steps.step: Provide periodic training to staff on access control policies and security best practices.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training records, attendance logs, awareness materials

GDPR.Description: Ensuring the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience of processing systems and services; access restriction measures.

NIST CSF.Description: Identity management, authentication, authorization, and access permissions are managed and enforced.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Technical safeguards: Access control and person/entity authentication; implementing procedures to control access to ePHI.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: Logical and physical access controls, user authentication, and authorization processes.

title: Identity management
description: The full life cycle of identities shall be managed.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.16, organizations must manage the entire identity lifecycle, from onboarding through modification to termination. Technically, this requires deploying an identity and access management (IAM) solution capable of integrating with HR systems and core applications, automating provisioning and de-provisioning, and enforcing least privilege principles. All user types—including privileged, non-employee, and service accounts—should be covered. Processes must include formalized workflows for identity creation, role or access changes, and prompt removal of access upon departure or role change, with clear accountability and segregation of duties. Documentation needs include an identity management policy, detailed procedures, identity inventories, access logs, and records of periodic reviews. Common pitfalls include reliance on manual processes, failure to promptly remove access after terminations, incomplete inventories of service accounts, and lack of regular review/audit activities. Avoid these by integrating with authoritative sources (e.g., HR databases), automating triggers for access changes, performing quarterly reconciliations between HR and IAM records, and ensuring all changes are logged and reviewed. Training staff on identity management best practices and maintaining evidence for audits are essential for compliance and effective risk mitigation.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document an identity management policy encompassing provisioning, modification, and de-provisioning processes for all user types (employees, contractors, third parties, service accounts).
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved identity management policy document; policy review records

compliance_steps.step: Implement an automated identity and access management (IAM) system to manage user onboarding, role assignment, and access rights throughout the identity lifecycle.
compliance_steps.evidence: IAM system configuration settings; system audit logs; access request records

compliance_steps.step: Perform periodic identity reviews (at least quarterly) to validate active users, roles, and privileges against current HR and organizational records.
compliance_steps.evidence: Identity review reports; user access reconciliation records; lists of terminated and transferred users

compliance_steps.step: Ensure timely de-provisioning of user access within 24 hours of employment termination or role change, including revoking credentials, disabling accounts, and removing physical access where required.
compliance_steps.evidence: De-provisioning logs; account termination requests; confirmation of access removal

compliance_steps.step: Maintain a centralized record of all identities (including privileged and service accounts) and their associated access rights, with regular updates and access restrictions.
compliance_steps.evidence: Identity inventory database; access rights lists; update logs

compliance_steps.step: Conduct annual identity management training for all staff to raise awareness of identity lifecycle management and responsibilities.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training attendance logs; training materials; completion certificates

compliance_steps.step: Monitor and audit identity management activities for anomalies and unauthorized changes, and retain audit trail logs for at least one year.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit logs; anomaly reports; incident investigation documentation

NIST CSF.PR.AC-4: Access permissions and authorizations are managed, incorporating the principles of least privilege and separation of duties

title: Authentication information
description: Allocation and management of authentication information shall be controlled by a management process, including advising personnel on appropriate handling of authentication information.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.17, organizations must establish a robust process for managing all forms of authentication information, such as passwords, cryptographic keys, biometrics, and tokens. Technically, this requires enforcing strong credential policies (e.g., complexity, length, expiry, lockout after failed attempts), implementing multi-factor authentication (MFA) for sensitive systems, and ensuring secure transmission and storage of credentials (e.g., hashing, encryption). All processes for issuing, resetting, revoking, and renewing credentials must be standardized and documented, with strict segregation of duties to prevent unauthorized changes. Users should be regularly trained on how to handle authentication information securely, including guidance on not sharing credentials, recognizing phishing attempts, and using password managers where appropriate. Audit logging and active monitoring of authentication events are essential to detect and respond to suspicious activity promptly. Documentation should include the authentication policy, procedures, user training records, and logs of authentication events and incident responses. Common pitfalls to avoid include using default or weak passwords, failing to revoke credentials promptly upon personnel changes, neglecting to enforce MFA where warranted, and not providing adequate end-user guidance. Regular reviews and updates of controls, informed by incident trends and technology changes, are necessary to maintain effectiveness and compliance.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document an authentication information management policy covering password, biometric, token, and multi-factor authentication (MFA) credentials.
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved authentication information management policy document; policy review logs

compliance_steps.step: Implement technical controls to enforce secure allocation, distribution, and lifecycle management of authentication credentials (e.g., initial issuance, reset, revocation).
compliance_steps.evidence: System configuration screenshots, logs of credential issuance and revocation, access management tool audit trails

compliance_steps.step: Provide mandatory training and awareness to all personnel on secure handling and protection of authentication information (e.g., not sharing passwords, recognizing phishing attempts).
compliance_steps.evidence: Training materials, attendance records, acknowledgment forms

compliance_steps.step: Monitor and review authentication events for unauthorized access attempts or credential misuse, and respond according to incident response plans.
compliance_steps.evidence: Authentication logs, incident tickets, monitoring system reports

compliance_steps.step: Ensure authentication systems enforce strong credential requirements (e.g., password complexity, expiry, reuse limitations, MFA where required).
compliance_steps.evidence: System configuration settings, password policy documentation, MFA rollout logs

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and update authentication information management procedures, incorporating lessons learned from incidents and changing business requirements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Procedure review meeting minutes, updated procedure documents

NIST CSF.PR.AC-1: Identities and credentials are issued, managed, verified, revoked, and audited for authorized devices, users, and processes.
NIST CSF.PR.AC-7: Users, devices, and other assets are authenticated commensurate with the risk of the transaction.

GDPR Articles.Article 32: Security of processing; includes the implementation of appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability (including access control and authentication).

HIPAA Security Rule.§164.312(d): Person or entity authentication; requires procedures to verify that a person or entity seeking access is the one claimed.
HIPAA Security Rule.§164.308(a)(3): Workforce security; implement procedures to ensure only authorized access to ePHI.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC6.1: Logical access security software, infrastructure, and architectures are implemented to support access restrictions and authentication.
SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC6.2: Procedures exist to identify and authenticate users prior to granting access.

title: Access rights
description: Access rights to information and other associated assets shall be provisioned, reviewed, modified and removed in accordance with the organization topic-specific policy on and rules for access control.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.18, organizations should establish a robust access management lifecycle covering the provisioning, reviewing, modification, and removal of access rights for all information assets. Technically, this involves deploying centralized identity and access management (IAM) solutions that support policy-based provisioning and de-provisioning, maintaining detailed access logs, and enforcing least privilege through role-based access controls. On the process side, access requests must be formally documented, reviewed by asset owners or managers, and periodically audited—ideally using automated tools where feasible. Clear procedures should define how access adjustments occur upon role changes, terminations, or transfers, requiring close coordination between HR and IT teams. All activities must be documented, including policy approvals, access requests, reviews, and removal actions, with evidence retained for audit purposes. Common pitfalls include neglecting regular access reviews, failing to update rights following organizational changes, or not maintaining granular access inventories. Organizations should also guard against excessive access by periodically verifying that users retain only necessary privileges and immediately revoking access for departing personnel. To ensure ongoing compliance, continuous staff training on access control best practices and the importance of credential protection is essential. Avoid manual or ad hoc provisioning, as these increase error risk and audit failures. Use automated, auditable workflows wherever possible to demonstrate consistent, repeatable control operation.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document an access control policy outlining provisioning, reviewing, modifying, and revoking access rights for all information systems and assets.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Approved access control policy document; policy review logs

compliance_steps.step: Implement a formal access request and approval workflow that captures user identity, business justification, asset details, and authorization from relevant managers.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Helpdesk / Asset Owner / Line Manager
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Access request forms/tickets; approvals with timestamps

compliance_steps.step: Provision access rights based on least privilege principle and segregation of duties, ensuring users receive only the minimum access required for their roles.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Access provisioning logs; role-based access matrices

compliance_steps.step: Conduct periodic (at least quarterly) reviews of user access rights to all critical systems and assets, documenting findings and corrective actions.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Asset Owners / Internal Audit / IT Security Team
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Access review reports; evidence of access changes or removals

compliance_steps.step: Immediately modify or revoke access rights upon role changes, terminations, or transfers by following a documented de-provisioning process.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Change of employment status notifications; de-provisioning logs

compliance_steps.step: Maintain an up-to-date inventory of users and their access rights for all systems and assets, with version control on changes.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Access inventory database; access history audit trails

compliance_steps.step: Regularly educate staff on access control procedures and the importance of protecting credentials, through mandatory training sessions.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Training attendance records; training materials

NIST CSF.PR.AC-1: Identities and credentials are issued, managed, verified, revoked, and audited for authorized devices, users, and processes
NIST CSF.PR.AC-4: Access permissions and authorizations are managed, incorporating the principles of least privilege and separation of duties

GDPR Articles.Article 25: Data protection by design and by default, including limiting access to personal data
GDPR Articles.Article 32(1)(b): Implement measures to ensure confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience, including access controls

HIPAA Security Rule.164.312(a)(1): Access Control—Implement technical policies and procedures to allow access only to those persons or software programs that have been granted access rights

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC6.2: System access is provisioned, modified, and removed based on policies and procedures

title: Information security in supplier relationships
description: Processes and procedures shall be defined and implemented to manage the information security risks associated with the use of suppliers products or services.
guidance: To implement A.5.19 effectively, organizations must develop a robust supplier management program that integrates information security into every stage of the supplier lifecycle. Technically, this involves maintaining an up-to-date inventory of all suppliers who access or process your information, conducting risk-based assessments before onboarding, and ensuring that suppliers meet defined security standards. Contracts must explicitly specify information security requirements, including data protection, breach notification, and the right to audit. Processes should be in place to periodically review supplier security posture through assessments, evidence reviews, or on-site audits. When offboarding suppliers, ensure all organizational data is either returned or securely destroyed and that all access rights are revoked. Documentation is crucial—retain records of risk assessments, contract clauses, ongoing reviews, and supplier termination actions to demonstrate compliance. Common pitfalls include failing to update the supplier list, inadequate risk assessment depth, neglecting to enforce contract clauses, and inconsistent monitoring. Organizations should also train staff involved in supplier management on security expectations and ensure that exceptions or high-risk suppliers receive heightened scrutiny. By embedding security requirements in supplier management, organizations can significantly reduce third-party risks and demonstrate due diligence in compliance audits.

title: Information security roles and responsibilities
description: Information security roles and responsibilities shall be defined and allocated according to the organization needs.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.2, organizations must take a structured approach to defining, allocating, and documenting information security roles and responsibilities. Technically, this involves identifying all business processes, assets, and systems that require security oversight, and mapping out the necessary roles (e.g., Information Security Officer, Data Owner, System Administrator) in alignment with organizational risk and complexity. Process-wise, a formalized method should be established for creating and maintaining job descriptions, assigning responsibilities, and ensuring segregation of duties to prevent conflicts of interest. Responsibilities should be communicated through policy documents, onboarding procedures, and ongoing security training. All assignments and changes must be documented and retained for audit purposes, including role acceptance forms and organizational charts. Review and update processes must be scheduled, particularly after organizational changes such as restructuring, mergers, or new technology adoption. Common pitfalls include failing to update roles after personnel or technology changes, lack of clarity or overlap in responsibilities, and poor communication, which can lead to security gaps or non-compliance. Documentation should be comprehensive, covering not just role descriptions, but also evidence of communication, reviews, and corrective actions, ensuring a demonstrable, auditable trail of compliance.

title: Addressing information security within supplier agreements
description: Relevant information security requirements shall be established and agreed with each supplier based on the type of supplier relationship.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.20, organizations must integrate information security requirements into supplier agreements based on the risk posed by each supplier relationship. Technically, this involves specifying security controls such as encryption standards, access controls, incident reporting timelines, and data handling requirements within contracts. Provisions for right-to-audit, ongoing compliance monitoring, and incident notification must be explicit. Process-wise, organizations should establish a formal supplier risk assessment procedure to determine which security requirements are necessary for each supplier type. This must be embedded into procurement and contract renewal workflows to ensure all agreements are reviewed and updated accordingly. Documentation is critical; maintain a current supplier inventory, a security requirements matrix, contract templates with standardized clauses, and evidence of periodic supplier reviews. Common pitfalls include using generic contract templates that overlook specific security needs, failing to update legacy agreements, and neglecting subcontractor or fourth-party risk. Additionally, some organizations overlook the need for ongoing monitoring, erroneously treating supplier security as a one-time activity. To avoid these issues, implement robust contract management practices, regular supplier compliance checks, and periodic staff training. This comprehensive approach not only supports compliance but also reduces the risk of security incidents originating from the supply chain.

title: Managing information security in the ICT supply chain
description: Processes and procedures shall be defined and implemented to manage the information security risks associated with the ICT products and services supply chain.
guidance: Implementing effective information security management within the ICT supply chain requires a comprehensive approach that integrates technical, procedural, and contractual measures. Technically, organizations must ensure that all ICT products and services sourced from external suppliers comply with internal security standards. This involves defining security requirements for suppliers, such as encryption protocols, access controls, and data segregation, and verifying their implementation through technical assessments or audits. Process-wise, organizations should establish and document a supply chain risk management policy, conduct risk assessments prior to supplier onboarding and at regular intervals, and maintain a centralized inventory of all ICT suppliers, including their risk ratings and service details. Contracts with suppliers should explicitly state information security obligations, including incident notification timelines, audit rights, and data handling procedures. Documentation is critical—retain records of assessments, supplier performance reviews, and communication logs related to security incidents. Common pitfalls include failing to regularly update the supplier inventory, neglecting ongoing monitoring of supplier compliance, inadequate incident reporting clauses in contracts, and insufficient documentation of supplier risk assessments. To avoid these, assign clear responsibilities, schedule periodic reviews, and implement automated tracking where possible. Ultimately, embed supply chain security in the procurement lifecycle, from vendor selection through offboarding, to ensure ongoing protection against evolving supplier-related threats.

title: Monitoring, review and change management of supplier services
description: The organization shall regularly monitor, review, evaluate and manage change in supplier information security practices and service delivery.
guidance: Effective implementation of ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.22 requires a systematic and proactive approach to supplier service management. Organizations must develop technical mechanisms such as automated monitoring tools, dashboards, and alerting systems to track supplier performance and detect deviations from agreed security standards. Process-wise, establish a documented supplier review schedule, define clear roles and responsibilities, and maintain a risk-based approach to review frequency and depth. Change management protocols should be integrated into supplier relationships, ensuring that any modifications in supplier personnel, service scope, or technical controls trigger immediate reassessment of associated risks and contractual obligations. From a documentation perspective, maintain a centralized repository for all supplier contracts, review logs, change records, risk assessments, and communication trails, ensuring auditability and ease of access for compliance reviews. Common pitfalls include neglecting to update risk assessments after supplier changes, failing to document reviews and actions, relying solely on initial due diligence without ongoing monitoring, and not aligning technical and process controls (e.g., missing notification when a supplier changes a key subcontractor). To avoid these, enforce periodic reviews, integrate supplier monitoring into the broader GRC framework, and ensure escalation and remediation procedures are defined and followed. Regular training of responsible personnel and leveraging GRC platforms for workflow automation can further strengthen compliance and resilience in supplier service management.

title: Information security for use of cloud services
description: Processes for acquisition, use, management and exit from cloud services shall be established in accordance with the organizations information security requirements.
guidance: Implementing effective information security for cloud service usage requires a structured approach that aligns technical controls, processes, and documentation. Begin by establishing a formal policy for cloud service acquisition, mandating risk assessments and due diligence on each cloud provider. This should cover provider security posture, compliance certifications (e.g., SOC 2, ISO 27001), and data residency. Integrate explicit information security requirements into all contracts and SLAs, such as obligations for encryption, access controls, incident notification, and audit rights, ensuring legal enforceability. Technically, enforce encryption for data at rest and in transit, enable multi-factor authentication, and implement role-based access controls within cloud platforms. Maintain an up-to-date inventory of all cloud services, including data classification and business ownership, to ensure visibility and accountability. Develop and test data exit and migration procedures to secure data upon service termination, including data deletion certificates or transfer logs. Regularly audit cloud service usage for compliance with internal policies and regulatory requirements. Document each process, from acquisition through exit, and retain supporting evidence such as risk assessments, contracts, access logs, and audit reports. Avoid common pitfalls such as shadow IT (unauthorized cloud service usage), inadequate exit planning, or over-reliance on provider assurances without verification. Continuous staff training on secure cloud practices and incident reporting is essential to maintaining an effective and compliant cloud security posture.

Implement and document technical controls for secure cloud usage, such as encryption (at rest and in transit), multi-factor authentication, and user access reviews.

title: Information security incident management planning and preparation
description: The organization shall plan and prepare for managing information security incidents by defining, establishing and communicating information security incident management processes, roles and responsibilities.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.24 effectively, organizations must take a holistic approach encompassing technical infrastructure, structured processes, and thorough documentation. Technically, establish centralized logging, monitoring, and alerting mechanisms to detect and track security events. Ensure incident reporting channels (e.g., ticketing systems, hotlines) are integrated with existing IT operations for swift escalation. Assign clear roles and responsibilities (e.g., incident handlers, escalation managers, communicators, forensic analysts) and document these in a RACI matrix. Process-wise, define step-by-step incident management procedures—covering identification, categorization, containment, eradication, recovery, and post-incident review—and ensure they are regularly tested through simulations or tabletop exercises. Documentation should include policies, procedures, training records, test/exercise results, and evidence of communication to staff. Common pitfalls include lack of staff awareness, outdated or overly generic procedures, infrequent testing, and unclear escalation paths. To avoid these, ensure all procedures are tailored to your organizational context, are regularly reviewed, and that staff at all levels are trained and aware of their responsibilities. Finally, integrate incident management planning into business continuity and disaster recovery frameworks to ensure a coordinated response to major incidents, and periodically update all documents and processes to reflect changes in the threat landscape and organizational structure.

title: Assessment and decision on information security events
description: The organization shall assess information security events and decide if they are to be categorized as information security incidents.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.25 requires technical, procedural, and documentation rigor. Technically, organizations should deploy centralized logging and monitoring solutions (such as SIEM platforms) to automatically capture and surface security-relevant events from networks, endpoints, and cloud environments. Process-wise, establish and formalize criteria that distinguish routine events from those of security concern (e.g., unauthorized access, malware detection, policy violations). This should be documented in an incident management policy and communicated through regular staff training. Each event flagged by the monitoring tools must be assessed promptly by trained personnel, with a clear workflow guiding whether it is elevated to incident status. Every assessment must be recorded, including the decision and supporting evidence, ensuring traceability and consistency for audits and management review. Common pitfalls include vague categorization criteria, inconsistent assessment practices, lack of evidence documentation, and failure to update processes as threats evolve. To avoid these, organizations should automate wherever possible, regularly review and refine assessment processes, and ensure strong management oversight. Finally, incident assessment statistics and trends should be reported to governance bodies to ensure continuous improvement and strategic alignment.

title: Response to information security incidents
description: Information security incidents shall be responded to in accordance with the documented procedures.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.26, organizations must establish and rigorously follow a structured incident response process. Technically, this involves maintaining a secure, monitored environment where potential incidents can be detected (via security information and event management—SIEM—or similar tools), and ensuring evidence is preserved for potential forensic analysis. Process-wise, the organization should document clear, actionable procedures that define how incidents are identified, classified, escalated, contained, eradicated, and recovered from. These procedures should specify responsibilities, escalation thresholds, and communication plans—both internally and, where required, with external parties or regulators (such as under GDPR or HIPAA). All staff must be regularly trained to recognize and report incidents, and response teams should conduct periodic incident simulations or tabletop exercises to ensure readiness. Documentation is critical: maintain detailed incident logs, action plans, communications, and post-incident review reports. Avoid common pitfalls such as vague procedures, lack of regular updates or testing, insufficient staff training, and failure to document actions taken. An effective incident response capability is not static—review and improve it continuously based on lessons learned and evolving threat landscapes. Integrate incident response tightly with risk management and compliance obligations to ensure regulatory alignment and rapid, coordinated action during events.

title: Learning from information security incidents
description: Knowledge gained from information security incidents shall be used to strengthen and improve the information security controls.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.27, organizations must systematically extract actionable intelligence from every information security incident, regardless of severity. Technically, this requires collecting detailed incident data (logs, timelines, impacted systems, attack vectors), performing root cause analysis, and mapping findings to existing control weaknesses. Process-wise, a cross-functional post-incident review should be mandated, with defined roles for incident handlers, IT, risk management, and process owners. All lessons learned must be documented in a centralized repository, and tracked to closure through a corrective action register. Documentation requirements include incident review reports, updated procedures, communication records, and training logs that reflect changes implemented as a result of incident insights. Organizations should update policies and controls in a timely manner and ensure these updates are communicated and reinforced via targeted staff training. Annual trend analysis of incidents is critical to identify recurring patterns and systemic risks. Common pitfalls include inconsistent documentation, failure to update controls, lack of stakeholder communication, and not following through on corrective actions. To avoid these, establish clear accountability, automate documentation where possible, and schedule regular reviews of the effectiveness of improved controls. This disciplined learn-and-improve loop strengthens the overall information security posture and satisfies both internal and external audit expectations.

GDPR.Article 32(1)(d): Requires regular testing, assessing, and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organizational measures, including updating measures based on incidents.

NIST CSF.ID.RA-5: Risk response planning incorporates lessons learned from past incidents.
NIST CSF.RS.IM-1: Response plans are updated with lessons learned and improvement actions.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(6)(ii): Implement response and reporting procedures for security incidents, including improvements based on incident analysis.

title: Collection of evidence
description: The organization shall establish and implement procedures for the identification, collection, acquisition and preservation of evidence related to information security events.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.28, organizations must establish a comprehensive evidence handling process that supports both technical and procedural rigor. Technically, deploy forensically sound tools for digital evidence acquisition, such as write-blockers for storage media and secure log export utilities, ensuring that collected evidence is not altered during the process. All evidence must be hashed and the hash values recorded at the time of collection to verify integrity. Process-wise, clearly define roles and responsibilities within your incident response team for identifying, collecting, and preserving evidence. Maintain a detailed chain-of-custody log for each piece of evidence, documenting who handled it, when, where, and for what purpose. Secure storage—preferably with encryption and physical security controls—is essential to prevent unauthorized access or tampering. Documentation is critical: all evidence collection actions should be logged, and evidence-related procedures must be kept up to date and regularly tested through tabletop exercises or mock incidents. Common pitfalls to avoid include failing to train staff, using non-forensic methods that might alter evidence, neglecting chain-of-custody documentation, or storing evidence in insecure locations. Regularly review your procedures to incorporate lessons learned from incidents and ensure compliance with legal and regulatory requirements. Comprehensive, tested, and well-documented procedures strengthen both incident response effectiveness and legal defensibility.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and document an evidence collection and preservation procedure, detailing roles, responsibilities, tools, and step-by-step processes for handling evidence related to information security events.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Manager; Incident Response Team Lead
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Approved procedure document; version control record

compliance_steps.step: Train all relevant personnel (e.g., IT, security, legal, HR) on the evidence collection procedure at least annually and upon onboarding.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Training records; attendance logs; training materials

compliance_steps.step: Utilize forensically sound tools and methods (e.g., write-blockers, log collection scripts) to collect digital evidence, ensuring integrity and chain-of-custody are maintained.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Forensics Specialist; Incident Response Team
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Tool inventory; acquisition logs; chain-of-custody forms

compliance_steps.step: Securely store collected evidence in a controlled environment (e.g., encrypted storage, locked physical storage) with restricted access, and log all access events.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Access logs; storage location records; access control policies

compliance_steps.step: Document each evidence collection event, including what was collected, by whom, when, where, and the justification for collection, to support legal admissibility.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Incident reports; collection forms; timestamped logs

compliance_steps.step: Periodically review and test the evidence collection process (e.g., tabletop exercises or mock incidents) to ensure effectiveness and update procedures as needed.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Test/exercise reports; process review meeting minutes; updated procedures

NIST CSF.DE.CM-3: Detection processes include monitoring for anomalous activity and collecting evidence for analysis.
NIST CSF.PR.IP-9: Response plans (Incident Response and Business Continuity) and recovery plans (Incident Recovery and Disaster Recovery) are tested; evidence collection is implied in response and recovery planning.

GDPR Articles.Article 32: Requires appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure data security, which includes incident response and evidence preservation when breaches occur.
GDPR Articles.Article 33: Obligation to document and report personal data breaches, which requires evidence collection.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.312(b): Audit controls for recording and examining access and activity; supports the collection of evidence.
HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(6)(ii): Requires procedures to respond to and report security incidents, which includes identifying and documenting evidence.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC7.2: The entity monitors system components for security events and gathers evidence to support investigations.
SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC7.4: The entity responds to identified security incidents by executing a defined incident response process, which includes collecting and preserving evidence.

title: Information security during disruption
description: The organization shall plan how to maintain information security at an appropriate level during disruption.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.29, organizations must ensure that information security controls are resilient and functional during any form of disruption, such as cyber incidents, natural disasters, or operational outages. Technically, this requires redundancy in critical systems, secure backup infrastructure, alternative communication channels, and the ability to quickly enact access restrictions or alternative authentication methods. Processes must integrate security continuity into business continuity and disaster recovery plans, specifying who is responsible for activating and maintaining controls under adverse conditions. Documentation should include a detailed information security continuity plan, records of regular BIA, periodic test results, and clear evidence of control adaptations during real or simulated disruptions. Assigning and training staff for these roles is essential. Common pitfalls include neglecting to update plans after organizational or technology changes, failing to test controls under real-world conditions, or overlooking third-party dependencies. Another frequent issue is assuming that IT disaster recovery alone is sufficient for information security—additional controls (e.g., temporary data access methods, manual override procedures) may be necessary. Regular reviews and improvement cycles ensure plans remain fit-for-purpose as threats and business environments evolve. Evidence of compliance is best demonstrated through documentation, test logs, and records of post-event reviews.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct a business impact analysis (BIA) to identify critical information assets and processes that must be protected during disruptions.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Completed BIA report highlighting critical assets and processes.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Business Continuity Manager, Information Security Manager

compliance_steps.step: Develop and document an information security continuity plan that specifies measures to maintain security controls during various disruption scenarios (e.g., natural disasters, cyber-attacks, system outages).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Approved and version-controlled information security continuity plan.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Manager, Risk Management Team

compliance_steps.step: Integrate security continuity requirements into the organization's broader business continuity and disaster recovery (BC/DR) plans.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: BC/DR plans with referenced information security requirements and control measures.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Business Continuity Manager, IT Operations Manager

compliance_steps.step: Assign roles and responsibilities for maintaining information security during disruptions, ensuring clear accountability.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Organizational chart or RACI matrix showing assigned roles for disruption response.

compliance_steps.step: Establish procedures to monitor and adapt security controls as needed during a disruption, such as activating alternative authentication methods or restricting access.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Procedures and logs showing activation or adaptation of security controls during incidents.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Security Operations, Incident Response Team

compliance_steps.step: Conduct periodic tests and simulations (e.g., tabletop exercises, incident response drills) to validate the effectiveness of the information security continuity measures.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Test schedules, exercise reports, and remediation action plans.

compliance_steps.step: Review and update the information security continuity plan at least annually or after any significant disruption event to incorporate lessons learned and changes in the threat landscape.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Plan review logs, change history, and post-incident review reports.

GDPR.Article 32(1)(b): Ensures ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience of processing systems and services.
GDPR.Article 32(1)(c): Requires ability to restore availability and access to personal data in a timely manner in the event of a physical or technical incident.

NIST CSF.PR.IP-9: Response and recovery plans incorporate cybersecurity; aligns with maintaining security during disruptions.
NIST CSF.RS.CO-2: Incident response roles coordinated and integrated during disruptions.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(7)(ii)(B): Disaster Recovery Plan—restore information after emergency.
HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(7)(ii)(C): Emergency Mode Operation Plan—maintain security during emergencies.

SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria.CC3.2: Considers continuity in organization risk assessments and control design.
SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria.CC7.4: Responds to identified security incidents and ensures continuity of system operations while maintaining security.

title: Segregation of duties
description: Conflicting duties and conflicting areas of responsibility shall be segregated.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 A.5.3 Segregation of Duties, organizations should start by mapping business processes and performing a comprehensive SoD risk assessment to identify where conflicting duties could lead to risk (e.g., fraud, unauthorized access). Technically, configure systems with robust role-based access controls (RBAC) ensuring that no single user can execute all stages of sensitive transactions, such as user creation and approval, or payment initiation and authorization. Use workflow automation in ERP and IAM platforms to enforce dual authorization and multi-person approval chains, and ensure all changes to access rights are logged and regularly reviewed. Process-wise, maintain up-to-date documentation of all roles, responsibilities, and critical process flows, updating them promptly after organizational changes. Establish and document a formal exception management process, requiring executive sign-off and compensating controls (like increased monitoring or peer review) when SoD cannot be maintained. Schedule recurring access rights reviews and recertification, supported by automated tooling where feasible, to ensure SoD integrity over time. Provide targeted training to personnel involved in sensitive processes, emphasizing the importance of SoD and clear reporting channels for violations. Common pitfalls to avoid include relying solely on manual controls, neglecting SoD after staff turnover or restructuring, and failing to audit or monitor exceptions. Maintain comprehensive records of SoD risk assessments, policy documents, exception logs, and training completion to demonstrate ongoing compliance.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct a segregation of duties (SoD) risk assessment across all business processes to identify areas with potential conflicts.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Documented SoD risk assessment report, risk matrix highlighting conflict areas

compliance_steps.step: Define and document roles and responsibilities, ensuring critical processes (e.g., financial transactions, user provisioning) are separated between at least two individuals.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Role and responsibility matrices, organizational charts, process flow diagrams

compliance_steps.step: Implement role-based access controls (RBAC) in all key systems to technically enforce SoD, ensuring no single user can perform all stages of sensitive transactions.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: RBAC configuration screenshots, access control policy documents, system audit logs

compliance_steps.step: Establish workflow automation and approval chains for sensitive operations (e.g., payment approvals, access requests), requiring dual authorization.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Automated workflow settings, approval logs, system configuration documentation

compliance_steps.step: Schedule and conduct regular access rights reviews and recertification to validate SoD compliance and update as organizational changes occur.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Access review reports, recertification records, change management logs

compliance_steps.step: Establish a formal process for managing and documenting exceptions to SoD, including risk acceptance, additional controls (e.g., increased monitoring), and executive approval.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Exception request forms, approval records, compensating control audit logs

compliance_steps.step: Deliver targeted training to all relevant personnel on SoD requirements, processes, and reporting channels for potential violations.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Training attendance logs, training materials, acknowledgment forms

GDPR.Description: Requires organizations to ensure that persons with access to personal data only process it as instructed, supporting SoD through controls and process separation.

NIST CSF.Description: Access permissions and authorizations are managed, enforcing separation of duties in critical processes.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Requires authorization and supervision of workforce members, supporting SoD through role assignment and supervision.

title: ICT readiness for business continuity
description: ICT readiness shall be planned, implemented, maintained and tested based on business continuity objectives and ICT continuity requirements.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.30 (ICT readiness for business continuity) requires a structured approach integrating both technical and organizational processes. Start by performing a comprehensive Business Impact Analysis (BIA) to identify critical business functions, supporting ICT systems, and precise continuity requirements, such as Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) and Recovery Point Objectives (RPO). Maintain a continuously updated inventory of ICT assets, ensuring all critical systems are accounted for. Based on the BIA, design and implement technical measures such as data backups, redundant infrastructure, failover capabilities, and geographically dispersed data centers to meet continuity targets. All ICT continuity strategies and procedures should be documented in alignment with the overarching Business Continuity Management System (BCMS), ensuring integration with organizational objectives and risk appetite. Test these plans regularly through both technical exercises (e.g., live failovers, backup restores) and scenario-based drills, documenting outcomes, issues, and improvement actions. Provide targeted training for all personnel involved in continuity processes, and keep records of training and competency assessments. Common pitfalls to avoid include failing to update plans after system or business changes, conducting only superficial tests (like tabletop exercises without technical validation), and lack of cross-functional alignment between business and IT priorities. Evidence of compliance should include not just documentation of plans, but also validated test results, proof of updates after changes, and demonstrated stakeholder involvement, ensuring the practical effectiveness of ICT readiness for business continuity.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct and document a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) to identify critical business processes, supporting ICT assets, and their continuity requirements (e.g., RTO, RPO).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Approved BIA report, asset inventory, endorsed RTO/RPO matrices
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Business Continuity Manager, IT Service Owners

compliance_steps.step: Develop and maintain an up-to-date inventory of all critical ICT systems, applications, and supporting infrastructure relevant to business continuity.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Signed-off ICT asset inventory, configuration management database (CMDB) extracts

compliance_steps.step: Define and document ICT continuity strategies and technical solutions (e.g., backups, redundancy, failover) to meet the identified RTOs/RPOs and continuity requirements.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: ICT continuity strategy document, solution architecture diagrams, vendor SLAs
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Disaster Recovery Lead, IT Infrastructure Manager

compliance_steps.step: Integrate ICT continuity plans into the organization’s overall business continuity management system and align with business objectives.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Integrated business continuity plan (BCP), meeting minutes showing alignment discussions

compliance_steps.step: Test ICT continuity plans regularly using both technical (e.g., failover, backup restoration) and process-oriented scenarios; document results and lessons learned.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Test schedules, test result reports, incident logs, post-mortem/lessons learned documentation

compliance_steps.step: Train relevant personnel on their roles and responsibilities within ICT continuity plans and maintain records of training completion.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Training attendance logs, training materials, competency assessments

compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Plan review logs, change management records, updated plan versions with approval
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Business Continuity Manager, IT Change Manager

NIST CSF.PR.IP-9: Response and recovery plans are tested (aligns with continuity testing).
NIST CSF.PR.PT-1: Audit/log records are determined, documented, implemented, and reviewed (relates to evidence of tests and changes).

title: Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements
description: Legal, statutory, regulatory and contractual requirements relevant to information security and the organizations approach to meet these requirements shall be identified, documented and kept up to date.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 Control A.5.31, organizations must establish a systematic, continuously maintained process to identify, document, and update all legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual requirements impacting information security. Technically, this entails building a centralized compliance register or leveraging a GRC platform where each requirement is entered, categorized, and mapped to relevant information security controls and business units. The process should involve designated owners for each requirement, ensuring accountability for monitoring and compliance. Regular monitoring is critical; subscribe to regulatory update feeds, collaborate with legal counsel, and review contracts for security clauses that may exceed statutory obligations. Schedule at least annual reviews, or more frequently when significant changes occur, to validate the completeness and accuracy of your compliance inventory. Documentation must include the inventory itself, mappings to controls, ownership assignments, review logs, evidence of regulatory monitoring, and training records. Avoid common pitfalls such as treating compliance as a one-time initiative, underestimating the specificity of contractual requirements, failing to assign ownership, or relying solely on automation for updates. Ensure evidence management is robust—maintain audit logs, policy acknowledgements, and corrective action records to demonstrate ongoing compliance. By embedding compliance into daily operations and maintaining rigorous documentation, organizations can demonstrate due diligence and readiness for external audits or regulatory inquiries.

compliance_steps.step: Establish a compliance inventory register that catalogs all legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual requirements related to information security.
compliance_steps.evidence: Completed and regularly updated compliance inventory register, with version history.

compliance_steps.step: Assign clear ownership for each requirement in the register, ensuring responsible individuals are documented and aware of their obligations.
compliance_steps.evidence: Ownership assignment log, signed role acceptance forms, organizational chart with mapped responsibilities.

compliance_steps.step: Map each requirement in the inventory to specific information security controls, policies, or processes implemented by the organization.
compliance_steps.evidence: Cross-reference matrix linking requirements to controls, review meeting minutes.

compliance_steps.step: Implement a formal process for monitoring regulatory, legal, and contractual changes, including subscription to regulatory update services and scheduled reviews with legal counsel.
compliance_steps.evidence: Regulatory update feed logs, review schedules, records of regulatory monitoring activities.

compliance_steps.step: Review and update the compliance inventory at least annually and after significant business or regulatory changes.
compliance_steps.evidence: Annual review records, change logs, updated inventory with timestamps.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct periodic training for all relevant staff on current legal, regulatory, and contractual obligations, and the organization’s compliance processes.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training attendance logs, training materials, policy acknowledgement records.

compliance_steps.step: Maintain audit-ready evidence for each compliance requirement, including records of due diligence, communications, and corrective actions taken.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit logs, compliance certifications, corrective action records, evidence repository access logs.

NIST CSF.ID.GV-6: Establish and maintain legal and regulatory requirements regarding cybersecurity (Governance).
NIST CSF.ID.RA-6: Identify and document applicable legal and regulatory requirements regarding risk assessment.

GDPR Articles.Article 32: Security of processing—requires implementation of appropriate technical and organizational measures.
GDPR Articles.Article 5(1)(a): Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency—processing must comply with all applicable laws.

HIPAA Security Rule.§164.308(a)(1)(ii)(C): Sanction Policy—addressing compliance with legal requirements.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC7.2: The entity restricts, identifies, and manages regulatory and contractual obligations relevant to security commitments.

title: Intellectual property rights
description: The organization shall implement appropriate procedures to protect intellectual property rights.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.32 on intellectual property rights, organizations must blend technical, procedural, and legal safeguards. Start by developing a comprehensive inventory of all IP assets, including those licensed from third parties, and regularly update this inventory as new assets are acquired or retired. Implement robust access controls—preferably role-based—and use encryption to protect sensitive IP data both at rest and in transit. For digital content, consider deploying Digital Rights Management (DRM) solutions to prevent unauthorized copying or distribution. Formalize policies and procedures that address the creation, use, and protection of IP, including clear guidance on handling third-party IP and steps to take if infringement is suspected. These policies should be reviewed and updated regularly, and communicated to all staff via mandatory training that covers legal and operational risks. Conduct periodic audits to verify that IP usage complies with internal policies and external licensing agreements. Ensure all contracts with vendors, partners, and customers contain clear terms regarding IP ownership and responsibilities; review these terms during contract negotiation and renewal. Document all aspects of the IP protection program, including asset inventories, policy versions, training records, audit reports, incident investigations, and contracts. Common pitfalls include neglecting third-party IP compliance, failing to update inventories, inadequate staff training, and assuming technical controls alone are sufficient. Avoid these by integrating people, process, and technology, maintaining vigilance over contract language, and establishing clear incident response procedures for suspected IP violations.

compliance_steps.step: Create and maintain an inventory of all intellectual property (IP) assets, including patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets, and licensed third-party IP.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Up-to-date IP asset register, records of periodic inventory reviews

compliance_steps.step: Establish and enforce access controls for IP assets, ensuring only authorized personnel can access, modify, or distribute these assets (using role-based access controls where applicable).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Access control lists, change audit logs, periodic access reviews

compliance_steps.step: Implement technical safeguards such as encryption for sensitive IP data at rest and in transit, and deploy Digital Rights Management (DRM) solutions for critical digital content.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Encryption policy, DRM deployment documentation, encryption key management logs

compliance_steps.step: Develop and communicate formal policies and procedures covering IP creation, protection, usage (including third-party IP), and incident response for suspected infringement.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Published IP policies, evidence of communication (e.g., email, intranet), version history

compliance_steps.step: Conduct regular training for all relevant staff on IP policies, legal obligations, handling of third-party IP, and reporting suspected violations.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Training records, attendance logs, training materials

compliance_steps.step: Perform periodic audits of IP usage and licensing compliance, covering both internally created and third-party IP.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Audit plans, completed audit reports, remediation tracking

compliance_steps.step: Ensure all contracts with vendors, partners, and customers have clear terms regarding IP ownership, use rights, and responsibilities.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Executed contracts, contract review checklists

compliance_steps.step: Establish procedures for investigating and responding to potential or actual IP infringements, including escalation paths and documentation requirements.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Incident response procedures, incident investigation logs, resolution documentation
