Both relate to protecting organizational assets, including IP, through documented processes and controls.

title: Protection of records
description: Records shall be protected from loss, destruction, falsification, unauthorized access and unauthorized release.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.33 requires a holistic strategy combining robust technical and procedural safeguards. Start by cataloging all records—both physical and digital—while assigning classifications based on sensitivity, regulatory requirements, and business importance. For digital records, enforce strong access controls using role-based permissions and multi-factor authentication, and apply encryption for sensitive data at rest and in transit. Physical records should be housed in locked, access-controlled areas with monitoring (e.g., CCTV or sign-in logs). All access and modifications must be monitored; deploy automated logging and integrity checking solutions, with logs reviewed regularly for suspicious activity. Develop and implement backup routines covering all critical records, ensuring backups are encrypted, stored offsite or offline, and restoration procedures are tested semi-annually. Record retention schedules must be defined in accordance with legal and regulatory obligations and reviewed at least annually. Upon expiration, records should be securely destroyed—using methods like shredding for paper or cryptographic wiping for electronic files—and these actions documented. Comprehensive policies and procedures should govern record management, access, retention, and destruction, and all staff must receive training on these requirements. Common pitfalls include neglected access reviews (particularly after staffing changes), inconsistent backup or destruction routines, lack of alignment with regulatory retention periods, and insufficient monitoring. Regular internal audits, continuous training, and cross-departmental collaboration are vital for sustainable compliance and risk minimization.

compliance_steps.step: Create and maintain an up-to-date inventory of all organizational records, classifying them by sensitivity, format (physical/digital), and retention requirements.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Documented record inventory; classification matrix; version history of inventory updates

compliance_steps.step: Implement and enforce access controls for all records, including role-based permissions for electronic records and secure, monitored storage for physical records. Review and update access rights at least quarterly and after personnel changes.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Administrator, HR Manager, Facilities Manager
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Access control lists; access review logs; documentation of access changes/removals

compliance_steps.step: Establish regular backup routines for critical electronic records, with at least monthly verification and secure offsite/offline storage. Test restoration procedures semi-annually.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Backup schedules; backup verification logs; restoration test reports

compliance_steps.step: Define and document record retention schedules in accordance with legal, regulatory, and business requirements. Review schedules annually and upon regulatory changes.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Compliance Officer, Legal Counsel, Records Manager
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Retention policy; documented retention schedules; evidence of annual reviews

compliance_steps.step: Implement secure destruction processes for records that have reached end-of-life, including shredding for paper and cryptographic wiping for electronic files. Maintain destruction logs.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Records Manager, IT Administrator, Facilities Staff
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Destruction certificates/logs; destruction procedures documentation

compliance_steps.step: Deploy technical controls such as encryption for sensitive data at rest and in transit, integrity checking mechanisms, and multi-factor authentication for record access.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: System configuration files; encryption key management logs; MFA implementation records

compliance_steps.step: Monitor and log all access and modifications to records, and review these logs at least monthly for unauthorized activities. Investigate and document any anomalies.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Security Operations Center (SOC) Analyst, IT Security Manager
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Access/modification logs; log review records; incident investigation reports

compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Training materials; attendance sheets; training completion certificates

NIST CSF.PR.DS-1: Data-at-rest is protected (aligns with encryption and integrity requirements).

GDPR Articles.Article 5(1)(f): Integrity and confidentiality of processing (security of personal data).

HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A): Risk analysis for confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

title: Privacy and protection of PII
description: The organization shall identify and meet the requirements regarding the preservation of privacy and protection of PII according to applicable laws and regulations and contractual requirements.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.34 (Privacy and protection of PII), organizations must blend technical, procedural, and documentation efforts. Technically, all PII must be encrypted both at rest and during transmission, with strong access controls (preferably role-based and enforcing least privilege) to limit exposure. Data masking and pseudonymization should be leveraged where full identification is not necessary. Regular system patching and vulnerability assessments are essential to minimize exploitable weaknesses. Process-wise, develop and communicate clear privacy policies aligned with applicable laws (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA), and ensure procedures exist for handling data subject requests, such as access, rectification, and erasure. Implement a breach response plan, including timely notification to authorities and affected individuals. Conduct Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) for new or modified processing operations to identify and mitigate risks. Document all processing activities in a PII inventory and maintain records of risk assessments, PIAs, data subject requests, and periodic control reviews. Contracts with third-party processors must include explicit privacy and security obligations. Common pitfalls to avoid include failing to identify all PII processing activities (especially in shadow IT or legacy systems), neglecting to update inventories or processes after changes, overlooking jurisdiction-specific obligations, and not monitoring third-party compliance. Regular training for all relevant personnel and periodic reviews of privacy controls ensure continued effectiveness and audit readiness. By integrating these technical safeguards, robust processes, and thorough documentation, organizations can demonstrate strong privacy and PII protection in line with ISO 27001:2022 and cross-framework requirements.

compliance_steps.step: Maintain an up-to-date inventory of all PII processed, stored, or transmitted by the organization, including data flows and storage locations.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Data Protection Officer (DPO), IT Asset Management
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Data inventory spreadsheet or database, data flow diagrams, review logs showing regular updates

compliance_steps.step: Implement technical safeguards such as encryption (at rest and in transit), access controls based on least privilege, and regular vulnerability scanning on all systems processing PII.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Encryption configuration screens, access control lists, vulnerability scan reports, change management records

compliance_steps.step: Establish and maintain privacy policies and procedures, including mechanisms for fulfilling data subject rights (access, correction, deletion) and breach notification processes.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Published privacy policy documents, documented procedures, logs or tickets of data subject requests, breach incident reports

compliance_steps.step: Conduct and document Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) for all new or significantly changed processing activities involving PII.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Completed PIA templates, approval records, risk assessment reports

compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Signed contracts with data protection clauses, third-party risk assessments, vendor compliance attestations

compliance_steps.step: Provide regular (at least annual) privacy and data protection training to all staff with access to PII, and maintain records of training completion.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Training attendance logs, training materials, employee acknowledgment forms

compliance_steps.step: Review and update all privacy and PII protection controls at least annually or following significant changes in processing activities, regulations, or identified risks.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Control review schedules, meeting minutes, updated policy versions, audit reports

NIST CSF.PR.IP-3: PII is managed consistent with the organization’s risk strategy to protect individual privacy.

GDPR Articles.Art. 24: Responsibility of the controller to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures.
GDPR Articles.Art. 32: Security of processing—requires encryption, confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.312(a): Access Control—unique user identification, access restrictions.
HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(1): Security Management Process—risk analysis and risk management for e-PHI.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC7.1: Ongoing risk assessments include privacy risks.
SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC8.1: System operations are designed to protect confidential information and PII.

title: Independent review of information security
description: The organizations approach to managing information security and its implementation including people, processes and technologies shall be reviewed independently at planned intervals, or when significant changes occur.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.35, organizations must establish a formal, risk-based process for independent review of their information security management system (ISMS). Technically, this requires a thorough evaluation of both the design and effectiveness of controls across people, processes, and technology. Examples include reviewing user access management, security awareness training participation, incident response drills, system configurations, and applied security patches. The process should start with a documented policy outlining review scope, triggers, frequency, and independence criteria for reviewers. Independence can be achieved by using internal audit teams not involved in daily operations or qualified third-party assessors. Reviews must be scheduled regularly (annually at a minimum) and triggered by significant organizational changes such as mergers, regulatory updates, or new technology implementations. Each review should follow a standardized methodology, be evidence-driven (e.g., interviews, document sampling, technical testing), and result in a formal report detailing findings and prioritized recommendations. All actions stemming from findings must be tracked to closure, with evidence retained for audit readiness. Common pitfalls include appointing reviewers with conflicts of interest, overlooking non-technical areas (e.g., staff security culture), or failing to remediate identified issues. To avoid these, clearly define reviewer qualifications, comprehensively cover all ISMS dimensions, and establish a robust remediation/validation workflow. Maintain a secure, centralized repository for all review artifacts to facilitate auditability and continuous improvement.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document an independent review policy and procedure specifying scope, objectives, frequency (at least annually), and triggers for ad hoc reviews (e.g., after major changes).
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved policy and procedure documents; version history

compliance_steps.step: Define and document criteria for reviewer independence, ensuring reviewers are not involved in day-to-day information security operations or subject to conflicts of interest.
compliance_steps.evidence: Reviewer selection criteria document; reviewer independence attestation forms

compliance_steps.step: Schedule planned independent reviews and update the audit plan/calendar to include both periodic and event-driven reviews.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit schedule/calendar; communications to stakeholders

compliance_steps.step: Conduct the review according to defined methodology, covering all aspects: people (e.g., awareness, roles), processes (e.g., procedures, incident response), and technology (e.g., controls, configurations).
compliance_steps.evidence: Completed review checklists; evidence of interviews, technical assessments, and sample testing
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Independent Reviewer / Internal Auditor / Third-Party Assessor

compliance_steps.step: Document findings, observations, and recommendations in a formal review report, prioritizing issues by risk and impact.
compliance_steps.evidence: Formal review report with executive summary, detailed findings, and recommendations

compliance_steps.step: Assign ownership for corrective actions, track remediation progress, and validate closure of issues with follow-up reviews where necessary.
compliance_steps.evidence: Remediation tracker; evidence of completed actions; follow-up reports

compliance_steps.step: Maintain a centralized, secure repository for all review-related records and evidence to support future audits and continuous improvement.
compliance_steps.evidence: Central repository access logs; document retention logs

NIST CSF.ID.GV-4: Governance: Processes are established to review cybersecurity policies, procedures, and controls at planned intervals and after significant changes.
NIST CSF.ID.RM-1: Risk Management: Risk management processes are reviewed and updated regularly by independent parties.

GDPR Articles.Art. 32(1)(d): Requires regular testing, assessing, and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organizational measures for ensuring security of processing.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(8) - Evaluation: Perform a periodic technical and nontechnical evaluation of implemented security measures in response to environmental or operational changes.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC5.3: The entity evaluates and communicates the results of ongoing internal control monitoring and separate evaluations (e.g., independent reviews).

title: Compliance with policies, rules and standards for information security
description: Compliance with the organizations information security policy, topic-specific policies, rules and standards shall be regularly reviewed.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.36, organizations must operationalize a structured, repeatable process for reviewing all information security-related policies, rules, and standards. Technically, this requires a secure, centralized repository—using a GRC platform or document management system—with robust version control, change tracking, and access management. Every document should be assigned a clear owner responsible for its periodic review and update. Establish a documented review cycle (at least annually or semi-annually), with additional ad hoc reviews triggered by significant internal or external changes, such as new regulations, threat intelligence, or business shifts. The review process should involve cross-functional stakeholders (Legal, IT, Security, Business) and leverage standardized checklists to assess continued alignment with operational needs, compliance obligations, and emerging risks. Findings and required changes must be tracked through actionable improvement plans, with closure monitored and documented. All updates should be communicated to affected stakeholders and incorporated into training programs to ensure awareness and effective implementation. Maintain audit trails of review activities, decisions, and communications for regulatory and certification evidence. Common pitfalls include treating reviews as a formality rather than a substantive risk management activity, lack of clear ownership, poor change management, and insufficient communication or training on updated policies. Avoid these by embedding accountability, automating workflows where feasible, and integrating review outcomes into operational and technical enforcement mechanisms (such as access controls, monitoring, and incident response). This approach strengthens compliance, supports audit readiness, and enhances overall risk management.

compliance_steps.step: Create and maintain a centralized, version-controlled repository for all information security policies, rules, and standards.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Manager / IT Governance Lead
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Repository access logs, change history, version control records

compliance_steps.step: Assign explicit ownership for each policy, rule, and standard, ensuring clear accountability for review and updates.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Policy Owners (typically department heads or process owners)
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Ownership matrix, documented responsibility assignments

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document a formal review schedule (e.g., annual or semi-annual) for all documents, including triggers for ad hoc reviews due to regulatory or business changes.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Review calendar, documented review triggers, historical review logs

compliance_steps.step: Conduct documented reviews of each policy, rule, and standard, assessing alignment with operations, regulatory requirements, and current risks.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Review Committees (cross-functional including Legal, IT, Security, and Business units)
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Completed review checklists, meeting minutes, review reports

compliance_steps.step: Document findings, required changes, and improvement plans, and track their implementation to closure.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Improvement/action plans, change logs, closure evidence

compliance_steps.step: Communicate all updates and changes to relevant stakeholders and ensure training is delivered where required.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Communication records, training attendance logs, updated policy distribution lists

compliance_steps.step: Perform periodic audits to verify that policies are being followed and that updates have been effectively implemented.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Audit reports, compliance checklists, evidence of enforcement (system controls, logs)

NIST CSF.ID.GV-1: Organizational governance structure is established and maintained; encompasses regular review of policies.
NIST CSF.PR.IP-1: A baseline configuration of information systems is established and maintained; relates to maintaining and reviewing standards.

GDPR Articles.Article 32: Security of processing – requires regular review and assessment of policies and technical measures for security.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D): Information System Activity Review – regular review of records and activities for security policy compliance.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC8.1: The entity monitors the system to identify security events and other needed updates, which includes reviewing policies and standards.

title: Documented operating procedures
description: Operating procedures for information processing facilities shall be documented and made available to personnel who need them.
guidance: Effective implementation of ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.37 requires a systematic approach to documenting operating procedures for all information processing facilities—such as physical data centers, cloud environments, and critical on-premise servers. Technically, procedures should cover all operational aspects: routine tasks, system startup and shutdown, scheduled and emergency maintenance, backup and restoration, change management, and incident response. Each procedure must be tailored to the specific system or process, avoiding generic instructions that may not be applicable. From a process perspective, establish a clear workflow for drafting, stakeholder review, approval, publishing, and periodic updates, ensuring procedures remain current and relevant. Documentation must be detailed, version-controlled, and include change histories and approval records to maintain auditability. Store procedures securely using a role-based access system such as a document management platform or controlled intranet, ensuring that only authorized personnel can access and update them. Training and awareness programs must ensure that all relevant staff are informed of and competent in following these procedures, with attendance and comprehension documented. Common pitfalls include outdated or generic procedures, lack of stakeholder engagement, insufficient access controls, and failing to update documentation after system changes. Avoid these by enforcing a review cycle aligned with system changes and annual audits, and by implementing monitoring mechanisms—such as periodic audits or spot checks—to verify adherence and address gaps promptly. This robust approach strengthens operational consistency, reduces risk of errors, and supports ongoing compliance.

compliance_steps.step: Identify and inventory all information processing facilities (e.g., data centers, cloud environments, critical servers) requiring documented operating procedures.
compliance_steps.evidence: Facility inventory list; asset registry

compliance_steps.step: Develop detailed operating procedures covering routine operations, system startup/shutdown, maintenance, backup, data restoration, change management, and incident response for each facility.
compliance_steps.evidence: Procedure documents for each facility; mapping of procedures to facility types

compliance_steps.step: Establish a standardized workflow for drafting, reviewing, and approving procedures, including mandatory stakeholder input and formal sign-off.
compliance_steps.evidence: Workflow diagram; approval records; change history logs

compliance_steps.step: Implement secure, role-based access to procedures using an enterprise document management system or controlled intranet location.
compliance_steps.evidence: Access logs; user access matrix; screenshot of document repository
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Security Administrator / Document Control Officer

compliance_steps.step: Train relevant personnel on the operating procedures and document attendance, comprehension assessments, and feedback.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training records; signed acknowledgements; training completion certificates

compliance_steps.step: Schedule and execute periodic review and update cycles for all procedures—triggered by system changes and at least annually.
compliance_steps.evidence: Review schedule; updated procedures; version control logs

compliance_steps.step: Conduct regular monitoring (spot checks or audits) to verify procedure adherence and identify gaps or obsolete instructions.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit reports; corrective action plans; checklists

NIST CSF.Description: A baseline configuration of information systems is created and maintained; operating procedures are developed and maintained.

title: Management responsibilities
description: Management shall require all personnel to apply information security in accordance with the established information security policy.
guidance: Effective implementation of ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.4 requires a blend of technical, procedural, and cultural measures. Technically, organizations must ensure that their information security policy is accessible to all personnel—typically via intranet portals or document management systems—and that systems enforce policy adherence through role-based access controls and automated compliance checks where feasible. Procedurally, management must embed security responsibilities into organizational workflows, starting with job descriptions, onboarding processes, and regular mandatory training sessions. Management should actively communicate their support for information security through visible actions, such as participating in training, addressing policy breaches, and allocating necessary resources. Documentation is critical: maintain records of policy approvals, training, disciplinary actions, and ongoing compliance monitoring. Common pitfalls include treating security policy as a 'tick-box' exercise, failing to regularly update documentation as the organization changes, and neglecting to close the feedback loop when policy breaches occur. To avoid these issues, integrate policy compliance into performance reviews, continuously reinforce messaging at all organizational levels, and ensure there is a documented, enforced process for addressing non-compliance. Regular audits and management reviews should be scheduled to assess both the effectiveness of policy implementation and staff understanding, ensuring a culture of accountability and continuous improvement.

compliance_steps.step: Update and approve information security policy, ensuring alignment with organizational objectives.
evidence: Latest approved information security policy document
Management meeting minutes showing policy review and approval

compliance_steps.step: Conduct mandatory awareness training for all personnel on information security policy and responsibilities.
Integrate information security responsibilities into job descriptions and employment contracts for all roles.
evidence: Signed employment contracts with security clauses

compliance_steps.step: Establish periodic (e.g., quarterly) compliance monitoring mechanisms to verify adherence to security policy.
Implement a disciplinary process for non-compliance with information security policy.
evidence: Records of policy violations and actions taken

compliance_steps.step: Communicate management’s commitment to information security through regular internal communications (e.g., emails, town halls, intranet posts).
Review and update information security policy and related procedures at least annually, or upon significant organizational changes.
