title: Contact with authorities
description: The organization shall establish and maintain contact with relevant authorities.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.5 (Contact with authorities), organizations must establish both technical and procedural mechanisms for maintaining relationships with relevant authorities. Start by identifying all authorities applicable to your business, including regulators, law enforcement, and sector-specific bodies across all jurisdictions of operation. Maintain an up-to-date, centrally stored contact list with designated owners responsible for routine updates. Technically, ensure secure storage and restricted access to authority contact details, possibly within a GRC or compliance management tool. Process-wise, develop and document clear procedures for when and how authorities should be contacted, such as during data breaches, regulatory investigations, or compliance checks. Integrate these procedures into your incident response and business continuity plans. Documentation range from authority contact registers, communication logs, procedural guides, and training materials that evidence staff awareness and process execution. Regularly review and test your procedures through tabletop exercises or real incident post-mortems, updating your documentation to reflect lessons learned and regulatory changes. Avoid common pitfalls such as outdated contact lists, unclear escalation paths, lack of documented communication, or staff unawareness of reporting obligations. Proactive engagement with authorities can foster trust and streamline regulatory interactions, reducing risk during actual incidents. Ensure all activities are auditable, with clear evidence trails supporting compliance and governance objectives.

compliance_steps.step: Identify all relevant authorities (regulatory bodies, law enforcement, data protection authorities, sectoral regulators) applicable to your organization's operations and jurisdictions.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Maintained list of authorities with contact details, reviewed annually

compliance_steps.step: Assign clear ownership for maintaining up-to-date contact information with each authority, ensuring someone is responsible for each relationship.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Documented roles and responsibilities matrix; designation in policy

compliance_steps.step: Establish documented procedures for when and how to contact authorities, including defined triggers (e.g., data breaches, regulatory requests, investigations) and escalation paths.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Incident response plan or external communication protocol with authority contact procedures

compliance_steps.step: Maintain a log of all communications with authorities, including date, purpose, content, and outcomes of each interaction.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Communication logs or registers; audit trail of correspondence

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review (at least annually) and update authority contact information and procedures to reflect changes in regulatory requirements or organizational structure.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Change log; annual review records; policy update notifications

compliance_steps.step: Ensure staff are trained on when and how to engage with authorities, including awareness of reporting obligations and internal escalation procedures.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Training records; attendance logs; awareness materials

compliance_steps.step: Test authority contact procedures as part of incident response and business continuity exercises, and document lessons learned for process improvement.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Manager; Business Continuity Manager
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Exercise/test reports; post-incident reviews

NIST CSF.ID.RA-3: Legal and regulatory requirements regarding cybersecurity, including privacy and civil liberties obligations, are understood and managed.
NIST CSF.RS.CO-2: Incidents are reported consistent with established criteria to relevant authorities.

GDPR Articles.Article 33: Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(6)(ii): Response and Reporting—Identify and respond to suspected or known security incidents; mitigate, document, and report incidents as appropriate.

SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria.CC2.1: The entity communicates relevant internal and external reporting requirements.
SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria.CC7.4: The entity responds to identified security incidents by executing a defined incident response program, which includes notifying appropriate external parties.

title: Contact with special interest groups
description: The organization shall establish and maintain contact with special interest groups or other specialist security forums.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 Control A.5.6, organizations must systematically establish and maintain relationships with external special interest groups such as security forums, industry alliances, and professional associations. Technically, this means identifying groups that offer actionable threat intelligence, regulatory updates, and best practices relevant to your sector and technologies. Process-wise, assign clear responsibility for managing these external contacts and participation, and document these responsibilities in policies and procedures. Set up mechanisms for regular engagement—such as joining mailing lists, participating in webinars, or attending conferences—and ensure that information gained is promptly evaluated and distributed internally, influencing risk assessments and control updates. Documentation needs include maintaining updated lists of groups, records of participation, communication logs, and evidence of how external insights are incorporated into your security program. Common pitfalls include failing to regularly review and update group memberships, ineffective dissemination of information internally, and lack of evidence for audit purposes. Avoid limiting contact to passive membership—active engagement is crucial for timely intelligence. Ensure all contacts and actions are tracked and that lessons learned from these groups are reflected in security controls and risk management processes for full compliance and improvement.

compliance_steps.step: Identify relevant special interest groups, industry forums, and security associations applicable to the organization's sector, geography, and technologies.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: List of identified groups, rationale for selection, documented in ISMS records.

compliance_steps.step: Formally assign responsibility for maintaining external contacts to a designated employee or team and define their role in a documented procedure.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Role assignments; written procedure; employee job descriptions.

compliance_steps.step: Establish membership or regular participation in selected groups (e.g., subscribe to mailing lists, attend meetings/conferences, join online forums).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Membership records; meeting attendance logs; subscriptions receipts; calendar invites.

compliance_steps.step: Document processes for receiving, evaluating, and disseminating relevant external threat intelligence, regulatory updates, and best practices from these groups within the organization.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Threat intelligence reports; internal newsletters; process documentation.

compliance_steps.step: Review and update contact lists, memberships, and participation frequency at least annually to ensure relevance and effectiveness.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Annual review checklist; updated contact lists; management review minutes.

compliance_steps.step: Integrate insights and recommendations from special interest groups into the organization’s risk assessments and security controls where appropriate.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Risk assessment records; change logs for controls; meeting minutes.

compliance_steps.step: Maintain records of all external contacts, communications, and participation, ensuring these are accessible for audit and review purposes.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Contact database; communication logs; audit trail.

NIST_CS_F.description: Knowledge of external threat events is maintained (NIST CSF v1.1).

GDPR_Articles.description: Security of processing—requires organizations to keep up-to-date with security practices and threats.

HIPAA_Security_Rule.description: Security awareness and training—ongoing security updates and reminders, including external sources.

SOC_2_Trust_Service_Criteria.description: The entity communicates information, including objectives and responsibilities for internal control, necessary to support the functioning of internal control.

title: Threat intelligence
description: Information relating to information security threats shall be collected and analysed to produce threat intelligence.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.7, organizations must establish a robust threat intelligence capability that is both technically sound and process-driven. Technically, this requires subscribing to multiple sources of threat data—commercial vendors, open-source feeds, and industry sharing groups (ISACs)—and ensuring the data is integrated into security monitoring platforms like SIEMs. Automation should be used to correlate threat intelligence with internal logs, enabling faster identification of relevant threats. Processes should be documented for the collection, validation, and prioritization of threat intelligence, ensuring that intelligence is actionable and fits your organization's risk profile. Regular analysis meetings should occur, where recent intelligence is reviewed in the context of your organization's assets and risks, and outputs should drive updates to incident response plans and security controls. Dissemination of intelligence must be timely and reach all relevant stakeholders, with secure communication channels and records of distribution. Documentation is critical—maintain logs of subscriptions, evidence of integration, meeting minutes, and change records to response plans. Common pitfalls to avoid include relying on a single intelligence source, failing to validate or contextualize external data, not integrating intelligence into operational processes, and neglecting regular effectiveness reviews. Ensuring threat intelligence is actionable, relevant, and continually improved is key to compliance and operational security.

compliance_steps.step: Subscribe to reputable threat intelligence feeds (e.g., commercial, open-source, ISACs) relevant to your industry and geography.
compliance_steps.evidence: Subscription records, contracts, feed access logs

compliance_steps.step: Establish a documented process for collecting, validating, and prioritizing threat intelligence from multiple sources.
compliance_steps.evidence: Process documentation, workflow diagrams

compliance_steps.step: Integrate threat intelligence into security monitoring systems (e.g., SIEM) to automate detection and correlation of threats.
compliance_steps.evidence: SIEM configuration files, integration logs, alert reports

compliance_steps.step: Conduct regular (e.g., monthly or quarterly) threat analysis meetings to review recent intelligence and update risk assessments.
compliance_steps.evidence: Meeting minutes, updated risk registers

compliance_steps.step: Disseminate actionable threat intelligence to relevant staff, including IT, incident response, and management, via secure channels.
compliance_steps.evidence: Distribution logs, internal communications

compliance_steps.step: Update incident response plans and playbooks based on newly identified threats and trends from intelligence analysis.
compliance_steps.evidence: Version history of response plans, change logs

compliance_steps.step: Periodically review and assess the effectiveness of threat intelligence activities, making improvements as required.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit reports, improvement action plans

GDPR.description: Requires measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability, including the ability to detect, respond, and recover from security incidents.

NIST CSF.description: Detection processes for monitoring threat events; external information sharing; risk assessment including threat identification.

HIPAA Security Rule.description: Risk analysis and response procedures that incorporate threat identification and intelligence.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.description: System monitoring for security events and anomalies; timely identification and response to risks.

title: Information security in project management
description: Information security shall be integrated into project management.
guidance: To effectively integrate information security into project management (ISO 27001:2022 A.5.8), organizations must embed security from project inception through closure. Technically, this requires defining baseline security requirements (e.g., access controls, encryption, data handling procedures) and ensuring these are considered in solution design, development, and deployment. Process-wise, mandate that all projects—IT and business—undergo security risk assessments, with outputs tracked in project risk registers and addressed through design or process controls. Assign security roles to project teams, require documented security checkpoints at key milestones, and incorporate security acceptance as a prerequisite for go-live. Document all security activities in the project lifecycle: requirements, risk assessments, test results, and sign-off records must be centrally stored and auditable. Common pitfalls include treating security as an afterthought, lack of security expertise in project teams, insufficient documentation, and inconsistent application of security reviews. Avoid these by training project managers on security, formalizing processes in the project management methodology, and establishing oversight mechanisms (e.g., regular audits or PMO reviews). Ultimately, security should be a visible, measurable, and traceable part of every project, reducing risk and ensuring compliance with both internal policies and external regulations.

compliance_steps.step: Update the organization's project management methodology to explicitly require the inclusion of information security considerations at all project phases (initiation, planning, execution, closure).
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Project Management Office (PMO) Lead, Information Security Manager
evidenceRequirements: Internal communications or training records on new requirements

compliance_steps.step: Develop and integrate an information security risk assessment process for all new and major change projects, ensuring that security risks are identified and addressed during project planning.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Project Manager, Information Security Risk Analyst
evidenceRequirements: Completed risk assessment templates for projects
Risk register entries specific to project risks

compliance_steps.step: Assign an information security representative to all project teams to provide ongoing security guidance and review throughout the project lifecycle.
evidenceRequirements: Project team charters or meeting minutes showing security representation

compliance_steps.step: Ensure that security requirements are documented as part of project requirements, and that security controls are incorporated into project deliverables (e.g., security testing, access controls, data protection measures).
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Project Manager, Lead Architect, Information Security Officer
evidenceRequirements: Project requirement documents with security sections
Design documentation and test plans including security controls

compliance_steps.step: Conduct periodic security reviews and checkpoints at key project milestones (e.g., design review, pre-launch) to verify security integration and address any gaps.
evidenceRequirements: Security review checklists and remediation actions

compliance_steps.step: Require formal security sign-off before project go-live, ensuring that all identified security requirements and controls have been implemented and tested.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Project Manager, Information Security Officer, Business Owner
evidenceRequirements: Final test results and security validation reports

compliance_steps.step: Maintain a repository of lessons learned from project security incidents or near-misses to inform future project security practices.

GDPR.Description: Data protection by design and by default—requires integrating data protection into processing activities and business practices, including projects.

NIST CSF.Description: ID.GV-3: Legal and regulatory requirements regarding cybersecurity are understood and managed; PR.IP-3: Configuration change control processes incorporate security considerations.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Risk analysis and evaluation of security measures when implementing new projects/systems.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: CC6.1: The entity implements logical access security measures; CC8.1: Change management processes include security impact assessments.

title: Inventory of information and other associated assets
description: An inventory of information and other associated assets, including owners, shall be developed and maintained.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.5.9, organizations must establish a comprehensive asset inventory that goes beyond basic listing. Technically, use automated discovery tools for hardware, software, and cloud resources, integrating with CMDBs or specialized asset management systems for accuracy and ongoing maintenance. The inventory should capture asset details including type, location, owner, classification, and lifecycle status. Process-wise, define clear procedures for asset onboarding, classification, transfer, and disposal, ensuring every asset is assigned a responsible owner who acknowledges their duties. Regular reconciliation—through both physical and logical audits—should be scheduled, with discrepancies promptly investigated and corrected. Documentation is critical: maintain a version-controlled asset inventory, audit logs, change records, and evidence of ownership assignment. Link asset records to related policies (e.g., information classification, risk management) and processes (e.g., incident response, business continuity) for holistic coverage. Common pitfalls include relying solely on manual inventories, neglecting to update records after changes, omitting cloud or virtual assets, and failing to assign clear ownership. Mitigate these risks by automating discovery, enforcing change management, and conducting periodic reviews. Ensure asset documentation is readily accessible but protected from unauthorized alteration. By following these technical and procedural steps, organizations will satisfy ISO 27001 and cross-framework requirements, supporting robust information security governance.

compliance_steps.step: Identify all information and associated assets (hardware, software, data, removable media, cloud services, etc.) within the organization.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Asset discovery reports, network scans, inventories exported from asset management tools

compliance_steps.step: Classify assets by type, criticality, and business function, ensuring alignment with information classification policies.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Officer, Business Unit Heads
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Asset classification matrix, documented asset categorization, policy references

compliance_steps.step: Assign asset ownership, ensuring each asset has a named owner responsible for its protection and lifecycle.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Asset inventory with ownership column, ownership acceptance forms

compliance_steps.step: Maintain and regularly update the asset inventory, including additions, disposals, transfers, and changes in ownership.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Versioned inventory logs, change records, disposal certificates

compliance_steps.step: Implement access controls and monitoring to secure the asset inventory against unauthorized changes.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Access logs, user permissions audit trail, change management records

compliance_steps.step: Periodically review and reconcile the asset inventory through physical and logical audits (at least annually).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Audit reports, reconciliation statements, remediation action plans

compliance_steps.step: Integrate the asset inventory with incident response, risk management, and business continuity processes.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Process maps, asset lists in risk registers, incident response documentation

NIST CSF.Description: Physical devices and systems within the organization are inventoried; Software platforms and applications within the organization are inventoried.

GDPR Articles.Description: Records of processing activities require maintaining an inventory of information assets and related activities.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Workforce security and device/media controls require tracking of information system assets and associated media.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: The entity maintains and periodically updates inventories of its system components and restricts logical access to assets.

title: Screening
description: Background verification checks on all candidates to become personnel shall be carried out prior to joining the organization.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 Control A.6.1 (Screening) requires organizations to establish a robust, documented process for background verification of all candidates prior to their employment. Technically, organizations must integrate screening procedures into the onboarding workflow, utilizing secure HR platforms that log and control access to sensitive verification data. Process requirements include defining the scope of checks (criminal, financial, education, previous employment), obtaining candidate consent, and ensuring checks are completed before granting system or facility access. All decisions and findings should be documented and retained securely for audit purposes. Organizations should select trusted third-party screening vendors and regularly review vendor performance and compliance with privacy laws (such as GDPR). Common pitfalls include skipping checks for temporary or contract staff, failing to update procedures for different jurisdictions, and insufficient documentation. Avoid blanket or non-specific screening policies; instead, tailor checks to role risk profiles and regulatory requirements. Periodically review and audit the effectiveness of the screening process, updating procedures as laws and organizational risks evolve. Maintain clear evidence trails—including signed consent forms, completed reports, and documented hiring decisions—to demonstrate compliance during audits and regulatory reviews.

compliance_steps.step: Define a formal background screening policy specifying types of checks (e.g., criminal record, education, employment history) and roles subject to screening.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Documented policy and procedures; date of last review

compliance_steps.step: Select and vet reputable third-party vendors for background verification, ensuring compliance with local laws and privacy regulations.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Vendor contracts and due diligence records

compliance_steps.step: Obtain written consent from candidates prior to initiating background checks, ensuring transparency and compliance with privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Signed consent forms retained in personnel files

compliance_steps.step: Conduct background checks for all candidates before issuing formal employment offers, ensuring all stipulated checks are completed.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Completed background check reports and verification logs

compliance_steps.step: Review screening results and document decision-making process for hiring or rejection, including risk assessments if discrepancies are found.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Hiring decision records, risk assessment reports

compliance_steps.step: Maintain records of completed background checks in secure, access-controlled HR systems for audit and compliance purposes.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: System access logs, record retention schedule

compliance_steps.step: Periodically audit the background screening process to ensure ongoing compliance and effectiveness, updating procedures as necessary.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Audit reports, process improvement plans

NIST CSF.Description: Personnel screening is performed prior to authorizing access to organizational systems.

GDPR Articles.Description: Requires processing personal data in a manner that ensures security, including appropriate vetting of employees.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Security management process including workforce clearance procedures to determine that persons have appropriate access.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: Criteria relating to background checks prior to granting system access and onboarding.

title: Terms and conditions of employment
description: The employment contractual agreements shall state the personnels and the organizations responsibilities for information security.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.6.2, organizations must embed clear, enforceable information security responsibilities within all employment contracts. Technically, this requires collaboration between HR, Legal, and Information Security teams to draft contract clauses that explicitly reference an employee’s duties regarding data protection, confidentiality, and compliance with internal security policies. Process-wise, ensure that these clauses are incorporated into all new hire contracts and that existing staff are transitioned to updated agreements when significant changes occur. Maintain a structured onboarding process where no system or data access is granted without a signed contractual acknowledgment. Regularly review and update contractual language to reflect evolving legal and regulatory requirements. Document all actions, including contract versions, signed agreements, policy references, and employee acknowledgments. Avoid common pitfalls such as generic or overly broad contractual language, failing to align contract clauses with current policies, or neglecting to audit and update existing agreements. Ensure that there is a clear disciplinary process for breaches of these contractual obligations. Finally, support contractual enforcement with ongoing information security awareness, ensuring employees understand their responsibilities and the consequences of non-compliance. This comprehensive approach not only strengthens your security posture but also provides strong evidence for audits and regulatory reviews.

compliance_steps.step: Review and update all employment contract templates to explicitly include information security responsibilities and obligations.
compliance_steps.evidence: Redlined and final contract templates with security clauses highlighted
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: HR Manager, Legal Counsel, Information Security Manager

compliance_steps.step: Incorporate specific references to relevant organizational policies (e.g., Acceptable Use Policy, Data Protection Policy) within employment agreements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Signed employment contracts referencing policy documents

compliance_steps.step: Ensure all new employees sign employment contracts that include information security clauses prior to system or data access.
compliance_steps.evidence: Dated, signed contracts stored in personnel files

compliance_steps.step: Conduct annual audits of existing personnel files to verify presence and completeness of security-related contractual clauses.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit reports, compliance checklists

compliance_steps.step: Communicate updates to information security responsibilities to all staff when contracts, policies, or regulations change and obtain documented acknowledgment.
compliance_steps.evidence: Change notifications, records of employee acknowledgments

compliance_steps.step: Establish a process for handling breaches of contract related to information security, including escalation and disciplinary action procedures.
compliance_steps.evidence: Documented procedures, incident records

compliance_steps.step: Provide regular (at least annual) training and refresher sessions on contractual information security obligations.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training materials, attendance logs, training completion certificates

GDPR.Article 32(4): Ensures that persons with access to personal data only process it upon instructions and are bound by confidentiality.
GDPR.Article 5(1)(f): Personal data must be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security.

NIST CSF.ID.AM-6: Personnel and roles are assigned and communicated; employment agreements support information security responsibilities.
NIST CSF.PR.AT-1: Awareness and training policies include information security roles and responsibilities.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(5)(i): Implement a security awareness and training program for all members of its workforce.
HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(3)(ii)(A): Implement procedures for the authorization and/or supervision of workforce members who work with ePHI.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC1.1: Control environment includes communication of responsibilities and expectations.
SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC2.2: The entity communicates information, including objectives and responsibilities for internal control, necessary to support the functioning of internal control.

title: Information security awareness, education and training
description: Personnel of the organization and relevant interested parties shall receive appropriate information security awareness, education and training.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.6.3, organizations must establish a comprehensive security awareness, education, and training program that addresses the diverse needs of personnel and relevant interested parties. Start by developing a formal policy that sets clear expectations for training scope, delivery frequency (e.g., onboarding, annual refreshers), and content coverage, such as threat identification, secure data handling, password management, and incident reporting. Leverage a mix of training formats—online modules, live sessions, and simulations—to cater to different learning styles and roles (e.g., IT, HR, executives, contractors). Deploy a secure, automated system for tracking participation, completion rates, and overdue training to ensure accountability and compliance. Extend awareness initiatives to third parties where relevant, based on contractual or risk-based requirements. Regularly assess training effectiveness via phishing simulations, quizzes, or feedback surveys, and use results to refine future sessions. Documentation is critical: retain training policies, attendance logs, assessment results, and version-controlled materials for audit purposes. Common pitfalls to avoid include generic, outdated content, lack of role-specific training, poor recordkeeping, and neglecting third-party awareness. Ensure training is regularly updated to address evolving threats, regulatory changes, and lessons learned from incidents. Ultimately, fostering a security-aware culture requires ongoing commitment and integration of awareness into daily business practices.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and maintain a formal Information Security Awareness, Education, and Training Policy that defines scope, frequency, and required topics.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Approved policy document; policy review logs

compliance_steps.step: Conduct baseline security awareness training for all personnel upon onboarding, covering topics such as password hygiene, phishing, data handling, and reporting incidents.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Training attendance logs; onboarding checklist; training materials
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: HR Manager and Security Training Lead

compliance_steps.step: Deliver periodic (at least annually) refresher and role-specific security training, ensuring coverage of current threats and organization-specific procedures.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Annual training schedule; completed training records; updated training content

compliance_steps.step: Administer regular phishing simulations or security awareness assessments to measure effectiveness and identify gaps in staff knowledge.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Simulation reports; assessment results; remedial action records

compliance_steps.step: Provide tailored security awareness and training to relevant third parties (e.g., contractors, vendors) as per contractual obligations or risk assessment.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Third-party training records; signed acknowledgments

compliance_steps.step: Maintain a centralized system for tracking all training activities, completion rates, and exceptions; ensure timely follow-up for overdue training.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Training management system logs; exception reports; follow-up communications

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and update training materials to address emerging threats, regulatory changes, and feedback from previous training sessions.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Version-controlled training materials; review meeting minutes

GDPR.Description: Data Protection Officer must monitor compliance with GDPR, including assignment of responsibilities, awareness-raising, and training of staff.

HIPAA.Description: Security Awareness and Training Standard: Implement a security awareness and training program for all workforce members.

NIST_CSF.Description: All users are informed and trained (Protect: Awareness and Training)

SOC_2_TSC.Description: The entity communicates information, including objectives and responsibilities, necessary to support the functioning of internal control (including security awareness training).

title: Disciplinary process
description: A disciplinary process shall be formalized and communicated to take actions against personnel who have committed an information security policy violation.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 control A.6.4 requires organizations to formalize, communicate, and rigorously enforce a disciplinary process for information security policy violations. Technically, this starts with the creation of a documented disciplinary policy, endorsed by management and legal counsel, that outlines what constitutes a violation and maps severity levels to specific consequences. The process should include secure digital or physical storage for investigation records, strict access controls, and audit logs to ensure all disciplinary actions are traceable and confidential. Process-wise, staff must be made aware of the policy through mandatory training sessions, onboarding, and periodic refreshers. Reporting channels—such as anonymous hotlines or secure emails—should be implemented to encourage prompt reporting of suspected violations. Investigations must follow a standardized procedure, ensuring fairness, consistency, and legal compliance, with clear escalation paths. Documentation is critical: maintain evidence of policy communication, investigations, decisions, and actions taken. Avoid common pitfalls such as vague policy language, inconsistent enforcement, lack of awareness among staff, and poor documentation. Regular reviews of the process, leveraging case studies and regulatory developments, ensure continued effectiveness and compliance. Above all, balance deterrence with fairness, ensuring disciplinary measures are proportional, transparent, and legally sound.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and approve a formal disciplinary policy specific to information security violations.
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved disciplinary policy document; meeting minutes showing review/approval.

compliance_steps.step: Communicate the disciplinary policy to all personnel via onboarding, training sessions, and internal communications.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training attendance records; signed acknowledgment forms; copies of communications (emails, intranet posts).

compliance_steps.step: Integrate reporting mechanisms so employees can confidentially report suspected information security violations.
compliance_steps.evidence: Procedure documents; hotline/email setup details; records of reports received.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document a clear investigation process for alleged violations, including roles, timelines, and escalation paths.
compliance_steps.evidence: Investigation process flowcharts or SOPs; investigation records; escalation logs.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: HR Manager, Information Security Lead, Legal Counsel

compliance_steps.step: Define and document disciplinary actions ranging from verbal warnings to termination, aligned with the severity of the violation.
compliance_steps.evidence: Matrix of disciplinary actions; case logs of applied disciplinary actions; records of decision-making rationale.

compliance_steps.step: Review and update the disciplinary process annually, considering lessons learned and evolving regulations.
compliance_steps.evidence: Policy review logs; updated policy versions; board or management review minutes.

compliance_steps.step: Ensure records of disciplinary actions and investigations are securely stored and protected against unauthorized access.
compliance_steps.evidence: Access control lists; audit logs; secure storage configuration documentation.

GDPR.Description: Article 32 requires appropriate measures for security; Recital 39 references enforcing compliance and consequences for breaches.

NIST CSF.Description: PR.AT-3 covers awareness and training with disciplinary actions for non-compliance; PR.IP-10 covers response and mitigation procedures for policy violations.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Requires a sanction policy for employees who fail to comply with security policies and procedures.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: CC1.2 requires policies for addressing violations; CC3.2 requires procedures for addressing breaches of standards.

title: Responsibilities after termination or change of employment
description: Information security responsibilities and duties that remain valid after termination or change of employment shall be defined, enforced and communicated.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.6.5 effectively, organizations must establish and enforce clear post-employment information security responsibilities. Technically, this requires robust offboarding processes where all physical and logical access (e.g., user accounts, email, building entry, remote access, and privileged credentials) are immediately revoked or disabled upon termination or change of employment. Automated systems should be used wherever possible to track and log these removals, and alerts set up to detect any post-termination access attempts. Processes should include updating employment contracts (and any related confidentiality or non-compete agreements) to specify ongoing obligations regarding intellectual property, data confidentiality, and return/destruction of organizational assets. HR and IT Security teams must collaborate to ensure these obligations are communicated during exit interviews and that written acknowledgements are obtained and retained. Documentation is crucial: maintain completed offboarding checklists, logs of access revocation, signed acknowledgements, and version-controlled procedures. Regular reviews of these processes, with input from Legal and Compliance, ensure continued effectiveness and alignment with legal or regulatory changes. Common pitfalls to avoid include failing to coordinate between departments (leaving access open), not updating contracts to reflect current risks, neglecting to document the process, or failing to enforce post-employment obligations. Consistent training for HR and managers on these requirements is essential to ensure policy is translated into practice and to minimize the risk of insider threats or data breaches from former employees.

compliance_steps.step: Update employment contracts and confidentiality agreements to explicitly define post-employment information security obligations, including non-disclosure and data handling requirements.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Signed employment contracts and NDAs with post-employment clauses

compliance_steps.step: Develop and maintain a documented procedure for offboarding that includes a checklist for removal of logical and physical access to all systems, facilities, and sensitive information.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Completed offboarding checklists and access revocation logs

compliance_steps.step: Communicate post-employment security responsibilities to departing or transferring employees during exit interviews, and obtain written acknowledgment of their understanding.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Exit interview records and signed acknowledgments

compliance_steps.step: Review and enforce any contractual or legal obligations regarding intellectual property, confidential information, and data retention/destruction post-employment.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Copies of relevant contractual clauses and enforcement records

compliance_steps.step: Set up automated alerts and reviews for any attempted post-termination access to organizational resources for at least 90 days after employment ends.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Access monitoring logs and incident reports

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and update post-termination procedures at least annually, or after any security incident involving former employees.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Procedure review logs and version-controlled policy documents

compliance_steps.step: Train managers and HR personnel on the importance of enforcing and documenting post-employment security responsibilities.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Training records and attendance logs

NIST CSF.ID.AM-3: Employees, contractors, and third-party users are managed throughout the employment life cycle (including termination or transfer).
NIST CSF.PR.AC-1: Identities and credentials for authorized users are managed, including removal after termination.

GDPR Articles.Article 32(4): Ensures any person acting under the authority of the controller/processor who has access to personal data does not process them except on instructions and maintains confidentiality obligations.
GDPR Articles.Article 5(1)(f): Personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized access.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(3)(ii)(C): Implement procedures for terminating access to electronic protected health information when employment ends.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC6.3: The entity removes access to information assets when personnel leave the organization or their job responsibilities change.
SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC7.2: Procedures exist for timely revocation of access and enforcement of ongoing obligations.

title: Confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements
description: Confidentiality or non-disclosure agreements reflecting the organizations needs for the protection of information shall be identified, documented, regularly reviewed and signed by personnel and other relevant interested parties.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.6.6, organizations must establish a robust process for managing confidentiality and non-disclosure agreements. Technically, this requires a secure document management platform for storing and tracking signed NDAs, with access restricted to authorized personnel. Processes should start by systematically identifying all individuals and third parties who may access sensitive information. Develop NDA templates in collaboration with legal and security teams, ensuring they address organizational requirements, applicable laws, and specific information protection needs. Integrate NDA signing into onboarding and contract initiation workflows, making NDA signatures a prerequisite for access. Periodically review and update templates and agreements to reflect changes in regulations, business context, or information classification. Maintain accurate records of all signed NDAs and train personnel on their obligations under these agreements, reinforcing this through regular awareness campaigns. Common pitfalls to avoid include using generic, outdated NDA templates, neglecting to update agreements when roles change, failing to track NDA compliance, and storing signed NDAs in insecure or decentralized locations. Organizations should also ensure that NDA obligations are enforceable and clearly communicated, with mechanisms to address breaches and non-compliance. Documentation should include NDA templates, signed agreements, review schedules, training materials, and evidence of compliance monitoring. By formalizing and actively managing this process, organizations demonstrate due diligence in protecting confidential information and comply with both ISO 27001 and cross-referenced frameworks.

compliance_steps.step: Identify all roles (employees, contractors, vendors, partners) with access to sensitive or confidential information.
compliance_steps.evidence: List of roles/personnel with access privileges; access logs; onboarding documentation

compliance_steps.step: Develop standardized confidentiality/non-disclosure agreement (NDA) templates that reflect the organization's specific information protection needs and legal requirements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved NDA templates; change logs for template updates

compliance_steps.step: Ensure all identified parties (internal and external) sign the NDA before being granted access to confidential information.
compliance_steps.evidence: Signed NDAs; onboarding checklists; contract management system records
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: HR Manager (internal), Procurement Manager (external), Legal Department

compliance_steps.step: Maintain a secure, centralized repository of all signed NDAs, accessible only to authorized personnel.
compliance_steps.evidence: Repository access logs; inventory of signed NDAs
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Records Management Officer, Information Security Manager

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and update NDA templates and signed agreements to reflect changes in business needs, legal requirements, or information classification.
compliance_steps.evidence: Review schedules; updated NDA versions; change management records

compliance_steps.step: Communicate NDA requirements and obligations to all relevant parties through training and periodic awareness sessions.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training records; attendance logs; awareness materials

compliance_steps.step: Monitor compliance and investigate any NDA breaches, taking appropriate disciplinary or contractual action where necessary.
compliance_steps.evidence: Incident logs; investigation reports; remedial action documentation
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Manager, HR Manager, Legal Department

NIST CSF.Description: Access permissions and authorizations are managed, including agreements such as NDAs for access to sensitive information.

GDPR Articles.Description: Requires appropriate safeguards, including contractual clauses (e.g., NDAs) for personnel and processors to ensure confidentiality of personal data.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Workforce security and agreements with business associates to ensure protection and confidentiality of electronic protected health information (ePHI).

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: The entity maintains agreements with personnel and external parties regarding confidentiality and information protection.

title: Remote working
description: Security measures shall be implemented when personnel are working remotely to protect information accessed, processed or stored outside the organizations premises.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 A.6.7 'Remote working' effectively, organizations must address both technical and procedural controls to secure information accessed or processed outside their premises. Start by developing a comprehensive remote work policy that clarifies acceptable use, device requirements, and employee responsibilities. Technical requirements should include the exclusive use of company-managed devices for remote access, with enforced endpoint security measures such as antivirus, disk encryption, and regular patching. Remote access should be restricted to secure channels like VPNs, with multi-factor authentication (MFA) mandatory for all connections. Endpoint configurations should disable local data storage where feasible, and data loss prevention (DLP) solutions should be implemented to monitor and control data transfers. Employees must be trained specifically on remote work risks, including safe use of home networks, identifying phishing attempts, and the dangers of public Wi-Fi. Regular monitoring of remote access logs and proactive review of remote work arrangements are essential for detecting anomalies and ensuring ongoing compliance. All processes must be thoroughly documented, including policies, device inventories, training records, and monitoring logs, to demonstrate compliance during audits. Common pitfalls include failing to keep policies updated as work patterns change, neglecting to enforce technical controls on all devices, inadequate user training, and insufficient monitoring. Avoid using unmanaged or BYOD devices for sensitive work unless robust MDM and security controls are in place. Ensure a feedback mechanism exists so remote staff can report issues or suggest improvements. Regularly review the effectiveness of controls and adapt as new threats to remote working emerge.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and enforce a Remote Work Security Policy that outlines acceptable use of organizational assets, data handling requirements, and security obligations for remote workers.
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved policy document, communication records to staff, employee acknowledgment forms

compliance_steps.step: Require the use of company-managed devices for remote access, ensuring all devices are configured with endpoint protection (antivirus, firewall, disk encryption) and kept up-to-date with security patches.
compliance_steps.evidence: Asset inventory, device configuration records, patch management logs

compliance_steps.step: Mandate the use of secure remote connectivity technologies, such as VPNs with multi-factor authentication (MFA), to access organizational systems from remote locations.
compliance_steps.evidence: VPN configuration documentation, MFA setup logs, access logs

compliance_steps.step: Implement controls to prevent unauthorized access or data leakage, including automatic screen lock, prohibited use of public Wi-Fi without VPN, and restrictions on data transfers to personal devices or cloud storage.
compliance_steps.evidence: System configuration settings, DLP solution logs, user awareness training records

compliance_steps.step: Provide mandatory security awareness training specific to remote working risks (e.g., phishing, secure home network setup) and regularly test user understanding.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training materials, attendance records, quiz results

compliance_steps.step: Monitor and regularly review remote access logs for unusual activity, and have incident response procedures tailored to remote work scenarios.
compliance_steps.evidence: SIEM logs, incident response plans, monitoring reports
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Security Operations, Information Security Manager

compliance_steps.step: Document and periodically review all remote work arrangements to ensure ongoing compliance with security requirements and adapt to changes in risk.
compliance_steps.evidence: Remote work arrangement records, periodic review reports

NIST CSF.PR.AC-3: Remote access is managed, including using secure methods for remote access.
NIST CSF.PR.AC-7: Users, devices, and other assets are authenticated (including MFA) when remote access is used.

GDPR Articles.Article 32: Security of processing, including measures to ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability when processing data remotely.
GDPR Articles.Article 5(1)(f): Principle of integrity and confidentiality, which applies to remote work environments.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.312(e)(1): Transmission Security: Protect ePHI during remote transmission.
HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D): Information System Activity Review: Monitor remote access activity.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC6.2: Authentication and authorization for remote access.
SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC6.7: System operations and monitoring of remote access.

title: Information security event reporting
description: The organization shall provide a mechanism for personnel to report observed or suspected information security events through appropriate channels in a timely manner.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.6.8 effectively, organizations must establish both technical and procedural mechanisms for timely security event reporting. Technically, this requires the deployment of accessible and secure reporting channels such as a dedicated email alias, a web-based reporting form integrated with ticketing systems, or a hotline number. These channels should be protected against misuse and monitored continuously. Processes must be clearly defined in a documented policy detailing what constitutes a reportable event, who is responsible for receiving and triaging reports, and the escalation workflow. All staff must receive regular, targeted training on how to recognize and report security events, with refresher sessions at least annually. Documentation should include the reporting policy, training records, logs of reported events, acknowledgment communications, and reviews of the reporting process. All reports must be logged, acknowledged promptly (within a predefined SLA), and stored securely for an appropriate retention period. Common pitfalls include unclear definitions of what qualifies as a security event, inaccessible or unknown reporting channels, lack of timely follow-up by security personnel, and inadequate protection of incident records. To avoid these, organizations should conduct periodic reviews and testing of reporting mechanisms, actively solicit feedback from users, and ensure robust access controls over incident data. A well-implemented reporting mechanism empowers personnel, enables rapid incident response, and demonstrates proactive compliance with multiple regulatory frameworks.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and implement a documented Information Security Event Reporting Policy that clearly defines what constitutes an information security event, reporting timelines, and escalation procedures.
Establish and publicize dedicated reporting channels (e.g., email address, hotline, web portal, ticketing system) accessible to all personnel for reporting security events.
Train all staff annually on identifying and reporting information security events, including practical examples and step-by-step guidance for using reporting mechanisms.
Implement a process to acknowledge receipt of security event reports within a defined timeframe (e.g., 24 hours) and document all reports in a centralized incident/event management system.
Regularly review and test reporting mechanisms (at least annually) to ensure effectiveness and accessibility, updating processes as necessary based on feedback or lessons learned from incidents.
Maintain logs and records of all reported events, investigations, and outcomes for a defined retention period, ensuring records are protected from unauthorized access or alteration.

GDPR.Description: Obligation to notify the supervisory authority and, where applicable, the data subject of personal data breaches without undue delay.

NIST CSF.Description: Monitoring for security events and ensuring anomalies and events are reported in a timely fashion.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Implement procedures to identify and respond to suspected or known security incidents; mitigate harmful effects of known incidents.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: Processes are in place to identify and report security events and incidents.

title: Physical security perimeters
description: Security perimeters shall be defined and used to protect areas that contain information and other associated assets.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 control A.7.1 requires a multi-layered approach combining physical, technical, and administrative safeguards. Begin by conducting a thorough risk assessment to pinpoint all physical locations where sensitive information and assets reside, such as data centers, communications rooms, and storage archives. Document these areas on detailed floor plans, clearly delineating the security perimeters. Technical measures should include the installation of robust physical barriers—such as reinforced doors, badge-controlled entry systems, CCTV surveillance, and intrusion alarms—at all entry and exit points. All access to secure areas must be strictly controlled, with access rights granted based on job role and regularly reviewed for appropriateness. Implement an access authorization workflow, ensuring that all requests are formally approved and documented, and that access logs (electronic or manual) are maintained and subject to regular review for anomalies. Place clear signage to demarcate restricted areas and reinforce security awareness. Complement these controls with regular staff training and drills covering both routine procedures and emergency response. All procedures, asset lists, access logs, and review records must be kept up-to-date and available for audit. Common pitfalls include poorly documented perimeters, outdated access rights, lack of signage, and failure to monitor or review access logs. Avoid relying solely on electronic controls—layering procedural and physical barriers is essential for effective perimeter security.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct a physical security risk assessment to identify areas containing sensitive information and associated assets.
Define and document physical security perimeters for each identified area (e.g., data centers, server rooms, document storage).
evidenceRequirements: Facility floor plans with marked boundaries

compliance_steps.step: Implement physical barriers (e.g., locked doors, badge readers, security gates, CCTV) to control and monitor access to defined perimeters.
evidenceRequirements: Photos or records of physical barriers installed

compliance_steps.step: Establish and enforce access authorization processes for entry to secure perimeters, including regular review and approval of access rights.
Post clear signage indicating restricted access areas and security requirements at all perimeter entry points.
Monitor and log entry/exit to secure perimeters using electronic or manual logs, and review logs regularly for unauthorized access attempts.
Train all relevant personnel on physical security policies and emergency procedures related to security perimeters.

GDPR.Article 32(1)(b): Implement measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, including physical access controls.

NIST CSF.PR.AC-2: Physical access to assets is managed and protected.
NIST CSF.PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.310(a)(1): Facility Access Controls - policies and procedures to limit physical access to electronic information systems and the facility.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC6.6: Logical and physical access controls are implemented to protect against unauthorized access.
SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC6.7: Procedures ensure only authorized access to sensitive information.

title: Storage media
description: Storage media shall be managed through their life cycle of acquisition, use, transportation and disposal in accordance with the organizations classification scheme and handling requirements.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.7.10, organizations must approach storage media management as a comprehensive life cycle process. Technically, all storage media—whether physical (e.g., hard drives, USBs, tapes) or virtual (e.g., cloud storage volumes)—should be tracked from acquisition through disposal. This requires robust inventory systems, logical and physical access controls (including encryption for classified/sensitive data), and secure configuration baselines. Processes must address the secure handling, transportation, and storage of media, with clear chain-of-custody procedures for media movement and tamper-evident packaging where risk warrants. For end-of-life, organizations should use industry-approved data destruction methods (e.g., cryptographic erase, degaussing, shredding) and ensure that destruction is witnessed and documented. Documentation is key: policies, asset registers, chain-of-custody logs, destruction certificates, and training records must all be maintained and regularly reviewed for accuracy. Common pitfalls include incomplete asset inventories, failure to align handling with data classification, inadequate erasure before media reuse or disposal, and lack of staff training. Regular audits and testing of procedures can identify these gaps. Finally, organizations should ensure that outsourced disposal vendors comply with agreed standards and provide evidence of secure destruction. Robust media management reduces the risk of data leakage and supports compliance with multiple regulatory frameworks.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document a storage media management policy aligned with the organization's classification scheme, covering acquisition, usage, transportation, and disposal.
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved policy document, version history, communication records to staff
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Manager, IT Asset Manager

compliance_steps.step: Maintain an inventory of all storage media (including hard drives, USBs, backup tapes, cloud storage devices), tracking ownership, location, classification, and life cycle status.
compliance_steps.evidence: Up-to-date storage media inventory, asset tracking logs

compliance_steps.step: Implement access controls and encryption for sensitive data stored on media according to data classification requirements; regularly review access rights.
compliance_steps.evidence: Access control lists, encryption configuration screenshots, periodic access review records

compliance_steps.step: Develop and enforce secure procedures for the transport of storage media, including physical protection, chain-of-custody documentation, and tamper-evident packaging where required.

title: Supporting utilities
description: Information processing facilities shall be protected from power failures and other disruptions caused by failures in supporting utilities.
guidance: Implementing the 'Supporting Utilities' control requires a holistic approach to safeguarding information processing facilities against failures in power, water, HVAC, and other essential services. Technically, organizations must deploy redundant power solutions, such as UPS and generators for critical infrastructure, and ensure HVAC and fire suppression systems are robust and regularly maintained. Process-wise, a documented contingency and recovery plan should be established, detailing steps for responding to utility outages, escalation protocols, and routine system testing. Continuous monitoring for utility status using sensors and automated alerts is crucial for early detection and swift response. Documentation should include risk assessments, utility provider contracts, maintenance logs, test records, and staff training materials. Common pitfalls include failing to regularly test backup systems, neglecting updates to response procedures, insufficient staff training, and overlooking dependencies on third-party utility providers. Organizations should also avoid over-reliance on a single utility source and ensure all supporting utilities are considered in their risk profile. Proper evidence collection—such as test outcomes and incident logs—is vital for audit readiness and compliance verification. Regular review and improvement of controls, informed by past incidents and changing facility requirements, will further strengthen resilience against utility disruptions.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct a risk assessment to identify all supporting utilities (e.g., electricity, water, HVAC, internet) critical to information processing facilities.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Risk assessment report listing critical utilities and associated risks.

compliance_steps.step: Implement uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and backup generators for critical systems to ensure continuity during power failures.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Installation records, maintenance logs, UPS/generator specifications.

compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Training attendance records, training materials, completion certificates.

title: Cabling security
description: Cables carrying power, data or supporting information services shall be protected from interception, interference or damage.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 A.7.12 (Cabling Security), organizations must take a holistic approach encompassing technical, process, and documentation requirements. Technically, all data and power cables, especially those supporting critical operations or sensitive information, should be routed through secure, access-controlled pathways such as conduits, raised floors, or locked cable trays. Physical protections like tamper-evident covers and lockable cabinets can further reduce the risk of interception or damage. Cables should be clearly labeled to minimize the risk of accidental disconnects and facilitate rapid troubleshooting. From a process perspective, organizations should establish a maintenance and inspection schedule (at minimum, annually) to proactively identify any signs of wear, unauthorized access, or interference. Access to cabling infrastructure should be tightly controlled and restricted to authorized personnel—this includes monitoring with access logs and periodic reviews of authorization lists. Comprehensive documentation is critical: maintain up-to-date cable inventories, diagrams of cable routes, access authorization lists, and records of inspections and incidents. Common pitfalls to avoid include relying solely on initial cable installation security (without ongoing checks), inadequate labeling, and failing to update documentation after changes. Organizations should also ensure that response procedures for physical breaches or cable faults are clearly documented and communicated to relevant staff. By combining these measures, organizations can significantly reduce the risk of interception, interference, or damage to cabling infrastructure, supporting overall information security and compliance objectives.

compliance_steps.evidence: Inventory list of all identified cables with locations and types

compliance_steps.evidence: Inspection and maintenance logs, incident reports

compliance_steps.evidence: Access control records, list of authorized personnel

compliance_steps.evidence: Incident response procedures, training records, incident logs

title: Equipment maintenance
description: Equipment shall be maintained correctly to ensure availability, integrity and confidentiality of information.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.7.13 (Equipment maintenance) effectively, organizations must take a structured approach that integrates both technical and procedural safeguards. Technically, maintain a comprehensive inventory of all information processing equipment, ensuring each asset is uniquely identified and classified based on criticality. Schedule regular preventive maintenance in accordance with manufacturer recommendations and the organization's risk assessment, ensuring all maintenance tasks are logged with details such as date, personnel, and actions taken. Access to equipment during maintenance should be tightly controlled: only authorized, vetted personnel should perform maintenance, and third-party service providers must sign NDAs and adhere to organizational security requirements. To protect information during maintenance, implement measures such as disabling user access, encrypting sensitive data, or using temporary, supervised access. All maintenance activities, including repairs and updates, should be documented in a centralized system. Review maintenance records periodically to spot trends, recurring issues, or potential vulnerabilities. Update inventory and configuration records after significant maintenance. Common pitfalls include failing to document ad-hoc maintenance, neglecting to vet third-party technicians, or not updating asset records post-maintenance, which can lead to gaps in security and compliance. Ensure procedures are audited regularly, and maintenance documentation is readily available for compliance reviews or incident investigations.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and maintain an inventory of all information processing equipment, including hardware, network devices, storage media, and critical peripherals.
compliance_steps.evidence: Up-to-date equipment inventory records; asset management system exports.

compliance_steps.step: Establish a documented preventive and corrective maintenance schedule for all equipment based on manufacturer recommendations and criticality assessments.
compliance_steps.evidence: Maintenance schedules; signed service level agreements (SLAs); maintenance logs.

compliance_steps.step: Ensure maintenance activities are performed by authorized personnel only, with background checks and non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) in place for third-party service providers.
compliance_steps.evidence: Access logs; staff training records; signed NDAs; vendor agreements.

compliance_steps.step: Document all maintenance actions, including date, type of service, personnel involved, and any discovered issues or corrective actions taken.
compliance_steps.evidence: Maintenance logs; service reports; ticketing system records.

title: Secure disposal or re-use of equipment
description: Items of equipment containing storage media shall be verified to ensure that any sensitive data and licensed software has been removed or securely overwritten prior to disposal or re-use.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.7.14, organizations must establish a comprehensive program for the secure disposal and re-use of equipment containing storage media. Technically, this requires the use of validated data destruction methods such as cryptographic erasure, degaussing, physical shredding, or certified software overwriting tools that ensure all sensitive data (including licensed software) is irretrievably removed prior to asset disposal or re-allocation. Procedures should clearly define steps for identifying equipment, performing data removal, and verifying destruction or overwriting using standardized checklists. All actions must be documented, including asset IDs, disposal dates, methods used, and the individuals responsible. Third-party vendors used for offsite destruction must provide certificates of destruction aligned with recognized standards. Training must be provided to all personnel involved in equipment handling, ensuring awareness of risks and procedures. Regular audits should be performed to validate compliance and identify any lapses. Common pitfalls include failing to verify the effectiveness of data destruction, neglecting to update asset inventories, inadequate documentation, and relying on unvetted third-party vendors. Avoid these by enforcing strict verification steps, maintaining detailed records, and periodically reviewing both procedures and vendor agreements. Proper implementation not only reduces risk of data leakage but also demonstrates regulatory compliance during audits.

compliance_steps.step: Maintain an inventory of all equipment containing storage media (e.g., servers, laptops, USB drives, smartphones) within the organization.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Updated asset inventory list with unique IDs and assigned custodians.

title: Physical entry
description: Secure areas shall be protected by appropriate entry controls to ensure that only authorized personnel are allowed access.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.7.2 (Physical entry), organizations must deploy a combination of technical and procedural safeguards to ensure only authorized personnel access secure areas. Technically, this entails installing robust access control mechanisms such as electronic badge readers, biometric authentication, or PIN-based locks at all entry points. These systems should be integrated with centralized access management software to automate permissions and maintain detailed access logs. Process-wise, organizations must establish and routinely update access authorization lists, ensuring only those with a legitimate business need are approved. Visitor access should be tightly controlled, requiring sign-in procedures, temporary badges, and staff escorts. Documentation is critical: maintain records of access authorizations, visitor logs, incident reports, and periodic audits. Regularly review access logs to identify suspicious activity and enforce prompt revocation of access for departing or role-changing staff. Common pitfalls include failing to update access permissions in a timely manner, neglecting to monitor access logs, and relying solely on manual sign-in sheets, which are less reliable and audit-friendly. Organizations must also avoid ambiguous policies—clear, standardized procedures and regular staff training are essential. By combining technical controls with well-documented, enforced processes, organizations can robustly safeguard their secure areas against unauthorized physical entry, supporting compliance and reducing risk.

compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Access control system deployment records, photographs of installed devices, vendor contracts

title: Securing offices, rooms and facilities
description: Physical security for offices, rooms and facilities shall be designed and implemented.
guidance: Implementing control A.7.3 requires a balanced approach combining physical safeguards, technical systems, and well-defined processes. Organizations should start by conducting a thorough physical security risk assessment to identify vulnerable areas and prioritize protection of sensitive zones (e.g., server rooms, records storage). Technical requirements include deploying robust access control mechanisms (electronic locks, badge systems, biometrics), surveillance systems to monitor entry/exit points, and alarm systems for intrusion detection. Processes must cover visitor management, equipment storage, regular inspections and maintenance of security systems, and incident response procedures for physical breaches. All procedures should be documented in physical security policies, facility security plans, visitor management protocols, and maintenance logs. Staff training is essential to ensure employees understand their roles in maintaining physical security and reporting incidents. Common pitfalls include failing to regularly update access permissions, neglecting to audit access logs, inadequate surveillance coverage, and insufficient documentation. Avoid relying solely on technology without supporting procedures or neglecting employee awareness. Regular reviews and audits of controls, combined with evidence collection (logs, reports, inspection records), ensure ongoing compliance and readiness for external assessments.

Implement access controls such as key cards, biometric systems, or PIN codes to restrict entry to authorized personnel only.

Establish procedures for visitor management, including visitor sign-in/sign-out, visitor badges, and escort requirements.
Ensure all physical security controls (doors, windows, locks, alarm systems) are regularly inspected, tested, and maintained.
Define and enforce a clean desk policy and secure storage requirements for sensitive equipment and information.
Train employees on physical security procedures, including reporting suspicious activity and emergency protocols.

title: Physical security monitoring
description: Premises shall be continuously monitored for unauthorized physical access.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.7.4, organizations must combine robust technical security with well-defined processes and thorough documentation. Technically, deploy physical access control systems (card readers, biometrics, PIN pads) at all entry/exit points and sensitive areas. Integrate these systems with centralized logging to capture every access event, ideally with timestamps and user identification. Complement access controls with continuous video surveillance (CCTV), ensuring coverage of all critical zones and secure storage of footage for a defined retention period. Process-wise, establish clear procedures for onboarding/offboarding staff with access rights, regularly review and update authorized personnel lists, and set up automated alerting for unauthorized or out-of-hours access attempts. Conduct quarterly audits of access logs and video footage to verify compliance and detect anomalies. Documentation should cover all aspects—system configurations, access lists, audit findings, incident responses, and staff training records on physical security protocols. Avoid common pitfalls: not monitoring secondary exits, failing to regularly review logs, neglecting updates to access rights, or keeping unclear documentation. Ensure staff are aware of incident reporting procedures and that all physical security policies are easily accessible. By combining technology, process discipline, and strong documentation, you can maintain a robust physical security monitoring posture that satisfies regulatory and audit requirements.
