title: Protecting against physical and environmental threats
description: Protection against physical and environmental threats, such as natural disasters and other intentional or unintentional physical threats to infrastructure shall be designed and implemented.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 control A.7.5 requires organizations to systematically safeguard their physical infrastructure from both natural and human-driven threats. Technically, this involves deploying robust access control systems—such as card readers, biometrics, and CCTV—to restrict entry to data centers and other critical areas. Environmental controls, including fire suppression systems, flood detection sensors, HVAC monitoring, and smoke alarms, must be tailored to the specific risks identified in a formal risk assessment. Process-wise, organizations should establish documented emergency response and evacuation procedures, regularly train staff through drills, and maintain up-to-date incident response plans. All controls should be supported by a regular maintenance and testing schedule, with logs and reports kept for audit purposes. Documentation is a key compliance requirement: maintain risk assessments, access policies, system maintenance and testing records, emergency plans, and logs of physical access or monitoring reviews. Common pitfalls include neglecting to update controls following facility changes, failing to test emergency systems regularly, or lacking evidence of implementation and review. Organizations should also ensure that roles and responsibilities for physical and environmental security are clearly assigned and communicated. Regular reviews and updates to controls are essential, especially after incidents or changes to physical infrastructure, to maintain compliance and minimize risks.

title: Working in secure areas
description: Security measures for working in secure areas shall be designed and implemented.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 Control A.7.6 requires organizations to establish robust physical and procedural safeguards for secure areas where sensitive information or critical assets are processed or stored. Technically, this involves installing physical controls such as access card readers, biometric authentication, CCTV surveillance, intrusion alarms, and environmental protections (e.g., fire suppression, climate controls). Process requirements include defining and documenting clear access procedures, including visitor management, regular access reviews, and emergency response protocols. Access to secure areas should be strictly limited to authorized personnel, with continuous monitoring and periodic audits to ensure compliance. Documentation is critical: maintain up-to-date secure area policies, access logs, visitor logs, training records, and incident reports. Common pitfalls to avoid include failing to update access rights when personnel change roles, neglecting regular reviews of physical security measures, and overlooking the importance of staff training. Additionally, inadequate documentation or poor incident response can undermine the effectiveness of secure area controls. Regular testing, staff awareness campaigns, and integration of physical controls with logical access management systems are recommended to strengthen the overall security posture.

title: Clear desk and clear screen
description: Clear desk rules for papers and removable storage media and clear screen rules for information processing facilities shall be defined and appropriately enforced.
guidance: A robust Clear Desk and Clear Screen program requires both technical measures and user-driven processes to limit unauthorized access to sensitive information. Technically, organizations should configure all workstations and devices to automatically lock screens after a short period of inactivity (e.g., 5-10 minutes) using centralized management tools (like Group Policy for Windows or MDM for Macs). Physical security controls must be in place, such as lockable drawers, restricted access to printer/copier areas, and secure shredding for document disposal. Employees should be trained to clear their desks of all sensitive papers and removable media (e.g., USB drives) at the end of each working day or when leaving their workspace for extended periods. The policy should explicitly define what must be secured and how to handle exceptions (e.g., in shared environments). Document the policy, communicate it regularly, and have all users acknowledge it. Conduct spot checks and regular audits for compliance, and document findings. Common pitfalls include unclear definitions of what constitutes 'sensitive' material, lack of follow-through on audit findings, and insufficient technical enforcement (e.g., screens not set to auto-lock). Ensure disciplinary procedures are in place and consistently enforced to maintain a strong security culture. Maintain evidence of training, audits, and corrective actions for auditability and ongoing compliance. Regularly review and update the policy to adapt to changing risks or business processes.

compliance_steps.evidence: Incident records; documentation of disciplinary actions taken

title: Equipment siting and protection
description: Equipment shall be sited securely and protected.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.7.8, organizations must ensure that all critical equipment is sited in secure, access-controlled areas. This requires a comprehensive approach that combines technical, procedural, and administrative safeguards. Begin by conducting a physical and environmental risk assessment to identify potential threats such as unauthorized access, theft, fire, water damage, or environmental extremes. Based on this assessment, physically locate equipment in areas that are not easily accessible to unauthorized personnel—preferably away from windows, external doors, and environmental hazards. Secure these areas using locked rooms, cages, or biometric access controls as warranted by risk. Install environmental controls such as temperature and humidity monitoring, fire suppression, and water leak detection to mitigate non-human threats. Maintain a detailed inventory of all equipment, noting exact placement and any movement. Document all procedures related to equipment placement, access, and protection, and ensure staff are trained on these protocols. Regularly inspect sites for compliance, and perform maintenance on all physical and environmental security systems. Avoid common pitfalls such as failing to update equipment inventories, neglecting environmental controls, or relying solely on physical locks without regular review and testing. Comprehensive documentation and audit trails are essential to demonstrate compliance and support continuous improvement in equipment protection.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct a risk assessment to identify threats to the physical environment and equipment.
compliance_steps.evidence: Completed risk assessment report, risk register documenting identified threats and vulnerabilities.

compliance_steps.step: Site critical equipment (e.g., servers, network devices) in secure areas with restricted access; use locked rooms or cages where appropriate.
compliance_steps.evidence: Access control logs, floor plans showing secure areas, photos of locked rooms/cages.

compliance_steps.step: Install environmental controls (e.g., temperature, humidity monitoring, fire suppression, water leak detection) to protect equipment from environmental hazards.
compliance_steps.evidence: Maintenance records, sensor logs, system configuration documentation.

compliance_steps.step: Ensure equipment is not placed near hazards such as windows, external walls, or water sources to reduce risk of theft or environmental damage.
compliance_steps.evidence: Equipment placement diagrams, site inspection reports, photographic evidence.

compliance_steps.step: Implement regular inspections and maintenance of security and environmental controls for all equipment locations.
compliance_steps.evidence: Inspection and maintenance logs, incident reports, maintenance schedules.

compliance_steps.step: Maintain an up-to-date inventory of all critical equipment and its physical location.
compliance_steps.evidence: Asset inventory records, physical inventory checklists.

compliance_steps.step: Document and enforce policies and procedures for equipment siting, access, and protection.
compliance_steps.evidence: Published policy documents, training records, staff acknowledgement forms.

title: Security of assets off-premises
description: Off-site assets shall be protected.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.7.9 (Security of assets off-premises), organizations must adopt a holistic approach encompassing technical, procedural, and documentation requirements. Begin by establishing and maintaining a comprehensive inventory of all assets likely to leave the organization’s premises, such as laptops, mobile devices, removable media, and paper records, capturing details such as asset owner, data classification, and physical location. All off-premises assets handling sensitive or critical data should be encrypted (e.g., full-disk encryption for laptops), protected by strong authentication (complex passwords, MFA), and physically secured when not in use (lockable cases, cable locks). Formalize policies outlining the conditions for asset use, transport, and storage off-site, with mandatory reporting procedures for lost or stolen assets. Ensure all employees receive regular training and acknowledge their responsibilities regarding off-premises asset security. Periodic audits and spot checks should be performed to validate compliance, and all incidents involving off-premises assets should be logged, reviewed, and used to improve controls. Document all related processes, inventory updates, policy communications, training, and incident reports for evidence during audits. Common pitfalls include failing to keep inventories up to date, neglecting asset classification, overlooking employee training, and not enforcing encryption or secure disposal processes. To maintain compliance, regularly review and update controls in response to emerging threats and organizational changes.

compliance_steps.step: Maintain and regularly update an inventory of all off-premises assets, including asset type, owner, location, and business purpose.
compliance_steps.evidence: Updated asset inventory records with asset details and location history.

compliance_steps.step: Classify off-premises assets according to their data sensitivity and criticality to determine required security controls.
compliance_steps.evidence: Asset classification register with assigned sensitivity levels.

compliance_steps.step: Implement physical and logical security controls for off-premises assets (e.g., device encryption, strong authentication, cable locks, GPS tracking for high-value assets).
compliance_steps.evidence: Configuration records (encryption enabled), device logs, photographs of physical controls.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and communicate clear policies for the use, transport, and storage of off-premises assets, including procedures for loss, theft, or incident response.
compliance_steps.evidence: Published policies, training records, employee acknowledgements.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Policy Manager, HR, Information Security Officer

compliance_steps.step: Conduct periodic audits or spot checks on off-premises assets to verify their location, condition, and compliance with security requirements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit reports, spot check logs, exception and remediation records.

compliance_steps.step: Ensure secure disposal or return of off-premises assets at the end of their lifecycle or upon employee departure.
compliance_steps.evidence: Disposal certificates, return checklists, exit procedure records.

compliance_steps.step: Monitor and review incidents involving off-premises assets, and update controls or policies based on lessons learned.
compliance_steps.evidence: Incident logs, post-incident review documentation, updated policies.

title: User endpoint devices
description: Information stored on, processed by or accessible via user endpoint devices shall be protected.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.1 effectively, organizations must take a comprehensive and multi-layered approach to endpoint device security. Technically, all endpoint devices (laptops, desktops, mobile devices, tablets) that store, process, or access organizational information should have robust endpoint security software (antivirus, anti-malware, endpoint detection and response) installed and kept up-to-date. Encryption should be enforced on all devices to protect data at rest, and strong user authentication—ideally multi-factor authentication (MFA)—should be mandated for device access. Regular patch management processes should ensure timely updates of operating systems and applications, reducing vulnerability exposure. From a process perspective, establish clear policies on acceptable use, device management, and software installation, and communicate these to all users. Maintain a detailed inventory of endpoint devices, updating it with every onboarding or decommissioning event. Monitoring should be continuous, leveraging centralized logging or SIEM to detect and respond to suspicious activity. Documentation is key: maintain evidence of technical configurations, inventory records, policy acknowledgments, and incident response actions. Common pitfalls to avoid include inconsistent device enrollment, lack of visibility into BYOD (bring your own device) usage, failure to enforce encryption or updates, and inadequate response to security alerts. Regularly review both technical controls and processes to ensure coverage as new device types or use cases emerge.

compliance_steps.step: Deploy and configure endpoint protection software (e.g., antivirus, anti-malware, EDR) on all user endpoint devices.
compliance_steps.evidence: Deployment reports, configuration screenshots, and license records.

compliance_steps.step: Enforce device encryption (e.g., BitLocker, FileVault) for all laptops, desktops, and mobile devices storing or accessing organizational data.
compliance_steps.evidence: Encryption policy, device audit logs, and encryption status reports.

compliance_steps.step: Implement and require strong authentication mechanisms (e.g., passwords, MFA) for accessing endpoint devices.
compliance_steps.evidence: Authentication configuration, MFA enrollment logs, and access control policy.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Security and HR (for policy communication)

compliance_steps.step: Apply regular security updates and patches to operating systems and applications on all endpoint devices, with automated update mechanisms where feasible.
compliance_steps.evidence: Patch management logs, update schedules, and compliance dashboards.

compliance_steps.step: Restrict installation of unauthorized software and enforce application whitelisting where possible.
compliance_steps.evidence: Application whitelisting policy, device audit logs, and exception request records.

compliance_steps.step: Monitor endpoint devices for suspicious activity and respond promptly to detected threats.
compliance_steps.evidence: Monitoring tool logs, incident response tickets, and investigation reports.

compliance_steps.step: Maintain an up-to-date inventory of all endpoint devices accessing organizational information.
compliance_steps.evidence: Asset inventory records, device enrollment logs, and periodic reconciliation reports.

GDPR.Article 25: Data protection by design and by default.
GDPR.Article 32: Security of processing: Organizations must implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including encryption of personal data.

title: Information deletion
description: Information stored in information systems, devices or in any other storage media shall be deleted when no longer required.
guidance: To comply with ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.10, organizations must establish a comprehensive, risk-based process for deleting information from systems, devices, and all forms of storage media when it is no longer required. Technically, this involves configuring automated retention mechanisms within all relevant applications and storage systems to identify data eligible for deletion, and implementing secure deletion methods such as cryptographic erasure, overwriting, or degaussing for both digital and physical media. Where possible, deletion should be automated to reduce human error, but manual verification steps must be included for high-risk data or exceptional cases. Process-wise, the organization should define and document retention periods for all data types in line with legal, regulatory, and business requirements, ensuring this is reflected in a formal Data Retention and Deletion Policy. Regular audits and reviews are essential to verify the effectiveness of deletion processes and identify gaps or failures. Documentation is critical: maintain detailed logs of all deletion events, including what was deleted, by whom, when, and how, along with periodic audit and training records. Common pitfalls include neglecting backup and archive copies, failing to update retention schedules, inadequate deletion methods (e.g., only deleting file pointers), and insufficient oversight of third-party or cloud environments. To mitigate these, include all data repositories and third-party services in the scope, validate deletion methods, and regularly review contracts and technical controls. Ensuring robust training and ongoing monitoring will help embed secure deletion practices organization-wide.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document a Data Retention and Deletion Policy specifying data types, retention periods, and secure deletion methods.
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved policy document and version history
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Data Protection Officer, IT Security Manager

compliance_steps.step: Configure all information systems and devices to flag and identify data that is due for deletion based on retention schedules.
compliance_steps.evidence: System configuration screenshots, retention schedule logs

compliance_steps.step: Implement secure deletion mechanisms (e.g., cryptographic erasure, multiple overwriting, degaussing) for all storage media, both onsite and offsite.
compliance_steps.evidence: Tool configurations, deletion logs, process documentation

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and audit deletion actions to ensure compliance with policy and technical effectiveness of deletion methods.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit reports, deletion logs, exception reports

compliance_steps.step: Train all relevant staff on secure deletion procedures and the importance of following retention schedules.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training records, attendance logs, training materials

compliance_steps.evidence: Contract clauses, vendor attestations, third-party audit results

title: Data masking
description: Data masking shall be used in accordance with the organizations topic-specific policy on access control.
guidance: Effective implementation of ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.11 (Data Masking) requires a combination of technical solutions, robust processes, and thorough documentation. Technically, organizations should utilize data masking techniques such as tokenization, redaction, or substitution within databases, applications, and data exports to ensure that sensitive data elements (like payment card numbers, national IDs, or health data) are obfuscated for users who do not require access to the full data. Masking should be applied both in production and non-production environments to prevent inadvertent exposure during development, testing, or analytics. From a process perspective, data masking must be governed by a documented policy that defines which data is masked, under what circumstances, and who may access original versus masked data. Access management processes should enforce that only authorized individuals with a legitimate business need can view unmasked data, while all others see masked values. Documentation should include the data masking policy, system inventories indicating where masking is applied, technical configuration records, and audit logs of access and masking activity. Regular reviews and technical validation are essential to ensure controls remain effective, especially as systems or data flows change. Common pitfalls include relying on manual masking, which is error-prone; failing to mask data in non-production environments; not updating masking as new data types are added; and lacking ongoing monitoring. Avoid these by automating masking, integrating with access control solutions, and embedding masking requirements into system development and procurement processes.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and document a data masking policy aligned with the organization's access control policy, specifying types of data to be masked, masking techniques, and applicable systems.
Perform a data inventory and classification to identify all systems and datasets containing sensitive information that require masking.
Implement data masking controls in relevant applications, databases, and reporting tools based on defined masking techniques (e.g., tokenization, character substitution, redaction).
Restrict access to unmasked data only to authorized personnel with a documented business need, and configure systems to provide masked data to all other users.
Test and validate that data masking controls are functioning as intended through periodic reviews and technical testing (e.g., test queries, application walkthroughs).
Train relevant staff on data masking procedures, the importance of masked data, and their responsibilities for handling masked and unmasked data.
Maintain ongoing monitoring and review of data masking effectiveness, updating controls and policies as new systems and data types are introduced.

title: Data leakage prevention
description: Data leakage prevention measures shall be applied to systems, networks and any other devices that process, store or transmit sensitive information.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.12 (Data leakage prevention), organizations must adopt a holistic approach that combines technical, procedural, and organizational measures. Technically, deploy Data Loss Prevention (DLP) solutions across endpoints, email servers, and network gateways, ensuring these tools are properly configured to monitor, detect, and block unauthorized data transfers based on your data classification scheme. Integrate DLP with existing security infrastructure (SIEM, IAM, etc.) for centralized monitoring and alerting. From a process perspective, establish and document clear DLP policies, including definitions of sensitive data, channels to be monitored, exception handling, and escalation protocols. Regularly review and update these policies in line with new business requirements and evolving threats. Conduct periodic DLP effectiveness tests and simulated data leakage scenarios to ensure readiness and continuous improvement. Employee awareness is crucial: provide targeted training so staff understand data handling responsibilities and how to recognize/report data leakage attempts. Document all DLP activities, including policy approvals, incident investigations, and training records, to demonstrate compliance. Common pitfalls include over-reliance on technology without robust processes, failure to keep DLP policies up to date, insufficient user training, and not monitoring less obvious data exfiltration vectors (e.g., cloud apps, removable media). Avoid these by adopting a layered, well-documented approach and ensuring ongoing oversight and accountability.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct a data classification exercise to identify and label all sensitive information stored, processed, or transmitted across systems, networks, and devices.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Data classification register; documented data flow diagrams; sample screenshots of labeling in systems

compliance_steps.step: Deploy and configure a Data Loss Prevention (DLP) solution across endpoints, email, and network gateways to monitor and control the movement of sensitive data.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: DLP solution deployment records; configuration screenshots; DLP policy settings

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document DLP policies that define acceptable use, alert thresholds, and automated response actions for various data types and channels.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: DLP policy documents; logs of policy approval; policy change history

compliance_steps.step: Regularly test and review the effectiveness of DLP controls through periodic simulated data leakage scenarios and incident response drills.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Test results reports; incident simulation logs; corrective action records

compliance_steps.step: Provide recurring, role-based training to staff on DLP controls, data handling procedures, and how to recognize and report potential data leakage incidents.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Training attendance logs; training materials; quiz/test results

compliance_steps.step: Monitor DLP alerts and data movement logs on an ongoing basis, and investigate anomalies promptly as per the incident response plan.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: DLP alert logs; investigation reports; incident tickets
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Security Operations Center (SOC), IT Security Team

compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Incident log register; root cause analysis reports; post-incident review records

title: Information backup
description: Backup copies of information, software and systems shall be maintained and regularly tested.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.13 (Information backup) effectively, organizations must establish a robust approach that includes technical, procedural, and documentation elements. First, systematically identify all data, software, and systems that are business-critical or contain sensitive information. Classify these assets to determine backup priority and regulatory requirements. Develop detailed, approved procedures specifying what data is backed up, how often (e.g., daily incrementals, weekly fulls), retention periods, and storage methods (onsite, offsite, or in compliant cloud environments). Use automated backup tools configured to encrypt data both in transit and at rest, ensuring only authorized personnel can access backup media or files. Regularly monitor backup jobs for failures and set up alerts for anomalies. Test backup restoration at least quarterly to confirm that data can be recovered, documenting each test and addressing any failures or gaps promptly. Document all backup configurations, schedules, test results, and access logs. Review backup policies annually or whenever there are significant system, business, or regulatory changes. Common pitfalls to avoid include failing to test restorations, neglecting to encrypt backups, not updating backup scopes after system changes, or storing backups in physically or logically insecure locations. Comprehensive documentation and proactive monitoring are essential to demonstrate compliance and ensure organizational resilience.

compliance_steps.step: Identify and classify all information assets, software, and systems that require backup based on business criticality and regulatory requirements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Asset inventory list with classification labels; documented backup scope

compliance_steps.step: Develop and implement documented backup procedures, specifying backup frequency, retention periods, storage locations (onsite/offsite/cloud), and encryption requirements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved backup policy and procedures; policy review logs

compliance_steps.step: Configure automated backup solutions for targeted systems and information, ensuring backups are performed as per defined schedules.
compliance_steps.evidence: Backup configuration screenshots; backup logs showing last run date/time

compliance_steps.step: Secure backup data through encryption in transit and at rest, and restrict access to authorized personnel only.
compliance_steps.evidence: Encryption configuration documentation; access control lists; access logs

compliance_steps.step: Regularly test backup restoration processes (at least quarterly or as per policy) to ensure backup integrity and recoverability.
compliance_steps.evidence: Backup restoration test reports; issue logs; remediation actions

compliance_steps.step: Monitor backup jobs and generate alerts for failures or anomalies, with documented incident response procedures for backup issues.
compliance_steps.evidence: Monitoring dashboard screenshots; incident tickets; resolution documentation

compliance_steps.step: Review and update backup policies and procedures annually, or upon significant changes to the IT environment or regulatory obligations.
compliance_steps.evidence: Policy review schedule; version history; meeting minutes

title: Redundancy of information processing facilities
description: Information processing facilities shall be implemented with redundancy sufficient to meet availability requirements.
guidance: To effectively implement redundancy for information processing facilities per ISO 27001:2022 A.8.14, organizations must first identify all systems critical to business operations through a structured Business Impact Analysis (BIA). Technical requirements include deploying redundant hardware (e.g., dual power supplies, RAID storage), network components (e.g., multiple ISPs, load balancers), and software failover mechanisms (e.g., high-availability clusters, automated replication). Redundancy may also involve geographically distributed data centers for disaster resilience. Process requirements center on maintaining current redundancy policies, conducting regular failover and recovery tests, and integrating redundancy checks into change management workflows. All redundancy architectures, test results, incident responses, and maintenance activities must be meticulously documented, ensuring traceability and audit readiness. Common pitfalls include failing to test redundancy setups regularly, neglecting updates after system changes, incomplete documentation, and lack of staff training—any of which can result in system downtime or failed recovery during incidents. Organizations should also monitor the operational health of redundant systems, proactively addressing issues. By embedding redundancy design and validation into both technical architectures and operational processes—with continuous oversight and improvement—organizations can reliably meet their availability commitments and regulatory obligations.

compliance_steps.step: Perform a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) to identify critical information processing facilities and their required availability levels.
evidenceRequired: List of critical systems with availability requirements

compliance_steps.step: Design and implement redundancy solutions for identified critical facilities, such as clustering, failover systems, or geographically dispersed data centers.
Establish and document redundancy policies and procedures, including failover testing schedules and restoration protocols.
Conduct regular failover and recovery tests (at least annually) to verify redundancy effectiveness and staff readiness.
Monitor the health and status of redundant systems using automated tools and generate periodic reports.
Review and update redundancy configurations and documentation after major system changes, upgrades, or following incidents.
Train relevant personnel on redundancy processes, failover protocols, and incident response related to system availability.

NIST CSF.description: PR.DS-4 (Data-at-rest is protected), PR.DS-5 (Data in transit is protected), PR.IP-9 (Response and recovery plans are tested). Redundancy is directly related to ensuring system availability through failover and backup mechanisms.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.description: CC7.1 (Infrastructure and software are designed to achieve availability objectives), CC7.2 (Backup and disaster recovery procedures meet availability commitments). Directly addresses redundancy and system recovery.

title: Logging
description: Logs that record activities, exceptions, faults and other relevant events shall be produced, stored, protected and analysed.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.15 (Logging) effectively, organizations must establish a comprehensive logging strategy that covers both technical and procedural aspects. Technically, all critical systems—including servers, network devices, applications, and cloud services—should be configured to capture security-relevant events such as authentication attempts, privilege changes, configuration modifications, faults, and exceptions. Logs must be directed to a centralized, secure log management platform that enforces access controls and supports tamper-evident storage (e.g., write-once read-many storage, cryptographically signed logs). Automated log rotation, archival, and retention mechanisms must align with regulatory and business requirements, ensuring logs are preserved for mandated periods and securely deleted thereafter. Process-wise, regular log reviews should be scheduled, with documented procedures for analyzing logs, escalating incidents, and maintaining audit trails of all review activities. Documentation should include a log management policy, system configurations, retention schedules, access logs, and reports of log review activities. Common pitfalls to avoid include logging too much (leading to storage and performance issues), failing to log critical events, inadequate access controls, and neglecting regular review and analysis. Additionally, organizations should ensure logs are protected from unauthorized alteration using hashing or digital signatures and periodically test the entire logging process to validate effectiveness. Regular training and awareness activities for relevant staff are also recommended to sustain compliance and operational effectiveness.

compliance_steps.step: Define logging requirements based on risk assessment, regulatory requirements, and business needs.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Manager, IT Risk Officer
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Documented logging policy specifying events to be logged, retention periods, and access controls.

compliance_steps.step: Configure all critical systems (servers, network devices, applications) to generate logs for security-relevant events (e.g., login attempts, privilege changes, configuration modifications, exceptions, faults).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Screenshots or exported configurations showing enabled logging on systems and applications.

compliance_steps.step: Store logs in a secure, centralized location with restricted access and tamper-evident measures (e.g., write-once storage, log management platforms).
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Infrastructure Team, Security Operations Center (SOC)
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Access control lists, system architecture diagrams, and records of log storage configurations.

compliance_steps.step: Establish log retention policies compliant with legal, regulatory, and business requirements (e.g., retain logs for a minimum of 12 months).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Retention schedule document, automated log rotation and archival settings, deletion logs.

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and analyze logs for suspicious activities, faults, and exceptions, and document the review process.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Security Operations Center (SOC), Incident Response Team
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Log review schedules, incident response logs, tickets, and reports of findings.

compliance_steps.step: Protect log integrity using cryptographic controls, hashing, or digital signatures to detect and prevent unauthorized alteration.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Configuration documentation, integrity verification reports, and logs of integrity checks.

compliance_steps.step: Regularly test the logging process, including log generation, storage, access controls, and analysis workflows.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Internal audit reports, test plans, and remediation records.

NIST CSF.Description: PR.DS-4: Audit/log records are determined, documented, implemented, and reviewed; DE.AE-3: Event detection information is analyzed to understand impacts.

GDPR Articles.Description: Article 32: Security of processing (includes log management for confidentiality, integrity, availability); Recital 39: Accountability and traceability (logging of access).

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: 164.312(b): Audit controls (mechanisms that record and examine activity); 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D): Information system activity review.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: CC6.6: System monitors for unauthorized changes to system components; CC7.2: Processes to detect and monitor anomalous or unauthorized system activity.

title: Monitoring activities
description: Networks, systems and applications shall be monitored for anomalous behaviour and appropriate actions taken.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.16, organizations should deploy robust technical solutions such as Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) systems, intrusion detection/prevention systems, and application monitoring tools. These should be configured to collect comprehensive logs from all key assets—including servers, network devices, databases, and critical applications—and to correlate events for real-time detection of anomalous behaviors. Baseline normal activity patterns for both users and systems, and set alert thresholds for deviations indicating potential security incidents. On the process side, define clear roles and responsibilities for monitoring, incident detection, and response. Create and maintain detailed procedures for responding to alerts, including triage, investigation, escalation, and remediation steps. Regularly update monitoring rules and detection logic in response to emerging threats and lessons learned from previous incidents or near-misses. Documentation is crucial: maintain evidence of monitoring coverage, alerting mechanisms, incident response activities, and periodic reviews of monitoring effectiveness. Retain logs and related records for periods mandated by legal, regulatory, or contractual requirements. Common pitfalls include monitoring too few assets, overwhelming teams with excessive false positives, failing to regularly update detection rules, and neglecting to document monitoring activities. Avoid these by routinely reviewing monitoring scope, fine-tuning alerting rules, and ensuring comprehensive documentation and evidence collection.

compliance_steps.step: Define monitoring scope and assets (networks, systems, applications) to be covered.
compliance_steps.evidence: Asset inventory list, monitoring scope documentation

compliance_steps.step: Deploy and configure Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) or equivalent monitoring tools to collect and analyze security events.
compliance_steps.evidence: SIEM deployment records, configuration screenshots, list of monitored event sources

compliance_steps.step: Establish baseline behaviors for systems and applications to detect anomalies (e.g., user activity, network traffic patterns).
compliance_steps.evidence: Baseline documentation, anomaly detection rules, logs showing baseline establishment

compliance_steps.step: Implement alerting mechanisms for anomalous or suspicious activities, ensuring prompt notification to relevant personnel.
compliance_steps.evidence: Alert configuration files, sample alert notifications, incident response contact list

compliance_steps.step: Develop and document incident response procedures for handling detected anomalies, including roles, responsibilities, and escalation paths.
compliance_steps.evidence: Incident response plan, escalation flowcharts, training records

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and update monitoring rules and thresholds based on evolving threats and lessons learned from incidents.
compliance_steps.evidence: Change logs, meeting minutes, updated monitoring rule sets

compliance_steps.step: Retain monitoring logs and related evidence for a defined period, ensuring compliance with legal and regulatory requirements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Log retention policy, sample stored logs, retention schedules

NIST CSF.description: Continuous monitoring of networks, physical environment, and personnel; monitoring for anomalous activity and potential cybersecurity events.

GDPR Articles.description: Implement processes to regularly test, assess, and evaluate the effectiveness of technical and organizational measures for ensuring the security of processing.

HIPAA Security Rule.description: Implement procedures to regularly review records of information system activity, such as audit logs, access reports, and security incident tracking; audit controls.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.description: Monitor infrastructure and software to identify and address security threats; implement processes to detect and address anomalies.

title: Clock synchronization
description: The clocks of information processing systems used by the organization shall be synchronized to approved time sources.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.17 (Clock synchronization), organizations must ensure that all critical information processing systems—including servers, network infrastructure, security appliances, and key workstations—automatically synchronize their clocks with a set of approved, authoritative time sources (such as national NTP servers or a trusted internal NTP hierarchy). Technically, this involves configuring each system to use secure NTP (Network Time Protocol) settings, enforcing authentication where possible to prevent malicious tampering, and scheduling frequent synchronization intervals to minimize clock drift. Process-wise, organizations should establish clear procedures for monitoring synchronization status, automatically alerting IT personnel if any systems fall out of sync, and promptly remediating detected issues. Documentation is essential: maintain detailed records of approved time sources, configuration settings, monitoring results, and response actions to ensure auditability and facilitate reviews. Common pitfalls to avoid include failing to apply synchronization settings to all relevant devices (especially network appliances), neglecting to monitor synchronization status, using unsecured or unreliable external time sources, or not updating configurations after infrastructure changes. To demonstrate compliance, retain evidence such as configuration files, monitoring logs, alert records, and periodic audit results. By integrating technical controls with robust processes and thorough documentation, organizations can ensure consistency in log data, enable effective incident investigation, and support regulatory requirements for accurate recordkeeping.

compliance_steps.step: Identify all information processing systems (servers, network devices, critical workstations, security appliances) requiring clock synchronization.
compliance_steps.evidence: Asset inventory list with systems marked for clock synchronization

compliance_steps.step: Select and document approved, authoritative time sources (e.g., internal NTP servers, national time servers) for clock synchronization.
compliance_steps.evidence: Time source configuration policy and records of approved sources

compliance_steps.step: Configure all identified systems to synchronize clocks automatically with the approved time sources at defined intervals (e.g., daily or more frequently).
compliance_steps.evidence: Configuration files or screenshots showing NTP settings and synchronization schedules

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document monitoring procedures to regularly verify the status of clock synchronization across all relevant systems.
compliance_steps.evidence: Monitoring logs/reports showing synchronization status, alerts for out-of-sync systems

compliance_steps.step: Implement automated alerts for synchronization failures or significant clock drift to ensure timely remediation.
compliance_steps.evidence: Alert configurations and incident tickets related to detected clock drift

compliance_steps.step: Review and test clock synchronization controls at least annually or after significant changes to infrastructure.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit reports, test results, and records of control reviews

compliance_steps.step: Maintain documentation of clock synchronization settings, monitoring procedures, and incident response actions.
compliance_steps.evidence: Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), change logs, and incident records

NIST CSF.ID.AM-1: Physical devices and systems within the organization are inventoried (supports system identification for synchronization scope).
NIST CSF.PR.PT-1: Audit/log records are determined, documented, implemented, and reviewed; accurate timestamps depend on synchronized clocks.

HIPAA Security Rule.45 CFR §164.308(a)(1)(ii)(D): Information System Activity Review—requires regular review of system activity, supported by accurate time logs.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC7.2: Controls to monitor system components and detect anomalies; synchronized clocks ensure log correlation.
SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC7.3: The entity evaluates security events; accurate logging requires synchronized system clocks.

title: Use of privileged utility programs
description: The use of utility programs that might be capable of overriding system and application controls shall be restricted and tightly controlled.
guidance: Implementing control A.8.18 requires a multi-layered approach that encompasses technical, procedural, and documentation elements. Technically, organizations must identify all privileged utility programs—such as password reset tools, disk editors, or system-level diagnostic programs—and maintain a current inventory. Access to these utilities should be strictly limited via role-based access controls and, where possible, multi-factor authentication. Usage should be monitored, with all executions logged and logs reviewed for anomalies. From a process perspective, establish and enforce a robust change management workflow for the installation, update, or removal of privileged utilities, ensuring that changes are authorized and documented. Regularly review access permissions and the necessity of each utility to maintain a tight security posture. Documentation should include inventories, access control configurations, change management logs, monitoring reports, and training records for authorized users. Common pitfalls include failing to maintain an up-to-date inventory, granting excessive or lingering access rights, not monitoring usage adequately, storing utility programs in insecure locations, and neglecting periodic reviews. Avoid assuming that default system controls are sufficient; regular, proactive management is essential. Additionally, ensure training and awareness for authorized users to minimize mistakes or misuse. By integrating these technical safeguards, process controls, and documentation practices, organizations can effectively mitigate risks associated with privileged utility programs and demonstrate compliance with ISO 27001:2022 and other frameworks.

compliance_steps.step: Identify and inventory all privileged utility programs (e.g., disk editors, debugging tools, password reset utilities) operating on all systems.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Documented inventory list of privileged utilities, updated at least quarterly.

compliance_steps.step: Restrict access to privileged utilities using role-based access controls and limit usage to authorized personnel only.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Security Team / Identity & Access Management Team
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Access control configuration records and user authorization logs.

compliance_steps.step: Implement monitoring and logging of all usage of privileged utility programs, ensuring logs are retained and reviewed regularly.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Security Team / Security Operations Center
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Log files showing usage of utilities, log review reports, and alert records.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and enforce a change management process for any updates to privileged utilities (installation, removal, or configuration changes).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Change request forms, approval records, and implementation logs.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct regular reviews (at least annually) of privileged utility program access and usage to validate continued necessity and appropriateness.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Audit reports, review meeting minutes, and documented actions taken.

compliance_steps.step: Ensure privileged utilities are stored securely and not accessible from general user accounts or public locations.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: System configuration documentation, directory access permissions, and periodic verification records.

compliance_steps.step: Provide training to authorized users on the secure use and risks of privileged utility programs.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Training materials, attendance records, and completion certificates.

title: Installation of software on operational systems
description: Procedures and measures shall be implemented to securely manage software installation on operational systems.
guidance: To securely manage software installation on operational systems, organizations must integrate both technical and process-based controls. Technically, restrict installation privileges using endpoint management and least privilege principles, ensuring only authorized administrators can install or modify software. Employ application whitelisting to block unauthorized software, and enforce software source validation to avoid malware. Process-wise, all installations should require documented approval, including risk assessment and justification, managed through a formal change or service request system. Maintain a comprehensive inventory of installed software, routinely reconcile with authorized lists, and promptly remove any unauthorized applications. Regularly update all software with vendor-released security patches and verify integrity before deployment. Training staff on installation policies and risks is essential to prevent social engineering or accidental violations. Documentation should cover the installation policy, approval records, inventory reports, and audit findings. Common pitfalls include vague policies, excessive installation privileges, lack of inventory management, inadequate patching, and insufficient audit trails. Avoid relying solely on technical controls without supporting policy or process, and ensure that staff understand both the why and how of secure installation. Continuous monitoring, periodic audits, and enforcement of disciplinary measures for violations will maintain compliance and reduce risks associated with unauthorized or vulnerable software installations.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document a formal software installation policy that defines authorized software, approval workflows, and installation restrictions.
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved and published software installation policy; revision history logs
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Manager / IT Governance Team

compliance_steps.step: Implement technical controls to restrict installation rights (e.g., via endpoint management tools, least privilege access, application whitelisting) on operational systems.
compliance_steps.evidence: System configuration reports; access control lists; screenshots of endpoint protection settings

compliance_steps.step: Require and log formal authorization for all software installations, including business justification, risk assessment, and management approval.
compliance_steps.evidence: Completed software installation request forms; approval records; change management tickets

compliance_steps.step: Maintain an up-to-date inventory of all installed software on operational systems, regularly review for unauthorized installations, and reconcile with approved software lists.
compliance_steps.evidence: Software inventory reports; audit logs; unauthorized software removal records

compliance_steps.step: Ensure all installed software is sourced from trusted vendors, verified for integrity, and kept up-to-date with security patches.
compliance_steps.evidence: Vendor verification checklists; patch management logs; software update records

compliance_steps.step: Conduct periodic audits of software installation activities and enforce disciplinary actions for policy violations.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit reports; incident investigation records; corrective action documentation

compliance_steps.step: Provide training to staff on secure software installation procedures and risks associated with unauthorized software.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training attendance logs; training materials; feedback forms

NIST CSF.PR.IP-1: A baseline configuration of information systems is created and maintained (relates to controlling software installation and configuration management).

GDPR Articles.Article 5(1)(f): Integrity and confidentiality - Ensures proper controls against unauthorized access and processing.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(1)(ii)(B): Security Management Process - Risk Management (includes managing risks related to software installation).
