SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC7.2: The entity implements change management processes for system changes (covers formal authorization and logging of software installations).

title: Privileged access rights
description: The allocation and use of privileged access rights shall be restricted and managed.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.2 requires a multi-layered approach that combines technical, procedural, and organizational measures. Technically, organizations should deploy solutions such as RBAC, multi-factor authentication, and session monitoring to restrict and manage privileged access. This includes enforcing strong password policies, segregating duties where feasible, and ensuring all privileged actions are logged and regularly reviewed. Process-wise, establish a formal privileged access management policy detailing the criteria for granting, modifying, and revoking privileged rights, and require documented managerial approval for every privileged access change. Conduct quarterly reviews of privileged account assignments to confirm continued necessity and immediately revoke access when roles change or employment is terminated. On the documentation front, maintain comprehensive records of policies, access requests, approvals, reviews, and training completion. Evidence such as SIEM logs and access control lists should be available for audit. Common pitfalls include failing to regularly review privileged accounts, neglecting to monitor account activity, and not providing adequate training to privileged users. Avoid generic access assignments, shared privileged accounts, and lack of real-time monitoring. By tightly integrating technical controls with robust processes and thorough documentation, organizations can effectively control and evidence compliance with privileged access management requirements.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and maintain a documented privileged access management policy that defines eligibility, approval, monitoring, and revocation procedures for privileged accounts.
Perform a quarterly review of all privileged accounts to verify necessity, appropriateness, and alignment with job roles, and document outcomes.
Implement technical controls such as role-based access control (RBAC), multi-factor authentication (MFA), and session monitoring for all privileged accounts.
Enforce approval workflow for provisioning, modifying, or revoking privileged access, requiring managerial authorization and audit trail maintenance.
Log and monitor all privileged account activities, including access, changes, and attempted breaches, with automated alerts for anomalous behavior.
Restrict privileged access to the minimum necessary, using the principle of least privilege, and immediately revoke access when no longer required.
Provide mandatory annual training for all users with privileged accounts on security responsibilities, acceptable use, and incident reporting.

NIST_CS_F.PR.AC-4: Access permissions and authorizations are managed, incorporating least privilege and separation of duties for privileged accounts.

GDPR_Articles.Art. 32(1)(b): Measures to ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability, including restricting access to personal data to only necessary personnel.

HIPAA_Security_Rule.164.308(a)(4): Information access management—implement policies and procedures for granting access to ePHI, including workforce clearance.

SOC_2_Trust_Service_Criteria.CC6.2: System components are assigned access rights based on job roles, with privileged access restricted and monitored.

title: Networks security
description: Networks and network devices shall be secured, managed and controlled to protect information in systems and applications.
guidance: To robustly implement ISO 27001:2022 A.8.20 (Networks security), organizations must secure, manage, and control all network infrastructure to ensure information protection. Technically, this requires instituting network segmentation to isolate sensitive systems, deploying firewalls and intrusion detection/prevention systems, and enforcing secure configurations on all network devices. Regular vulnerability scanning and prompt patching of firmware and software are essential to mitigate known threats. Process-wise, document and periodically update network inventories and topology diagrams. Establish and follow strict access controls for network devices, including multi-factor authentication for management interfaces. All network changes should be tracked using change management procedures, and incident response plans should address network security breaches. Continuous monitoring—via SIEM or equivalent tools—should capture logs and alert on anomalies. Documentation should include network security policies, device configuration standards, access control lists, incident logs, and evidence of regular reviews and tests, such as backup restoration. Common pitfalls include failing to maintain up-to-date inventories, neglecting segmentation, overlooking patch management, and poorly configured access controls. Avoid reliance on default configurations, unrestricted administrator access, and inadequate monitoring. Regular training for network administrators and periodic audits are vital to sustaining compliance and responding effectively to emerging threats.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct a comprehensive network inventory to identify all network devices, segments, and connections.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Network inventory report; network topology diagrams; asset register updated within last 12 months.

compliance_steps.step: Implement network segmentation to separate critical business systems from general user networks and public-facing services.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Network segmentation policy; VLAN/Firewall configuration documentation; change management records.

compliance_steps.step: Apply secure configuration baselines to all network devices (routers, switches, firewalls), disabling unused services and ports.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Configuration baseline procedures; device configuration files; change logs; configuration audit results.

compliance_steps.step: Regularly monitor and log network traffic for security events, unauthorized access, and anomalies.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Security Operations Center (SOC) / IT Security Analyst
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Network monitoring policy; SIEM/log samples; incident response tickets; evidence of daily/weekly review.

compliance_steps.step: Enforce strong authentication and access controls for network device management interfaces (e.g., SSH, console access).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Access control policy; list of authorized administrators; authentication logs; periodic access reviews.

compliance_steps.step: Ensure regular patching and firmware updates for network devices based on vendor advisories and internal vulnerability assessments.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Operations Team / Patch Management Coordinator
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Patch management records; firmware update logs; vulnerability assessment reports.

compliance_steps.step: Backup network device configurations and test restoration processes at least quarterly.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Operations Team / Disaster Recovery Coordinator
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Backup schedules; backup files; restoration test results; backup policy documentation.

NIST CSF.Description: PR.IP-1: Baseline configuration established and maintained; PR.PT-4: Communications and control networks are protected; PR.AC-5: Network access control implemented.

GDPR Articles.Description: Article 32(1)(b): Ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems; Article 25: Data protection by design and by default.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Technical safeguards for access control, integrity, and transmission security of electronic protected health information.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: CC6.1: Logical access controls; CC6.2: System operation and monitoring; CC6.6: Network security controls.

title: Security of network services
description: Security mechanisms, service levels and service requirements of network services shall be identified, implemented and monitored.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.21, organizations must address both technical and process elements governing network services. Begin with a comprehensive inventory of all network services in use, including internal and external connectivity, cloud interfaces, and remote access solutions. Define explicit security requirements for each service, addressing authentication, encryption, access controls, and resilience. These requirements must be integrated into service level agreements (SLAs) with both internal stakeholders and third-party providers, ensuring accountability for security, availability, and incident response. Technically, deploy robust controls such as firewalls, IDS/IPS, secure VPN configurations, and segment networks where appropriate to limit risk exposure. Ongoing monitoring is essential; leverage SIEM, NMS, or other monitoring platforms to detect anomalous activities, service disruptions, or policy violations. Regularly test network controls through vulnerability scans and penetration testing, documenting findings and remediation steps. Maintain up-to-date documentation covering service inventories, requirements, SLAs, monitoring records, and test results, with at least annual reviews. Common pitfalls include neglecting to update service inventories, failing to specify security requirements in SLAs, and inconsistent monitoring or testing. Avoid relying solely on legacy controls or assuming providers deliver adequate security—validate through evidence and review. Effective implementation hinges on clear responsibility assignments, measurable outcomes, and rigorous documentation supporting ongoing compliance.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct an inventory of all network services (e.g., VPNs, firewalls, MPLS, cloud connectivity) used within the organization.
compliance_steps.evidence: Completed network services inventory document, asset register

compliance_steps.step: Define and document security requirements for each network service, including authentication, encryption, access controls, and monitoring.
compliance_steps.evidence: Network service security requirements specification, approved by relevant stakeholders

compliance_steps.step: Establish and formalize service level agreements (SLAs) with internal teams and external service providers, covering security mechanisms, incident response, and uptime.
compliance_steps.evidence: Signed SLAs and contracts including security clauses

compliance_steps.step: Implement technical security controls such as firewalls, intrusion detection/prevention systems (IDS/IPS), secure VPN configurations, and network segmentation.
compliance_steps.evidence: Network diagrams, configuration files, change logs

compliance_steps.step: Continuously monitor network services for security events, unauthorized access, and performance against SLAs using automated tools and manual review.
compliance_steps.evidence: Monitoring logs, alert records, SLA performance reports

compliance_steps.step: Periodically review and test network service controls and SLAs through vulnerability assessments and penetration testing.
compliance_steps.evidence: Penetration test reports, vulnerability scan results, remediation records

compliance_steps.step: Maintain documentation of network service security requirements, SLAs, monitoring procedures, and testing results, ensuring they are reviewed at least annually.
compliance_steps.evidence: Documented policies, procedures, review meeting minutes

NIST CSF.description: Protective Technology (PR.PT-4): Communications and control networks are protected; Access Control (PR.AC-5): Network integrity is protected.

GDPR Articles.description: Requires implementation of appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including network security.

HIPAA Security Rule.description: Access Control (164.312(a)(1)): Technical policies and procedures for electronic protected health information (ePHI); Transmission Security (164.312(e)(1)): Protects ePHI against unauthorized access during transmission over networks.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.description: CC6.6: Restricts logical access to network services and monitors activity; CC7.1: Monitors infrastructure and controls to detect anomalous activity.

title: Segregation of networks
description: Groups of information services, users and information systems shall be segregated in the organizations networks.
guidance: Effective implementation of network segregation (ISO 27001:2022 A.8.22) requires a multi-layered approach combining technical controls, documented processes, and periodic review. Technically, organizations must use VLANs, firewalls, or similar tools to divide the network into logical segments, ensuring that information services, users, and systems with different security requirements are isolated from one another. Access control lists and firewall rules should strictly limit traffic between segments, with exceptions clearly documented and justified. From a process perspective, ensure a formal change management process is in place so any modifications to network segmentation are reviewed, tested, and approved. Maintain up-to-date network diagrams and segmentation policies in your ISMS, and train relevant staff on the importance and use of segmentation controls. Documentation should include network diagrams, segmentation policies, access control procedures, and monitoring logs. Regular reviews and audits of network segmentation are critical to ensure ongoing effectiveness, particularly as business needs and IT infrastructure change. Common pitfalls include over-permissive segmentation (e.g., 'flat' networks with no isolation), lack of documentation, failing to update configurations as systems evolve, and weak monitoring of inter-segment traffic. Avoid these by implementing strong controls, rigorous documentation, and continuous oversight.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct a network segmentation assessment to identify all groups of information services, users, and systems requiring segregation.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Assessment report, network diagrams, asset inventory

compliance_steps.step: Design and implement VLANs or equivalent network segments for each identified group based on business and security needs.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Updated network topology diagrams, configuration screenshots

compliance_steps.step: Enforce access controls between segments using firewalls, ACLs, or similar technologies to restrict unauthorized inter-segment traffic.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Firewall/ACL rulesets, change management records

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and update segmentation rules and configurations to accommodate changes in business processes or new systems.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Review logs, change review meeting minutes, updated network diagrams

compliance_steps.step: Monitor network traffic between segments for anomalies and unauthorized access attempts using IDS/IPS or SIEM solutions.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Monitoring logs, incident response reports

compliance_steps.step: Document and maintain segmentation policies, procedures, and network diagrams in the information security management system (ISMS).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Policy documents, procedure manuals, ISMS records

compliance_steps.step: Conduct regular (at least annual) audits of network segmentation effectiveness and compliance with defined policies.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Audit reports, remediation plans, audit checklists

GDPR.Description: Implementation of measures to ensure the ongoing confidentiality and integrity of processing systems, including network segmentation as a means to limit access.

NIST CSF.Description: Network integrity is protected; network segmentation is implemented to limit access and contain potential impact of events.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Implementation of security measures sufficient to reduce risks and vulnerabilities; network segmentation as a technical safeguard.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: Logical access security controls restrict access to system components and data based on user roles; includes network segmentation as a method.

title: Web filtering
description: Access to external websites shall be managed to reduce exposure to malicious content.
guidance: Implementing web filtering for ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.23 involves a blend of technical, process, and documentation components. Technically, organizations should deploy a robust web filtering solution that supports features such as URL categorization, real-time threat intelligence, malware scanning, and HTTPS inspection. Integration with directory services (e.g., Active Directory) enables user-based policies and granular access control. All endpoints and network egress points must be covered, including remote and mobile users, to prevent bypass. Process-wise, a formal web access policy should be established and approved by relevant stakeholders, detailing which categories of websites are allowed, blocked, or restricted. Exception handling processes must be defined, ensuring risk assessments and documented approvals for business-justified access to otherwise restricted sites. Continuous monitoring is essential; configure the system to generate alerts for policy violations and potential malware downloads, and review logs regularly for suspicious activity. Documentation should include the policy, configuration records, deployment logs, review reports, and evidence of exception management. Common pitfalls include failing to enforce filtering on all devices (especially remote users), overlooking encrypted traffic (lack of HTTPS inspection), and not updating filtering categories in response to emerging threats or business changes. Regular reviews, user awareness, and effective incident response processes are vital for ongoing compliance and risk reduction.

compliance_steps.step: Assess and document all network points where web access is possible, including endpoints, servers, and mobile devices.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Network diagram, asset inventory, assessment report

compliance_steps.step: Select and deploy a web filtering solution (hardware, software, or cloud-based) that supports URL categorization, malware detection, and HTTPS inspection.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Vendor selection documents, deployment records, configuration screenshots

compliance_steps.step: Define and approve a web access policy specifying allowed and blocked categories (e.g., social media, gambling, adult content), incorporating business and security requirements.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Web access policy document, policy approval record

compliance_steps.step: Configure web filtering controls on all applicable systems, ensuring enforcement for all users and devices (including remote and guest access if applicable).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Configuration files, deployment logs, enforcement test results

compliance_steps.step: Establish monitoring and alerting for web filtering violations and potential malware detections, with regular review of logs and automated alerts for suspicious activity.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Alert configuration, log review reports, incident records

compliance_steps.step: Conduct periodic reviews (at least quarterly) of web filtering effectiveness and policy relevance, updating categories and rules as needed based on threat intelligence and business changes.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Review meeting minutes, updated policy documents, change logs

compliance_steps.step: Document exceptions to web filtering (e.g., business justified access to restricted sites), including risk assessments and management approval.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Exception request forms, risk assessment documents, approval records

GDPR.Description: Security of processing; requires appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure data protection, including mitigating exposure to malicious content.

NIST CSF.Description: Data is protected; includes controls for restricting unauthorized access to data, relevant to web filtering to prevent malicious content.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Protection from malicious software; mandates procedures for guarding against, detecting, and reporting malicious software, which web filtering supports.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: Logical access security; addresses technical controls to restrict internet access and protect systems from external threats.

title: Use of cryptography
description: Rules for the effective use of cryptography, including cryptographic key management, shall be defined and implemented.
guidance: Implementing effective cryptography under ISO 27001:2022 A.8.24 requires a blend of robust technical controls, well-defined processes, and thorough documentation. Technically, organizations must select strong, vetted cryptographic algorithms (such as AES-256 for data at rest and TLS 1.2+ for data in transit), using secure key lengths and avoiding obsolete protocols (e.g., SSL, MD5, SHA-1). Key management is equally vital: keys must be securely generated, stored (preferably within hardware security modules or encrypted vaults), rotated periodically, and destroyed when obsolete. Process-wise, organizations should establish clear policies governing when and how cryptography is applied, which systems require encryption, and how exceptions are handled. Regular reviews and audits help ensure controls keep pace with emerging threats, while staff training mitigates risks from human error. All activities must be documented—policies, inventories, key management logs, and audit trails are essential for demonstrating compliance and supporting investigations. Common pitfalls include using weak or deprecated algorithms, poor key management (e.g., storing keys in plaintext or sharing them via insecure channels), and failing to update cryptographic controls as threats evolve. Additionally, lacking documentation or not training staff can lead to non-compliance or accidental data exposure. By integrating strong technical solutions with disciplined processes and comprehensive documentation, organizations can ensure cryptography effectively protects their sensitive information.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and approve a formal cryptography policy outlining acceptable cryptographic algorithms, key lengths, usage scenarios, and lifecycle management requirements.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Signed and dated cryptography policy document; policy approval records

compliance_steps.step: Identify all systems, applications, and data flows where cryptography is required (e.g., data at rest, data in transit) and document these in an inventory.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Up-to-date cryptographic asset inventory; network/data flow diagrams highlighting cryptographic usage

compliance_steps.step: Implement cryptographic controls using industry-standard algorithms (e.g., AES, RSA, SHA-256), ensuring deprecated protocols are not used.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: System configuration files; code review records; deployment scripts showing cryptographic settings

compliance_steps.step: Establish and enforce key management procedures, including key generation, distribution, storage, rotation, archival, and destruction.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Key management procedure documents; key lifecycle logs; audit trails of key activities

compliance_steps.step: Conduct regular reviews and audits to ensure ongoing compliance with cryptography policies and update controls in response to new threats or technology changes.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Audit reports; review meeting minutes; action plans from findings

compliance_steps.step: Train relevant personnel on cryptographic policies, procedures, and secure key handling practices.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Training attendance records; training materials; employee acknowledgement forms

compliance_steps.step: Document exceptions to cryptographic policy and obtain formal risk acceptance for any deviations.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Exception logs; risk acceptance forms; risk assessment documentation

NIST CSF.Description: Protect Data-at-Rest and Data-in-Transit using cryptography; Key management is part of protecting data integrity and confidentiality.

GDPR Articles.Description: Requires pseudonymization and encryption of personal data; Ensures ongoing confidentiality, integrity, and resilience of systems.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Encryption and decryption of electronic protected health information; Transmission security using encryption.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: Logical and physical access controls include cryptographic protections; Key management and encryption are required for confidential information.

title: Secure development life cycle
description: Rules for the secure development of software and systems shall be established and applied.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.25, organizations must embed security practices throughout the entire software and systems development life cycle (SDLC). Technically, this requires integrating secure coding standards, automated vulnerability scanning, and regular code reviews into CI/CD pipelines. Process-wise, security requirements should be captured during the requirements and design phases, followed by threat modeling, and validated through security testing (static, dynamic, and penetration tests) before deployment. Third-party components must be inventoried and assessed for vulnerabilities and licensing risks. Access to development, testing, and production environments should be tightly controlled and monitored, enforcing segregation of duties. Documentation is crucial: maintain up-to-date SDLC policies and procedures, code review and test records, component inventories, and training logs. Regular secure development training should be provided to all relevant staff to keep them abreast of current threats and secure practices. Common pitfalls include treating security as an afterthought, inadequate documentation, inconsistent application of controls across projects, and failing to keep up with emerging threats or new technologies. To avoid these, ensure policies and procedures are periodically reviewed and updated, and verify consistent execution through internal audits or metrics. Automated tools should supplement, not replace, manual review and testing. Ongoing stakeholder engagement and early security involvement in projects are critical for long-term compliance and risk mitigation.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and formally approve a Secure Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) policy that outlines security requirements for each development phase.
evidenceRequirements: Change management records for policy approval

compliance_steps.step: Integrate security requirements and threat modeling into requirements gathering and design phases for all new software and system development projects.
Conduct secure code reviews and utilize automated code analysis tools prior to code promotion to production.
Perform security testing (e.g., static/dynamic analysis, penetration testing) during the testing phase and before release.
evidenceRequirements: Test results with documented remediation actions

compliance_steps.step: Ensure all third-party code, libraries, and components are vetted for vulnerabilities and license compliance before integration.
Restrict and monitor access to development, testing, and production environments based on least privilege.
Provide regular secure development training for all personnel involved in software and system development.

NIST CSF.description: PR.IP-3 (Lifecycle processes are managed), PR.DS-7 (Development and testing environments are separate from production)

GDPR Articles.description: Art. 25 (Data protection by design and by default), Art. 32 (Security of processing, including measures for ensuring ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience)

HIPAA Security Rule.description: Security Management Process (Risk Analysis), Evaluation of security measures, including in development

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.description: CC8.1 (Logical and Physical Access Controls over system development), CC8.2 (System changes are authorized, designed, developed, and implemented)

title: Application security requirements
description: Information security requirements shall be identified, specified and approved when developing or acquiring applications.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.26 effectively, organizations must integrate security requirements into every stage of their application lifecycle—whether applications are developed in-house or acquired from vendors. Begin by establishing a formal, repeatable process for gathering security requirements, aligning with organizational security policies, applicable regulations (GDPR, HIPAA, etc.), and industry standards like OWASP. Technical requirements should cover authentication, authorization, secure data handling (encryption, validation, storage), logging, error handling, and vulnerability management. For process requirements, ensure each application project includes a risk assessment to inform tailored security controls, and that requirements are documented, reviewed, and approved by stakeholders such as security, privacy, and business representatives. Embed approved requirements into SDLC artifacts (e.g., business requirements, design documents, procurement specs) and verify vendor-supplied applications also meet these standards. Documentation needs include the security requirements process, project-specific requirements, approvals, and evidence of periodic reviews. Common pitfalls include using generic, non-specific requirements; neglecting third-party and SaaS applications; failing to update requirements as threats or regulations evolve; and missing stakeholder sign-off. Regular training and communication with all relevant teams reinforce compliance and help avoid these issues, ensuring security is built-in, not bolted on.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document a security requirements gathering process for all new application development or acquisition projects.
compliance_steps.evidence: Documented security requirements process/procedure, meeting records
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Application Development Manager, Information Security Officer

compliance_steps.step: Conduct a formal risk assessment for each application project to identify relevant information security threats, vulnerabilities, and regulatory requirements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Completed risk assessment reports, risk registers specific to applications

compliance_steps.step: Develop and maintain a checklist or template covering minimum application security requirements based on organizational policies and relevant frameworks (e.g., OWASP ASVS).
compliance_steps.evidence: Approved security requirements checklist/template, version history

compliance_steps.step: Review and tailor application security requirements for each project and obtain documented approval from stakeholders (e.g., business owner, IT security, data privacy officer).
compliance_steps.evidence: Signed approval records or emails, project documentation with finalized requirements

compliance_steps.step: Integrate approved security requirements into system development lifecycle (SDLC) documentation and procurement processes.
compliance_steps.evidence: SDLC documentation, RFP/RFI documents with embedded security requirements

compliance_steps.step: Periodically review and update application security requirements to reflect changes in threats, business context, and regulatory landscape.
compliance_steps.evidence: Review meeting minutes, updated requirements documents, change logs

compliance_steps.step: Conduct training for development, procurement, and project management teams on identifying and specifying application security requirements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training attendance records, training materials

GDPR.description: Data protection by design and by default—embedding privacy and security requirements into applications from the outset.

NIST CSF.description: Security requirements for applications are identified and integrated into organizational processes; data-in-transit and at-rest are protected based on risk assessment.

HIPAA Security Rule.description: Risk analysis and integrity controls—identification of security requirements to protect ePHI in application design and acquisition.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.description: System processing integrity and confidentiality addressed through identification and documentation of security requirements during system design and acquisition.

title: Secure system architecture and engineering principles
description: Principles for engineering secure systems shall be established, documented, maintained and applied to any information system development activities.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.27, organizations must establish, document, and maintain a clear set of secure system architecture and engineering principles. Technically, this involves defining and codifying principles such as defense in depth, least privilege, secure defaults, fail-safe defaults, and minimizing attack surface. These principles should be embedded into the organization's SDLC, ensuring that every phase—from requirements gathering through deployment—considers security. Process-wise, conduct mandatory security architecture reviews for all new or significantly changed systems, and enforce the use of secure coding and design standards. All stakeholders, particularly developers, architects, and project managers, should receive regular training on these principles. Documentation requirements include up-to-date secure architecture principles, traceability matrices mapping principles to system designs, and records of all architecture reviews and training sessions. Periodic review (at least annually) is critical to align with emerging threats and technology changes. Common pitfalls include lack of integration with the SDLC, outdated principles, insufficient training, and poor documentation. To avoid these, ensure ongoing engagement with stakeholders, maintain a living document for security principles, and use auditing procedures to verify adherence. Failing to enforce security reviews or neglecting updates to principles can leave systems vulnerable and non-compliant.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and document secure system architecture and engineering principles tailored to the organization's risk profile and business context.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Documented secure design and engineering principles; approval records
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Manager, Lead Solution Architect

compliance_steps.step: Integrate secure architecture principles into system development lifecycle (SDLC) policies and procedures, ensuring all new and updated systems are covered.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Updated SDLC documentation; change management records
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: SDLC Process Owner, IT Governance Lead

compliance_steps.step: Conduct mandatory training for all developers, architects, and engineers on the documented secure system design and engineering principles at least annually.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Training attendance records; training materials
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: HR Training Coordinator, Application Security Lead

compliance_steps.step: Perform security architecture reviews for all new systems and significant system changes, ensuring compliance with established principles before approval.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Security architecture review reports; approval logs

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and update secure architecture and engineering principles to reflect changes in threats, technology, and regulatory requirements (at least annually).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Review meeting minutes; updated principle documents

compliance_steps.step: Maintain traceability between secure architecture principles and actual system designs through design documentation and security requirements traceability matrices.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Traceability matrices; system design documents

compliance_steps.step: Implement technical controls (e.g., secure coding standards, network segmentation, least privilege access) as per the documented principles and verify through code reviews and technical assessments.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Code review logs; technical assessment reports

NIST CSF.description: Design and implement secure development lifecycle processes; ensure security principles are incorporated into system architecture and engineering practices.

GDPR Articles.ID: Art. 25 (Data protection by design and by default)
GDPR Articles.description: Requires data protection to be integrated into system design and engineering, applying appropriate technical and organizational measures.

HIPAA Security Rule.description: Requires risk-based implementation of security measures and technical safeguards during system design and engineering.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.description: Logical and physical access controls; security design and implementation of systems and infrastructure.

title: Secure coding
description: Secure coding principles shall be applied to software development.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.28 (Secure Coding), organizations must embed security throughout their software development lifecycle (SDLC). Technically, this involves adopting recognized secure coding standards (e.g., OWASP, CERT) and ensuring all code is routinely scanned using automated tools like SAST (Static Application Security Testing) and DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing). Code reviews should be mandatory for all high-risk modules, with security specialists participating in reviews of critical components. From a process perspective, integrate secure coding requirements into SDLC documentation, define clear acceptance criteria for security, and ensure regular secure coding training for all developers. Document each stage: guidelines, review outcomes, vulnerability management processes, and evidence of patching or updating dependencies. Maintain logs of code review activities and resolution of vulnerabilities to provide an audit trail. Common pitfalls to avoid include treating secure coding as a one-time activity, failing to keep guidelines or training current, neglecting third-party libraries, and lacking evidence of ongoing activities. Effective implementation requires not only technical controls but also a culture of security awareness and continuous improvement, with clear responsibilities and accountability at each stage of development.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document secure coding guidelines aligned with industry standards (e.g., OWASP Top Ten, SEI CERT).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Published secure coding policy; version-controlled guidelines document; acknowledgment of policy by developers.

compliance_steps.step: Integrate secure coding training into the developer onboarding process and conduct annual refresher sessions.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Training attendance logs; training materials; completion certificates.

compliance_steps.step: Embed security requirements into the software development lifecycle (SDLC), including code review checklists and acceptance criteria.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: SDLC documentation; project artifacts showing security checkpoints; code review records.

compliance_steps.step: Implement automated tools (e.g., SAST/DAST) to scan for vulnerabilities in source code during development and prior to deployment.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Tool configuration screenshots; scan reports; remediation tracking logs.

compliance_steps.step: Require peer or security expert code reviews for all critical application components before release.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Peer review logs; pull request comments; approval workflow records.

compliance_steps.step: Maintain and document a process for remediating identified code vulnerabilities, including timelines and escalation paths.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Vulnerability management policy; issue tracking system screenshots; closure reports.

compliance_steps.step: Regularly update development environments and libraries to address new security threats and vulnerabilities.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Patch logs; dependency update records; change management tickets.

GDPR.Description: Data protection by design and by default – secure coding is part of technical and organizational measures to ensure data protection.

NIST CSF.Description: Development and testing environments are separate from the production environment and secure coding practices are implemented to prevent vulnerabilities.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Security management process including risk analysis and safeguards to protect ePHI, which can be addressed by secure coding.

SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria.Description: Application security controls are in place, including secure coding, to prevent, detect, and correct processing errors and unauthorized changes.

title: Security testing in development and acceptance
description: Security testing processes shall be defined and implemented in the development life cycle.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.29 requires organizations to embed security testing throughout the software development and acceptance lifecycle. Technically, this means integrating automated tools (such as static and dynamic application security testing, code reviews, and vulnerability scanning) at various SDLC stages—development, testing, and pre-production. Processes should mandate security testing as a non-negotiable checkpoint before software moves to acceptance and production. Clearly define roles and responsibilities for security testing, remediation, and verification, and establish escalation procedures for critical vulnerabilities. Documentation should include security testing policies, detailed test plans, execution records, remediation logs, and evidence of approvals prior to deployment. Common pitfalls include treating security testing as a one-time event (rather than iterative), failing to follow up on identified vulnerabilities, or neglecting documentation. Avoid reliance on manual testing alone—automated tools should complement human expertise. Regularly review and update security testing procedures in response to new threats and technology changes. Ensure all relevant staff are trained in secure coding and security testing practices. By institutionalizing security testing and maintaining robust records, organizations can demonstrate due diligence and compliance with ISO 27001 and align with best practices from other security frameworks.

compliance_steps.step: Define security testing requirements and standards for all software development projects.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Head of Application Development, Information Security Manager
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Documented security testing policy and standards approved by management.

compliance_steps.step: Integrate security testing activities (e.g., static code analysis, dynamic testing, vulnerability scanning) into the Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: SDLC process documentation, project plans showing security testing phases.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct security testing at defined stages: pre-release (development), acceptance (pre-production), and post-release (production monitoring).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Security test reports, logs of completed tests, evidence of test execution at each stage.

compliance_steps.step: Remediate identified vulnerabilities and verify fixes through re-testing before acceptance or production deployment.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Vulnerability management logs, re-test results, sign-off records for deployment.

compliance_steps.step: Maintain records of all security testing activities including methodologies, outcomes, and corrective actions taken.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Central repository with test plans, results, remediation actions, and approvals.

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and update security testing processes to reflect changes in technology, threat landscape, and business requirements.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Review meeting minutes, updated process documents, change logs.

compliance_steps.step: Train relevant staff (developers, QA, project managers) on secure development practices and security testing techniques.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirement: Training records, attendance sheets, training materials.

NIST CSF.Description: Data is tested to verify security functionality during development and acceptance.

GDPR Articles.Description: Implement processes to test, assess, and evaluate the effectiveness of technical and organizational measures for ensuring security.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Evaluation - Perform periodic technical and non-technical evaluations for security measures.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: System components are tested for security vulnerabilities prior to release; Change management and testing of system changes.

title: Information access restriction
description: Access to information and other associated assets shall be restricted in accordance with the established topic-specific policy on access control.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.3 (Information access restriction), organizations must establish both robust technical and process controls to ensure that information and associated assets are accessible only to authorized individuals. Begin by classifying your information assets and mapping them to access requirements in a formal access control policy. This policy should detail roles, responsibilities, and criteria for access, referencing principles such as least privilege and need-to-know. Technically, deploy centralized access management solutions (such as IAM platforms, directory services, or RBAC systems) to control and enforce access restrictions. All access rights should be provisioned and de-provisioned through a documented workflow, with appropriate approvals and records. Regularly (at least quarterly) perform access reviews and promptly address any discrepancies, such as unnecessary or orphaned accounts. Maintain comprehensive logging and monitoring of access events, leveraging SIEM tools for alerting on unauthorized or anomalous access attempts. All staff must be trained on access control policies and their responsibilities, with evidence of completion recorded. Documentation is critical at each stage: retain policy documents, workflow records, review reports, training logs, and evidence of exception approvals. Common pitfalls include failing to maintain up-to-date access rights after role changes, inadequate documentation of access decisions, or neglecting to regularly review and monitor access logs. Avoid these by automating key processes where possible and embedding access control requirements into onboarding, offboarding, and asset lifecycle processes.

compliance_steps.step: Develop and document an access control policy that defines roles, responsibilities, and access levels based on classification of information and assets.

Implement technical controls to enforce role-based or attribute-based access restrictions (e.g., using Active Directory, IAM tools), ensuring only authorized users can access specific information and assets.

Conduct initial and periodic access reviews (at least quarterly) to validate that access rights correspond to job responsibilities and classification requirements; promptly remove any unnecessary or inappropriate access.
Establish and enforce a formal user provisioning and de-provisioning process, ensuring all access requests are approved, documented, and logged.
Monitor and log all access to sensitive information and associated assets; regularly review logs for unauthorized access attempts and respond to incidents as per incident management procedures.
Communicate access control policies and procedures to all staff through mandatory training sessions and maintain training completion records.
Document exceptions to access control policies (if any), obtain formal approval, and ensure compensating controls are in place.

NIST CSF.ID.AM-3: Assets are formally managed throughout removal, transfers, and disposition.
NIST CSF.PR.AC-4: Access permissions and authorizations are managed, incorporating the principles of least privilege and separation of duties.

GDPR Articles.Article 5(1)(f): Processing must ensure appropriate security of personal data, including protection against unauthorized access.
GDPR Articles.Article 32(1)(b): Implement measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, including access restriction to personal data.

HIPAA Security Rule.45 CFR §164.308(a)(4): Information Access Management — Implement policies and procedures for authorizing access to ePHI.
HIPAA Security Rule.45 CFR §164.312(a)(1): Access Control — Implement technical policies and procedures for electronic information systems that maintain ePHI to allow access only to those persons or software programs that have been granted access rights.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC6.1: Logical access security software, infrastructure, and architectures are implemented and maintained to support restriction of access to authorized users.
SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.CC6.2: System operations, including user access, are formally authorized, documented, and reviewed.

title: Outsourced development
description: The organization shall direct, monitor and review the activities related to outsourced system development.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.30 requires organizations to establish robust governance over outsourced system development. Technically, all outsourced development activities should be subject to the same security controls as in-house projects, including secure coding practices, vulnerability scanning, and access management. Contracts must specify security requirements, data handling, incident response, and audit rights to ensure vendors adhere to your standards. Process-wise, organizations should perform risk assessments before onboarding vendors, maintain a current inventory of all outsourced projects, and conduct regular monitoring—such as code reviews and periodic security assessments. Documentation is critical: retain contracts, risk assessment reports, code review logs, training records, and audit findings as evidence of compliance. Common pitfalls include failing to specify security requirements in contracts, lack of ongoing monitoring, inadequate vendor due diligence, and insufficient documentation. To avoid these, ensure that outsourced partners receive security training, that SLAs are enforced, and that you have mechanisms to track and remediate non-compliance. Regular reviews and audits of outsourced development partners will help maintain alignment with your organization’s security policies and regulatory obligations.

compliance_steps.step: Establish and formally document outsourcing development requirements, including security, privacy, and compliance obligations.
compliance_steps.evidence: Signed outsourcing contracts, documented requirements, RFP documents

compliance_steps.step: Conduct due diligence and risk assessment on potential outsourced development partners prior to engagement.
compliance_steps.evidence: Vendor risk assessment reports, due diligence checklists, approval records

compliance_steps.step: Include explicit security clauses and Service Level Agreements (SLAs) in all outsourced development contracts, covering data protection, access controls, incident response, and audit rights.
compliance_steps.evidence: Signed contracts with security clauses, SLAs, contract review records
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Legal Counsel, Procurement Lead, Information Security Manager

compliance_steps.step: Review and monitor outsourced development activities regularly, including periodic security assessments and code reviews.
compliance_steps.evidence: Code review logs, vulnerability scan reports, monitoring logs, meeting minutes

compliance_steps.step: Ensure outsourced developers undergo appropriate security awareness training and are familiar with organizational security policies.
compliance_steps.evidence: Training completion records, signed policy acknowledgements

compliance_steps.step: Maintain an up-to-date inventory of all outsourced development engagements and associated systems.
compliance_steps.evidence: Inventory lists, vendor engagement logs
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: IT Asset Manager, Vendor Management Lead

compliance_steps.step: Perform regular reviews and audits of outsourced development partners to verify compliance with contractual and security requirements.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit reports, remediation tracking documents
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Internal Audit Lead, Vendor Management Lead

GDPR.Description: Processor obligations and security of processing; contractual requirements for data processors.

HIPAA.Description: Business associate contracts and arrangements; evaluation of external partners.

SOC_2.Description: Risk assessments for vendor relationships; communication and monitoring of third-party service providers.

NIST_CSF.Description: Data-in-transit and data-at-rest protection; Configuration change control in vendor-managed systems.

title: Separation of development, test and production environments
description: Development, testing and production environments shall be separated and secured.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 A.8.31 requires both technical and process-driven measures to ensure that development, testing, and production environments are securely separated. Technically, this involves setting up distinct network segments (VLANs, subnets) and access control groups, ensuring that only authorized personnel can access each environment. Firewalls and routing rules should strictly enforce this separation, preventing unauthorized cross-environment communication. Data used in development or test should never be copied from production unless it is sanitized or anonymized to protect sensitive information. Process requirements include establishing clear policies that define environment purposes, access rights, and responsibilities. Change management procedures must be in place to prevent unauthorized deployment of code or data between environments, with all changes requiring documented approval and logging. Documentation is critical: policies, environment inventories, access rights assignments, and audit logs must be maintained and reviewed regularly. Training all relevant staff on these requirements helps prevent accidental or intentional breaches of separation. Common pitfalls include shared credentials between environments, lack of network segmentation, insufficient monitoring of access, and failure to update documentation after changes. Regularly test and audit controls to ensure ongoing compliance, and always review third-party practices if external vendors are involved in any environment.

compliance_steps.step: Establish physically and logically separate environments for development, testing, and production systems.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Network diagrams, environment inventory lists, access control configurations

compliance_steps.step: Implement access controls to restrict permissions to only authorized personnel for each environment (e.g., developers access development, testers access test, operations staff access production).
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Role-based access control (RBAC) documentation, access logs, user access reviews

compliance_steps.step: Prohibit data transfer from production to development/test environments unless data is appropriately sanitized or anonymized.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Data sanitization procedures, data masking logs, approval records for data transfers

compliance_steps.step: Establish and document change management processes to prevent unauthorized movement of code or resources between environments.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Change management policy, change request records, deployment logs

compliance_steps.step: Configure network segmentation and firewall rules to ensure environments are isolated and cannot communicate directly without explicit authorization.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Firewall configuration files, network segmentation diagrams, test results of segmentation controls

compliance_steps.step: Conduct periodic audits and reviews to verify separation and security measures are maintained and effective.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Audit reports, review checklists, remediation action plans

compliance_steps.step: Document all environment separation policies and procedures and provide training to relevant staff.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequirements: Policy documents, training attendance logs, training materials

NIST CSF.Description: PR.DS-5 (Sensitive data is protected in development and testing environments); PR.IP-3 (Configuration change control processes are maintained and tested).

GDPR Articles.Description: Article 25 (Data Protection by Design and by Default), Article 32 (Security of processing, including appropriate technical and organizational measures).

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Risk management and access controls to ensure separation and protection of ePHI in various environments.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: CC6.1 (Logical access controls to restrict access to systems and data); CC7.2 (User and system activity monitoring in production environments).

title: Change management
description: Changes to information processing facilities and information systems shall be subject to change management procedures.
guidance:
Effective implementation of ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.32 requires a comprehensive, documented change management process governing all modifications to information processing facilities and information systems. Technically, organizations should deploy a centralized change management tool or ticketing system to capture change requests, approvals, test results, implementation details, and post-implementation reviews. All changes—whether hardware, software, or configuration—must be formally requested and logged, with unique identifiers for traceability. Process-wise, a Change Advisory Board (CAB) or equivalent should evaluate risks, potential impacts, and required mitigations for each proposed change. Risk assessments and rollback plans must be documented for every significant change. Testing must occur in a separate staging environment, with evidence of successful results and stakeholder acceptance prior to production deployment. Communication with affected parties before and after changes is essential to minimize disruption and ensure awareness.

Documentation is key: maintain a change management policy, detailed procedures, change logs, risk assessments, test results, approvals, and review reports for audit readiness. Avoid common pitfalls such as bypassing formal approvals for 'urgent' changes, insufficient testing, inadequate rollback planning, or failing to retain evidence. Regularly review the change management process for effectiveness and continuous improvement. By ensuring robust controls, clear roles, and comprehensive records, organizations can meet compliance obligations, minimize operational risk, and preserve the security and integrity of their information systems.

compliance_steps.step: Establish a documented change management policy and procedure that defines the scope, roles, responsibilities, approval workflow, and types of changes (e.g., emergency, standard, major).

Implement a change request and approval system (manual or automated) to formally log, track, and approve all changes to information processing facilities and information systems before implementation.
Assess and document potential security, business, and compliance impacts for each change request, including risk assessment and rollback plans.
Test changes in a controlled, non-production environment to validate functionality and security before deployment; document test results.
Communicate approved changes to all relevant stakeholders, including users, support teams, and management, prior to implementation.
Monitor and review implemented changes to ensure expected outcomes and absence of unintended effects; document post-implementation reviews.
Maintain an auditable log of all change management activities, including requests, approvals, testing, implementation, and reviews, for a defined retention period.

NIST CSF.ID.AM-3: Organizational communication and data flows are managed (includes change management implications).
NIST CSF.PR.IP-3: Configuration change control processes are in place.
NIST CSF.PR.IP-11: Cybersecurity is included in human resources practices (including change management roles).

GDPR Articles.Article 25: Data protection by design and by default – change management is part of system design and modifications.
GDPR Articles.Article 32: Security of processing – requires measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience, including change management.

HIPAA Security Rule.164.308(a)(8): Evaluation – periodic technical and non-technical evaluation of security measures, including after system changes.

title: Test information
description: Test information shall be appropriately selected, protected and managed.
guidance: Implementing ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.33 requires organizations to rigorously manage test information used in application development, QA, and other non-production activities. Technically, this means ensuring test data is anonymized or masked, particularly if it originates from production datasets containing sensitive or personal information. Access to test environments and test data should be strictly limited using role-based access controls, and all activities involving test information must be logged and monitored. Process-wise, organizations are expected to establish documented procedures for the selection, protection, and eventual disposal of test data, ensuring that only necessary information is used and that it is protected throughout its lifecycle. Documentation should include inventories of test data, records of data masking/anonymization steps, access control policies, and logs of reviews and changes. Common pitfalls include using live production data in test environments without masking, insufficient access controls, lack of formal test data management procedures, and failure to regularly review test data for compliance with privacy requirements. To avoid these, organizations should automate test data masking, conduct periodic audits of test environments, and ensure training for all staff involved in testing. Effective implementation not only protects sensitive data but also supports regulatory compliance and reduces the risk of data breaches originating from non-production environments.

compliance_steps.step: Identify and classify all test information and data used in development, QA, and staging environments.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Test data inventory, data classification records

compliance_steps.step: Implement data masking or anonymization procedures for test information that contains sensitive or production data.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Documentation of masking/anonymization processes, sample masked data sets

compliance_steps.step: Restrict access to test information to authorized personnel only, using role-based access controls.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Access control lists, user access audit logs

compliance_steps.step: Regularly review and update test data sets to ensure they do not contain live production data or personally identifiable information (PII) unless strictly necessary and properly protected.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Review logs, test data update records, PII risk assessments

compliance_steps.step: Maintain documented procedures for the selection, protection, and management of test information, including disposal after use.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Test data management procedure documents

compliance_steps.step: Monitor and log all access and modifications to test information to detect unauthorized activities.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Security event logs, monitoring reports

compliance_steps.step: Train staff involved in testing and development on secure handling and protection of test information.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Training attendance records, training materials

GDPR.Description: Security of processing and data protection by design and by default, including pseudonymization and minimization of personal data in test environments.

NIST CSF.Description: Data is destroyed according to policy (test data must be properly managed and disposed of).

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Workforce security and technical safeguards for access control and data protection, relevant for test data containing ePHI.

SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria.Description: Logical access security and protection of confidential information, including test data.

title: Protection of information systems during audit testing
description: Audit tests and other assurance activities involving assessment of operational systems shall be planned and agreed between the tester and appropriate management.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.34, organizations must establish a disciplined approach to planning and conducting audit tests on operational information systems. Technically, this requires setting up isolated test environments or scheduling audits during periods of low system activity to minimize operational risk. All audit activities should be clearly scoped, with objectives and boundaries documented and communicated to both testers and system owners. Process-wise, a pre-audit risk assessment is essential to identify potential business or operational impacts, and formal approvals must be secured from relevant management before testing begins. Comprehensive procedures should be in place for monitoring systems during audit tests, including clear methods for reverting changes or restoring services in the event of disruption. Documentation is critical—maintain detailed records of audit plans, risk assessments, approval forms, test schedules, activity logs, and post-audit reviews. Common pitfalls to avoid include lack of communication between auditors and system owners, performing tests on live systems without contingency plans, and failing to track changes or impacts. Ensure that all stakeholders are aware of the audit scope and potential risks, and conduct thorough post-audit reviews to capture lessons learned and further strengthen controls. By following these steps, organizations can maintain the integrity and availability of operational systems while achieving robust assurance through audit activities.

compliance_steps.step: Define and document the scope and objectives of audit testing for each information system.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit testing scope document, approved audit plan
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Internal Audit Manager or Information Security Manager

compliance_steps.step: Conduct a risk assessment to identify potential impacts on operational systems before audit activities begin.
compliance_steps.evidence: Risk assessment report, risk mitigation actions

compliance_steps.step: Obtain formal approval from system owners and relevant management prior to commencing audit testing.
compliance_steps.evidence: Signed approval forms, email correspondences

compliance_steps.step: Establish and communicate procedures for monitoring, controlling, and restoring systems in case of audit-induced disruptions.
compliance_steps.evidence: System monitoring logs, incident response procedures, communication records

compliance_steps.step: Ensure audit tests are performed in a controlled environment (e.g., test environment or during low-usage periods) whenever feasible.
compliance_steps.evidence: Testing schedules, environment access logs

compliance_steps.step: Log and review all audit activities performed on operational systems, including access and changes made.
compliance_steps.evidence: Audit activity logs, change management records

compliance_steps.step: Conduct post-audit reviews with relevant stakeholders to identify any system impacts and lessons learned.
compliance_steps.evidence: Post-audit review meeting minutes, impact analysis reports

GDPR.description: Processes for regularly testing, assessing, and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organizational measures for ensuring data security.

SOC 2.description: System operations are monitored, and change management processes ensure operational systems are protected during testing and audit activities.

NIST CSF.description: Testing of security controls is planned and conducted periodically to ensure continued effectiveness; audit activities are coordinated to minimize risk to operational systems.

HIPAA Security Rule.description: Perform periodic technical and nontechnical evaluations, including audit activities, ensuring minimal impact to operational systems.

title: Access to source code
description: Read and write access to source code, development tools and software libraries shall be appropriately managed.
guidance: To effectively implement ISO 27001:2022 A.8.4, organizations must take a multi-layered approach to managing access to source code, development tools, and libraries. Technically, this requires deploying role-based access controls (RBAC) within version control systems (e.g., Git, SVN) and development platforms, ensuring only authorized users can read or modify code. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) should be enforced to prevent unauthorized access, and all access should be logged for auditing purposes. From a process perspective, a formal access request and approval workflow must be established. This workflow should require justification for access, managerial approval, and periodic review of user privileges. Quarterly access reviews are recommended to promptly revoke access for departing staff or those whose roles have changed. Documentation is critical: maintain inventories of repositories, access control lists, change management records, and training materials on secure source code handling. Training developers and relevant staff helps reinforce the importance of these controls and proper procedures. Common pitfalls to avoid include failing to review access regularly, relying on default permissions, neglecting to log access events, and not updating inventories as new repositories or tools are introduced. By addressing both technical and administrative requirements, organizations can significantly reduce risks related to unauthorized source code access and manipulation, supporting both security objectives and regulatory compliance.

compliance_steps.step: Maintain an up-to-date inventory of all source code repositories, development tools, and software libraries.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Repository inventory list; tool/library asset register

compliance_steps.step: Implement role-based access controls (RBAC) for all source code repositories, ensuring only authorized personnel have read/write permissions.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Access control policy; access permission logs; RBAC configuration screenshots

compliance_steps.step: Enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users accessing source code repositories and development platforms.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: MFA enforcement documentation; authentication logs

compliance_steps.step: Review and approve access requests to source code and development tools through a formal change management or access request process.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Access request forms; approval workflow records; change management logs

compliance_steps.step: Conduct quarterly access reviews to validate that only current, authorized users retain access to source code and development assets.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Access review reports; user access reconciliation logs

compliance_steps.step: Log and monitor all access and modification activities on source code repositories for suspicious or unauthorized actions.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Audit logs; monitoring reports; incident response logs

compliance_steps.step: Document and train development staff on secure source code access procedures and protocols.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Training records; documented procedures; attendance logs

NIST CSF.Description: Controls governing access permissions, authentication mechanisms, and protective controls for code repositories and development environments.

GDPR Articles.Description: Requires measures ensuring confidentiality and integrity, including access controls for personal data within source code and development assets.

HIPAA Security Rule.Description: Technical safeguards for access management and audit logging, relevant if source code contains ePHI or supports regulated applications.

SOC 2 Trust Service Criteria.Description: Logical access controls, change management, and monitoring for source code and software assets.

title: Secure authentication
description: Secure authentication technologies and procedures shall be implemented based on information access restrictions.
guidance: To implement ISO 27001:2022 control A.8.5 'Secure authentication' effectively, organizations must establish a layered authentication framework that aligns with their risk environment and information access restrictions. Technically, this means deploying multi-factor authentication (MFA) for high-risk access points, enforcing robust password policies (minimum 12 characters, complexity, rotation, and reuse prevention), and using secure authentication protocols (e.g., SAML, OAuth2, OpenID Connect). From a process standpoint, organizations should maintain formal procedures for account provisioning, periodic access reviews, and immediate de-provisioning upon role changes or terminations. All authentication events should be logged and monitored for anomalies, such as repeated failed attempts or access from unusual locations, with integration into the incident response process. Documentation is critical: maintain an Authentication Control Standard detailing technologies, procedures, and exceptions, and review this document annually. Common pitfalls to avoid include relying solely on passwords, neglecting legacy systems that cannot support MFA, failing to monitor authentication logs proactively, and omitting regular review of access rights. Organizations must also ensure user training on secure authentication practices and immediate reporting of suspicious login activity. Continuous improvement should be driven by regular vulnerability assessments and simulated attack exercises. By combining robust technology, disciplined processes, and thorough documentation, organizations can achieve compliance and enhance their security posture.

compliance_steps.step: Conduct an authentication risk assessment to identify systems and data requiring secure authentication based on access restrictions.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Completed risk assessment report; asset inventory with authentication requirements documented.

compliance_steps.step: Implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all remote access, privileged accounts, and critical systems.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: MFA configuration reports; screenshots from identity provider; list of systems enforced.

compliance_steps.step: Enforce strong password policies (length, complexity, expiration, reuse restrictions) for all users.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Password policy documentation; system configuration screenshots; sample password change logs.

compliance_steps.step: Establish procedures for provisioning, de-provisioning, and periodic review of user access and authentication settings.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Access control procedures; onboarding/offboarding records; periodic access review reports.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: HR / IT Operations / Access Management Team

compliance_steps.step: Monitor authentication logs for unusual activity (e.g., failed logins, location anomalies) and integrate with security incident response.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Log review summaries; SIEM correlation rules; incident response records.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Security Operations Center (SOC) / IT Security Analyst

compliance_steps.step: Regularly test authentication controls through vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, and simulated phishing.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Test reports; remediation tracking logs; phishing campaign results.
compliance_steps.responsibleParty: Information Security Manager / External Security Assessors

compliance_steps.step: Document all authentication technologies, procedures, and exceptions in an Authentication Control Standard and review annually.
compliance_steps.evidenceRequired: Authentication control standard; annual review log; change management records.

GDPR.Article 25: Data protection by design and by default—implement access controls including authentication.
GDPR.Article 32(1)(b): Measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability, and resilience of processing systems—includes secure authentication.

NIST CSF.PR.AC-1: Identities and credentials are issued, managed, verified, revoked, and audited for authorized devices, users, and processes.
NIST CSF.PR.AC-7: Users, devices, and other assets are authenticated commensurate with the risk of the transaction.

HIPAA Security Rule.§164.308(a)(5)(ii)(D): Log-in monitoring—procedures for monitoring log-in attempts and reporting discrepancies.
